div.head: BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
div.p: BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY.
Before Mr. R. T. Fairclough (in the chair), Alderman Tinnion, and Messrs. A. J. Jolley

and J. Upson. " PITCHING THE TALE."—John Byrne, a young Irishman, was brought tip on remand for beg- ging in Museum-street 'When before the Court the week before he denied that he had ever been before in,trouble, and told a long story to show that he led an exemplary life.—The Chief Con- stage now said that Byrne had a bad record, as a finger print investigation showed. His record started in Dublin, and he had been in trouble elsewhere since 1906, and all he had said at the previous hearing was false. He went to the Orford Barracks and offered to enlist. Byrne was detained in the inspection room, but escaped by climbing over a wall, and soon after was arrested for begging. He was sentenced to a month in prison, with hard labour.—Byrne: .It is not fair.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.

Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Smethurst, Bolton and James Evans, Coun- cillor Wilkinson, and Mr. G. Pilling. • AFTER THE MATCH.—JaMeS M. Kendrick, a St. Helens supporter, got drunk on Saturday and was locked up for being drunk and disorderly.— It was stated that he said he would fight any- one in Warrington.—Prisoner said he had no recollection of the affair.—The Chief Constable: He wanted to fight in the 'cells because War- rington had beaten his town's team.—Prisoner : I have lived in Warrington as well. Both teams , are mine, but I like to support the one from the town I. am living in.—The case was , dis- missed on payment of costs. A POCKET-STREET Row.—There was a row in Pocket-street on Saturday night, and a sequel • was heard on Monday at the Court, when Joseph Steen, Pocket-street, gave evidence against Mary Ellen Moore, Pocket-street, who was charged with assaulting him.—Steen said that he was having words with his brother, when Mr. Moore (prisoner's husband) said that he would fight anyone. Witness went to the door and Moore said "Come out and see what we can do." Prisoner came along and threw things, including a bottle and a bowl, and a kettle of boiling water, at him (witness). He was dragged about and kicked on the floor. He tried to get in the house, but prisoner hit him on the head with a poker. He was taken to the Infirmary.—Mrs. Humphries and her daughter, 12, Dolan's-yard, deposed to seeing prisoner strike Seen on the head.—P.C. Cameron said that when charged prisoner said: "I did not do it. He had a bottle and I took the poker to frighten him."---Prisoner said she was going to go to confession. Steen, she alleged, kicked her in the chest and on the face.—Her sister said that she was hit on the head with the poker. She could not say whether it was done acciden- tally.—A fine of 10s. was imposed.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

Before Councillor H. Roberts (in the chair), Colonel Edelsten, Messrs. W. -Richardson and C. Jackson Holmes. Moron CAR OFFENCE.—CharIes Fitzhenery Baucher, colliery manager, Strangeways House, Hindley, near Wigan, was summoned for driv- ing a motor car in Winwick-road at a speed dangerous to the public.—Mr. Jackson (Price and Jackson, Wigan) defended.—P.C. Vost said that at 11.10 on Sunday, SeVt-ember 'l4th, the defendant drove a motor car, 1J1782, along Win- wick-road, at about 40 miles per hour. There were a number of people about at the time, and if there had been a vehicle coming out of Ker- foot-street or Longford-street, there would have been an accident. Defendant never sounded his horn, as he went past the Horse and jockey lane ends.—Mr. Jackson: How did you -calcu- late the speed?—Witness : L have never seen a car go so fast.—Acting-Sergeant Newey said he believed the car was going at about 50 miles per hour.—Mr. Jackson said defendant had driven a car for seven years, and had never committed an offence against the Motor Acts before. He would state that he was driving at a reasonable rate. It would need a vastly 'different car to go at the speed stated. The car was al6 h.p., and defendant would say he was going at about 20 miles per hour. Motorists had not such a nice time of it now, but if officers were enabled to , give what they thought was the speed from watching the car, it was going to set a bad pre- cedent.—Def end ant having given evidence, which was supported by his wife, a fine of 20s. and costs was imposed.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

Before Mr. J. W. Hayward (in the chair), Messrs. C. Jackson Holmes and W. T. Williams. Wivn ASSAULTED.—Joseph Clancy, 6, Dial- court, was charged' with assaulting his wife, Catherine Clancy, on the 30th, September.—De- tective Clough said he saw the complainant fol- lowing her husband in Buttermarket-street. They were quarrelling, and prisoner turned round and struck his wife a violent blow in the face, which felled her to the ground and ren- dered her insensible. She was taken to the In- firmary, where it was found she had a severe wound on the wrist. The woman admitted that the wound was caused by a cup, with which she was striking her husband.—Prisoner stated that he was aggravated at the time, because he came home from work and found his wife drinking with other women.—The magistrates imposed a fine of 20s. sand costs or one month, and, aa- dressing the wife, the Chairman said the mag- istrates were of the opinion that she was re- sponsible for the trouble, and they were sorry that she, was not in the same position as her hus- band.

WIFE TO PAY.—Thomas Griffin, 14, Buckley- street, was summoned by his wife, Margaret Griffin, for an assault on October 211d.—The wife said she did not wish to press the case.— The magistrates, in dismissing the case, ordered the wife to pay the costs of the summons, 6s.

div.head: MURDERED WHILE AT HIS PRAYERS.
div.p: MURDERED WHILE AT HIS PRAYERS.

An unheard of tragedy took place at Cairo. While Sheikh Tazzani, a professor at the Al Azhar University, and one of the most pictur- esque figures in Cairo, was absorbed in his mid- day prayer, a student, who is a French subject, came up to him from behind and plunged his knife three times into the neck of the old man, killing him on the spot. The miscreant was arrested, though knot before he had wounded two other students who had 'thrown themselves on him.

div.head: MUSICAL CO-OPEFATCRS.
div.p: MUSICAL CO-OPEFATCRS.
Choir Competitions at Warrington.

"Music is the greatest regenerative force in the way of recreation and pleasure." This statement was made by Dr. Henry Coward (conductor of the famous Sheffield Choir), who adjudicated at the eleventh annual co-operative choir contest, which was held in the Parr Hall on Saturday afternoon. Eleven ohoirs com- peted, and the pieces were "The nights" (Chal- linor) and "On Himalay " (Granville Bantock). Accrington and Church -Choir (150 marks), with Mr. G. Whittaker as conductor, were awarded the first prize, and they become the holders of the challenge shield for twelve months, and received a prize of £lO 10s, Brightside and Carbrook (Sheffield) were second with 148 marks, and Hull Choir were awarded third place with 148 marks. The other choirs.were : Bradford, Failsworth, Huddersfield, Radcliffe and Pilkington, Bingley, Haslingden, Halifax, and Blackley.

Dr. Coward said the winners had entered into the spirit of the pieces, although not one choir sang badly. He had been informed that the object of the Co-operative movement in pro- moting these contests was to raise the aims and aspirations of the people. Music , was the greatest regenerative force in the way of recrea- tion and pleasure. Picture palaces would not satisfy people with high aspirations for ever; they would require something which, every time' they took part in it, made them feel better, improved the spirit and enlarged the mind. ,(Applause.) In the evening a concert and male voice con- test were held, with Mr. J. Upson in the chair. The following choirs _competed St. Helens, Accrington and Church, Burnley, Haslingden and Blackley. The test pieces were "In absence" (Dudley Buck) and "A war song" (Granville Bantock).

Dr. Coward announced that Accrington and Church had, for the second time, taken first place, with 150 marks. Haslingden were second with 147 marks, and the other choirs were placed as follows: Blackley, Burnley and St. Helens. -

Mr. Upson presented the prizes and apologised for Mr. W. Gregory's absence. Commenting upon the advantages of the Co-operative move- ment, Mr. Upson said he iiished to emphasise the fact that there was very much altruism in the movement. It was said repeatedly that after all co-operators were "keen on the divi " —(laughter)—and that the sole object of the movement was the production of dividend, and that it was woe betide the committee which had not a very handsome profit for those who had been trading with the society. The pro- motion of such concerts and contests was an answer to those who said co-operators were entirely selfish in their aims. He thought the movement was becoming less and less selfish and more and more altruistic. The only one source of regret that day was that there was not a Warrington choir contesting. If there should be a similar contest in the town in the future, possibly there would be a Warrington choir taking part—at any rate, co-operators in Warrington all hoped it might be so. ,(Ap- plause.) The Accrington. and Church Choir rendered "Woodmen, shepherds, come Etway," and "A love symphony," and Blackley Choir rendered "How soft the moonlight" and "Gipsy life." The Failsworth party sang very beautifully "Queen of the night" and "Music all power- ful," while the selections "Dim-lit woods" and "When winds breathe soft" were sung by Rad- cliffe and Pilkington representatives.

div.head: BLACKPOOL TOURNAMENT.
div.p: THE BLACKPOOL TOURNAMENT.
Defeat of Mr. Charles Roberts of Padgate.

Mr. Charles Roberts, ,in the course of the fifth round on Monday, at Blackpool, met his "Waterloo." At one time Mr. Roberts looked like having a fairly easy victory, for, he was leading by 16 to 11. Mr. R. Dickinson, of Blackburn, from this point bowled splendidly, and, singular to say, won every end afterwards, the score finally reading: Dickinson, 21; Roberts, 16. Mr. Roberts, after the match, /n a sportsmanlike manner, stated that his opponent deserved his victory, for the manner in which he bowled at the finish.

div.head: AUSTRALIAN FARMERS AND THE TARIFF
div.p: AUSTRALIAN FARMERS AND THE TARIFF
Freehold Tenure of Land.

Meeting in an extraordinary session on August 15th, the West Alistralian Farmers' and Settlers"- Association, representing what is rapidly becoming a force to be reckoned with in Australian politics, namely, the "Country Party," drew up a scheme for the political section of the constitution. The scheme read :

"The following are declared to be funda- mental political principles of the association : Revision of the tariff downwards; freehold tenure in land; freedom of contract; Promotion of- agricultural settlement by the proviston transit facilities, adequate water supplies, decentralisation in expendittlre of public funds, cheap money, and a broad and vigorous policy of immigration by State and Commonwcalti." After some discussion, the first clause was altered to read: "Abolition of Protection in favour of a revenue tariff." The scheme was passed unanimously. Thus, the Austialian agriculturists are adopting the attitude of their Canadian brethren toward Hie tariff.

" Braves" or men stricken with the ". Carsonitis" whereas they are simply Members of a, friendly society limited to Catholics ,of any 'nationality, and simply carry on • the work of any other_ society, such as the Prudential, or Oddfe'llows. I.have never yet read of a case "of the present day" when the Hibernians have scalped any- one, and would ,be obliged for information upon the point from "Mon Ami," "Phil Squod." I quite,- agree.- that the Home, Rule ..-question should be settle&once and 'for but hardly accept "Phil Squod's " suggestion that it should be interred. Certainly, Ireland has been gov-,- ernal .by enbugh "Boards "ito make her coffin, but not enough to break her spirit of nation- ality. The " Imperi4.l" aspect of Home Rule is certainly the exordium and preoration of every discussion on the Irish question, and that the success of the Home Rule 13i11 depends upon its consistency with the Empire. To take an ex- ample of the "Imperial aspect," let us consider Canada. At one time Canada was in every de- tail in the same position as Ireland—twO creeds, Catholic and Protestain; two instincts, bureau- cratic and democratic; two races, English ,and French; were in continual opposition. The home authorities in London spoke in much the same spirit as do the ".Castle ".officials to-day. The language of Sir Edward •Carson was used by a more .famous, yet not less misguided, of our countrymen, the Duke'of Wellington ; Lord Stanley made a similar declaration to that of Bonar Law. Yet Canada got- Home Rule, just as will Iretand, because she was more than a nation, she was like England—like Ireland—.a race with an inherent right to, and economic necessity for, self-government. Everywhere Canada is looked 'upon as the model of loyalty and prosperity to the Empire. Let Ireland have a similar chance to that of Canada. Let her take her rightful position _amongst the nations of the world with the " Esto Perpetua " motto, she will welcome all Irishmen, according to Thomas Davis:
Irish born man, if you're to Ireland true, We heed not race nor creed nor clan, We've hearts and hands for you.

MONEY LENDING AND OTHER THINGS. *Sir,—lt is, with great pleasure that I read your correspondents letter, published .in last ,week's issue, on the above subject,.and I do not wonder at his earnest denunciation of the evil habits of the residents of this town. In my daily employment I go into every, part of this town, and am disgusted with -what I see in regard to the evil he mentioned in his letter. When I visit Sankey Bridges Saturday after Saturday,and see men,and boys also,playing at pitch and toss in .open daylight, I often wonder where the police duties come in, for it is a dis- grace to the credit of this town that such doings should be tolerated. " In regard to the drinking propensities of the town, it will never decline until the temperance workers, as a party,- Wake up and make their influence felt. Why should Warrington be be- hind any other town in regard to having a tem- perance hall, run on temperance lines? In the past 20 years I have travelled north, south, east and west in: this country, and have, with very few exceptions, found that the temperance workers have a room or a hall of their own, where thosewho do not wish to visit the public- house can go and spend an enjoyable evening, after their hlard day's toil, and, knowing how strong the temperance party is, I am more sur- prised that this has not been done. It is not, however, numbers .that count in respect to the work Ofaia party, but practical work which the workers of Mat party does that makes their influence felt to the masses.
-A:--"IEMFEnANCt WORKER.

, do not think your correspondent, "Spades are Trumps," can have much mason for saying "the money-lending evil will cure itself when men have got a thirst for some- thing better than beer." The money-lending evil exists, not only in ,Warrington, but also in all our great centres of, population; it even extends to' the rural districts. As a rule, the victims of the money-lender are not of the heavy beer-drinking class. _ Many a sober, Steady, working man (whose wages do not in- crease as regularly as his farnily does), ill:paid clerks, and even parsons„ poorly-paid parsons, fall within his clutches from time to time. People write and talk glibly about drink and the evils caused thereby. They fail to realise that in our great centresiof industry there are thousands of steady, hardworking men and women, who, through no fault of their own, cannot always.,make both ends meet. These have to resort to the money-lenders because there is ,no institution, national or otherwise, to come to 'their assistance. Beer has little, oi nothing, to do with the evil , October Bth, 1913

div.p: rtitas to the Oita

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS, Tag EDITOR of the " Examiner " invites corre- spondence on all subjects of public interest. LETTERS should be brief and pointed. Their object must be to .impart or seek information, not abuse.
LErrEss must in all cases be accompanied by the name and address of the writer. COMISVNICATIONS received early in the week— except urgent matters—can always be given the best attention.
SIR J. S. HARMOOD BANNER, M.P., AND THE INSURANCE ACT,

Sir,—At the yearly meeting -of the sharehold- ers of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, I notice that the Chairman, Sip Harmood Banner, M.P., in his report, said that the Insurance Act had cost the company £6,180, and that they failed to see ,how any benefit had accrued to the workman from it. He did not say, however, that if this money had not gone to the Insurance Act, it would have gone in increased wages to the workmen. No; 141 t ,he did say that it would have meant one per cent. increase in dividend to the shareholders. .1 am sure it would be an cask matter to find out how many of his workmen .have received, on behalf of their wives, the maternity benefit of 305., and how many 10s. per week. have been received by them when off sick ; also .the amount they have saved in money and .anxiety through hav- ing no doctor's 'bills to pay. But I doubt if tie wants to see these things, for,. being a. capitalist and Tory, with two eyes, one is fixed on dividends, and the °then-bllnd. to any benefit that can come from Liberal measures. A WORKMAN.

div.head: INCREASE OF CONVICTIONS FOR DRUNKENNESS.
div.p: INCREASE OF CONVICTIONS FOR DRUNKENNESS.

--- Sir,—Ther recei illy published Government , . Blue, Book, entitled Licensing , Statistics," shows Ufa), while a number .of public-houses were closed -last year tfie number of convictions for drunkenness had increased. ,At the confer_ ence of the Licensed Victuallers! Defence League a resolution was passed suggesting that in face of these figures it could no -longer be main- tained ttiat a reduction iri the facilities to obtain drink effected a reduction in the consumption of drink. May I venture to point out that the suggestion made by the Trade",S is quite un- warranted. In 1905 the total number Of "on" and off" public-houses and clubs in England and \Vale§ was 131,472, while in 1912 they numbered 121,873. The convictions for drunkenness in 1905 numbered 207,171,. while. in 1912 they num- bered 182,592, though the population had in- creased of 91),y5,(33/ of That is to say, a reduc- tionplaces had been accom- panied by a iednetio f 24,579 in the convic- tions for drunkenness. • Hence- instead of -disproving tile efficacy of reduetion, the figures suggest the very con- trary. I think I may say without much fear of contradiction that every civilised nation Oh-, to the horrors of intemperance is seeking to re- duce the facilities i for obtaining drink M order to promote temperance. J. T. pllys.

SPIRITISM AND ROMAN CATHOLICISM. , sir _The Holy Boman Church is becoming very much alarmed -about the progress of Spiritualism turoughout the world. it is not , long since the editor of the "New Catholic News," of U.S.A., called attentirm to itsadvanc- ino stridds all over- America, and bewailed the - fdraeiscp'etleytnhetaoetrigtilnulegeisir priests " found themselves, with yt increased frequency, obliged to ions concerning it, which were not put from. Mere -curiosity." Now Mgr. Bsintn ape is rs tryingto stem the tide in England, and from his lecture at Warrington • that he has not yet, in Spite of recent scientific pronouncements, got beyond the irrational appears ' idea of Satanic origin. Mgr. Benson has been repeatedly challenged by Spiritualist papers to justify a single one of his statements by any- thing in the nature, of evidence, and he has failed to do so. He prefers to rely upon the ignorance, prejudice and bigotry of his audi- ence4s. He knows perfectly well that spiritual Manifestations and phenomena have appeared in the Church of Home from the earliest times, and that her priests and leaders have made capital out of them whenever • it ' suited their purpose. But when similar manifestations. occur anywhere else they call them devilish. Many instances can be given, but it will suf- fice to mention one now as a challenge. It happened eight years ago, and the facts were widely published. Briefly, the Rev. - Father Hubert, of the Passionists' Church, Ardoyne, Belfast, declared publicly, in one of his sermons, that three out of the five Passionist fathers had recently seen and recognised the ghost of a formoc member of the community, who had died. He said that one night, after he had retired to rest, a knock came to his bedroom door, a similar knock was heard on an adjacent door, and both opened their doors and saw the figure of a Passionist father pacing the corridor and finally disappearing or melting into thin air. The visitation .was repeated on other occasions, and finally Father Hubert .accosted the apparition in the presence of other fathers hos a w it. The ghost spoke and- said 'that he (the preacher) had not fulfilled a promise made' to him in the flesh to pray for him a certain number' of times. Father Hubert admitted hav- ing made such a promise and had overlooked it. He had since kept it and the ,ghost had ceased to appear. There is nothing extraordinary about thN case, except that Father Hubert acted in a rational common-sense manner, instead of talking wildly about devilish influences. Scien- tific and open-minded investigators have pub- lished,thousands of cases equally-well attested. It is all consistent_with science, reason and natural laws, 4and it is dishonouring God to suggest that th'e poWers can a greater or more transcendent than His own. div.head: TREATMENT OF DECREPIT HORSES.
div.p: TREATMENT OF DECREPIT HORSES.

Sir,—Becent disclosures concerning the trade in worn-out, horses furnish horrible reading, and show. that the rules made by the Board of Agriculture for regulating this disgusting tvallic are somewhat of a farce. If, as one wit- ness says, it is vastly better than it was two Years ago, that only shows that there are de- grees even in devilry.- The old abuses all ap- parently exist still; if the number of .victims has been somewhat reduced, and if some boats and some men are not so bad as others. Mr. P. Carpw. Essex, Who has recently investigated the -condiltion under which the traffic is carried on, says that " the -accommodation- is shock- ing," and gives details ,to substantiate his assertion./

_ There are "terrible sufferings all round." On one journey two horses, certified fit to travel, fell down in the night, and, being too weak to rise, had to be. killed. In another place "there was no One besides the .man who brought the horses to see that things were even decently conducted, and you may imagine the stamp of man who does this sort of work."

The poor creature when condemned to death, IS not spared even then; a metal button is put, through the ear and clenched, to denote his fate ;:and the method of ;killing on some lines, With a hammer, is ghastly in its primitiveness: 1 doubt if it is realised by tile English public that over' 42,000 old horses are exported an- nually for slaughter abroad, and of this num- ber (according to the Report of the Board of Agriculture for 1912) 17,027 were shipped from London, Hull and other ports, to Antwerp. Of these, 16,988 arrived without injury. The others died on the voyage. . Why is this allowed to go on, we may ask? Presumably for., the same reason that many Other abuses are allowed to continue. Becausp

they have become a trade, and our legislators dare not interfere with trade, however immoral it may be. They make regulations, which ills no one's business to carry out, and the abuses go on as before.
ERNEST BELL (Editor, "The Animals' Friend "). York House, Portugal-street, Kingsway, London, E.C., October, ,1913.

div.head: IRISH DIFFICULTY.
div.p: THE IRISH DIFFICULTY.

Sir,—l ,father4rom the rew -remarks of O'Brien that he is unable or unwilling to con- trovert my alternative scheme to i-lothe I cannot conceive for My own part why We, born of an Imperial race, as we undoubtedly are, and ruling-subject races in every part of the inhabitable globe, should be so miserable that we cannot unite in one homogeneous whole for the benefit of ourselves in particular and mankind in general. What has given us our pre-eminence as a' civilising power in the world's history? Is it not the sterling vigour, honesty and 4 courage of our admirustrators, gaiderby that Divine Providence which, acts and moves. in the affairs of men; and cannot we govern this small group_ of islands in the corner of the Atlantic without miserably squab- bling over its affairs?.. • - If all Irishmen, or the majority of them, were like our good friend Mr. O'Brien; the Irish diffi- culty wOuld very soon settle itself, and there would be an end of the matter, but, -unfortun- • ately, they are not, and so long as we have men like " F.W.R.," so long will that question remain unsettled.

It seems regrettable to me that with so many subject races in a subordinate position, under our jurisdiction and control, we cannot Coalesce to form a homogeneous community ,irA these little islands. What- must these subject races think of dor quarrels here? Has it not a ten- dency to loosen the bonds of control over those subject peoples, and .to weaken the vigour of Empire?
Irishmen have in the past been amongst our greatest Empire builders. They have been second to none among our warriors, adrninis-

_ . trators and_statesmen,.ancl.it seems to me_soine- thing to regret that they Cannot fall into line to consolidate rather than divide the heart of the Enipire-. As I said in my last, and repeat here, there is no section or division of the Brit- ish Isles where the inhabitants. are of one dis- tinct race or creed; they are all inextricably mixed up, and any claim for special treatment of any part must therefore be on other lines than racial. .

We TUdY• all be proud of our 'descent, for' in all conscience, there is in the history of our ancestry plenty of noble deeds and heroic actions, both English, Scotch, Irish and Welsh. There is plenty of work And there is plenty of room in the broad acires which own Britain's sway for Britons to do. _
PHIL SQUOD.

div.head: MILITARY TRAINING
div.p: MILITARY TRAINING

Sir,--7-A remarkable manifesto in favour of universal military training has lately been issued, signed by most distinguished represen- tatives or leaders of public opinion. This manifesto has received wide circulation/ in the Press, but the varied character of the siima- tories-has apparently escaped notice. Among those who have come forward to appeal to the public to base the Territorial Force upon the oßfisitor obligatory principle of National Service are dlleard oo fwt, he such men as Earl Grey, the Roman Catholic Bishop of Newcastle (Dr. Collins), the Anglican Bishop gotfr oNnegwcc Newcastle, Principal educa- tional world in Newcastle. Nonconformity supplies its leaders in the persons of Mr. Elliott, JP., Mayor of Walisend, a prominent Wes- leyan, and ,Alderman A. Logan, Mayor of Ber- wick-on-Tweed. The presence of influential trade unionists is, however, still more signifi- cant, especially when they are such men as Alderman Allan, a leading member of the Boilermakers' and Iron Shipbuilders' Society; Alderman G. B. Hunter, of the Peace and Arbi- tration, Society; and Mr. J. O'llanlan, of the Shipwrights' Society, a member of the Ancient Order of Hiberniaris, and ex-Nationalist andi- date for Jarrow. Surely such a varied list of supporters of Lord Roberts will convince even the most timid politician that public opinion is rapidly being converted to,-reeognise the neces- sity of accepting the .duty of being trained for home defence as an obligatory principle. B. S. TOWNROE. Warrington.

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
CHANGE OF SEED.

There is no need to have a change of seed 'every year. The locality from which new seed comes is said to have its influence, and it is only reasonable to stippoSe that this is true. Seed from a southern county may be expected to give an earlier crop, than seed from a. less favoured climate, whilst that from the 'North gives 'a hardy crop that should withstand severe weather in early spring. However, there is no need to pay much attention to these Ideas. •

With regard to the quality of seed wheat, it is generally agreed that a good heavy sample is best. As like produces like in the vegetable world, as among animals, it is certainly rehson- able to expect the best results from good plump grain. it ,may be imentioned, however, that some experiments carried out at Woburn showed equal results from large and small seed grain. The large went ahead better at first, but the small drew up level in the later stages.

div.head: SEWAGE AS A MANURE.
div.p: SEWAGE AS A MANURE.

Dr. J. Grossmann, in discussing "The Util- isation of Sewage in Agriculture," before the British Association Agriculture Section, said the total value of the. nitrogenous .matter, phosphates and potash compounds contained in the liquid part of sewage was equal to 20 million pounds per anpurn. The value of its solid matter, termed sewage sludge, was •about two million pounds per annum,. and he had succeeded in designing a practicable method by which this amount could be made available. By his process' the dried sludge was mixed with a small percentage of acid and subjected to the actiOn of superheated steam, which carried off the fatty matters (which were condensed in water) and left an inodorous, brown powder, completely sterilised, -which contained, on an ,average, 1,5 per cent. of nitrogen, 3 per cent. of phosphate of lime, and .5 per cent. of potash, distrfiluted in almost molecular state over from 30 to 40 per cent. of organic matter similar to humus, and mixed with a certain amount of carbon in an extremely fine state of division. The process did not add to the cost of sludge disposal, was automatic, ad worked day and night without a break. _

The solution of the problem of sewage sludge disposal should place the much larger problem of the application of liquid sewage to farming within closer reach of solution. Up to the pre- sent, the tendency in sewage treatment had been to reduce the amount of sludge, as in practically every place it had been a source of great 'expense and nuisance. It was now pos- sible; and even advisable, to produce more sludge, . and by doing so to obtain better effluents with reduced purification plants. So far the great drawback in sewage farming had been that the sewage had had to be used whether . the land required it or not. The enormous strides which had been !made in the last seventy years in erigineering, chemistry, and agricultural science, the use of oil and gas engines, improvements in pumping machinery, the distribution of electricity, the improvements in motor traction, all seemed to point to the fact that within a measurable distance we shOuld,be able to utilise, if not all, at any rate a considerable part, of the sewage which was now wasted.

Plants for spring bedding should be put out while • the ground is still ward. They can be placed between summer occupants of the borders. Stir the soil with: the hoe to make the ,Plants grow vigorously. - Forget-me-nots, Wallflowers, Ara,bis, Primroses, Polyanthuses, Aubriptias, Daisies, Yellow Alystiun are - sonic fit subjects. Wallflowers, charming old-fashioned plants, are •always appreciated" in the spring; and stocky. seedlings should now be put in their final quarters. They are the better for being transplanted at once, and where this is done the final shift should be made. A FRAGRANT SHRUB.

The Mock, Orange, Philadelphus, or Syringa, as it is variously named, is the,Most fragrant of flowering shrubs. The pure white blossoms closely resemble the flower of the orange. It is a shrub both accommodating and hardy. Those ,desirous 'of. growing this beautiful shrub 'should plant as soon as possible in the autumn in ordinary' good soil in a sunny position. It may be utilised for pot culture; putting in the cold greenhouse December to May. Those who already have plants should do what pruning is required at the, present time. Next season's flowers will be produced on the new growth of .the present season, , and this must be borne in mind when pruning. All old spent shoots may be cut. away. The young growths will have a better chance to ripen. No further pruning will be needed next spring, with the exception of removing tht second crop of young shoots which may grow from the cut hack .sterns. If these shoots,were left on they Nvould,be of no use, and it is better to cut them off as Soon as they form. Grown in a sunny position, it is not particu- lar as to a dry or moist soil; but on dry soils there is generally a larger display of flowers. On Moist soils the flowers are fewer, but finer. Plants for small gardens or narrow borders should be of the dwarf-growing varieties. The tall-growing kinds are best adapted for a high wall.

div.head: QUEER WAY TO MAKE CONVERTS.
div.p: QUEER WAY TO MAKE CONVERTS.

Mr. SMITH: Two days ago I was in a cottage in Frederick-street, and I went to see a political oppqnent of mine. A VOICE: "Chuck up playing to the gallery." Mr.. SMITH: "The man asked the why I wasted my time addressing crowds at street corners, and I told him that I did not waste my time or ever intend to. I also told him that my audi- ences were generally composed of nay opponents, Certain people whiz) 'held no pronounced views, and others who shared my views. When the people who held no pronounced views heard me trying to reply to my opponent hecklers they went away in disgust, but as soon as they got home they quietly pondered over the whole matter, with the result that they came to the conclusion that what I had been saying must have been of great value or the opponents would have let me say ‘it without heckling. Thus, every time I address.audiences at street corners, I make at least a dozen converts or so. -That is the result of interruptions, and I am content to go on." Judging by the numerous interruptions this week there will not be a Liberal left in the town if what Mr. Smith says is correct.

div.head: " THE LAST VOTE."
div.p: " THE LAST VOTE."

The audience must have become satiated in humour, for when Mr. Smrra began "Let us re- member," a diminutive boy who had been most vociferous in his "[Tear, hears," throughout the meeting, caused roars of laughter when he fol- lowed Mr. Smith's • "Let Us remember," with "The Fifth of November." •

Mr. Smith did not seem to appreciate the joke or probably he was jealous that his remarks had not been treated so enthusiastically by the audience, as were this boy's chance remark, for in a very serious manner he continued, "Let us remember that the reason this Bill has reached its presdnt stage is the result of a base political bargain between the Radical Government and the Redmond party. It is because of this base political bargain that I, propose to fight this campaign in Warrington against all comers until the last vote has been dropped into the ballot box and the people have decided that I am not afraid of.a few who make a noise.

div.head: NOTHING BUT HOME RULE CHALLENGE.
div.p: A NOTHING BUT HOME RULE CHALLENGE.

In conclusion, he said: I will make this. bar- gain With my opponent, whoever he might be: I will contest the election with him on the Home Rule question only. I make this offer to Mr. Crosfield : That nothing shall be saixr in his election address; nothing on the posters or in the speeches except Home Rule. I will stand or fall by that challenge. My voice is bad now and I cannot go on. A VOICE: You will not be able to shout to your men then.
Then came the startling climax to this cam- paign when cheers were repeatedly given for Mr. Lloyd George, and the response to the call for "Cheers for the Member" was very weak.

Some workmen who were repairing the sewers of Milan—the largest in Italy, extending over 200 miles—were startled by the apparition of a gaunt, tattered man, covered with mud, whO, in a much exhausted state, invoked their aid. The man was rescued with difficulty, and con- veYed to hospital, where food and restoratives were given him.

He said he was a painter, aged 18. A month ago, while sleeping in the open air, he was assaulted by . three hooligans, who robbed him and then threw .him into the sewer. By sheer force of will he had succeeded in living a month underground, continually wandering along the sewers, vainly trying to find an exit, groping in the darkness, fighting rats, eating refuse, and drinking filthy water.
The painter's exhaustion is so great that he needs three months' hospita,l treatment, and his recovery is uncertain.
From reynolds's Newspaper.

div.head: "LIBERTY OF SPEECH."
div.p: "LIBERTY OF SPEECH."
Interruptions were the principal features of the meeting. At the ou4et Mr. Smith had ap- pealed for a fair hearing. A member of the audience asked: What anout liberty of speech in Belfast?

SMITH': My friend asks me, What about liberty of speech in Belfast? Well, I will reply to him by asking him a question: What about liberty of speech in Dublin? But I say, let us assume the Belfast men were .wrong in re- fusing a hearing, why perpetrate another wrong by refusing me a hearing? (Laughter.) There was now considerable uproar, and in answer to a remark•from the crowd, Mr. SMITH said: "I think that we are right, and .1 have said so in Warrington before. I am prepared at any) time to debate with Mr. Crosfield any phase of the Home Rule question, and I do say to you gentlemen-"

A VOICE: Don't be personal. Mr. SMITH: I am not personal. I put it to you, men of Warrington, by whose votes I gained my seat in Parliament, and by whose votes I hope to retain it at the next election, that I am at any rate an English sportsman. I-don't say, and never have said, a word against Mr. Crosfield. If he desires to conduct his cam- paign in his own way be is free to do so, as far as I am concerned, but I say it is only fair that a man who is prepared to discuss questions with his opponent is deserving of a fair hearing. A VOICE: Let us have something about Home Rule.
Mr. SMITE: Yes, and when I have said it, you can never say I was insincere in my beliefs, and that I lacked the courage to. meet my constitu- ents at street corners.

div.head: "ULSTER" WILL FIGHT. Mr. Smith's Sincere Prophecy.
div.p: "ULSTER" WILL FIGHT. Mr. Smith's Sincere Prophecy.

After conjuring up the visiorf of the "clash- ing of swords" in -Ulster, Mr. SMITH said: "1 am sincere in what I say, although it is only a prophecy. But when the time arrives, and the Bill is forced upon Ulster-" A VOICE: 'lt will be; and another VOICE: It is passed., Mr. SMITH: It is not passed. A VOICE: It is passed, and you are fighting' against it. ' Mr. SMITH: r cannot argue against Men who are dominated by such false notions. (Laugh- ter.) It is not passed yet,. but depend upon it, if it is, then the working men of, Ulster, who are toilers like you in Warrington, will resist it by force of arms on a question of their own freedom.

A VOICE: It is not true. You are talking rot. Mr. SMITH: You are entitled to your own Opinion, certainly, but you will find the truth of that prophecy when the time arrives. (Laugh- ter.) A VOICE: Take the troops out and cut them down, but they, will never rise up in arms for us to do it.

Mr. SMITE: This gentleman declares to you, with all his knowledge of Ulster—Which may be great or small, I don't know which—that itt is not true that -Ulster will fight for her freedo)n, and he suggests this is all a pantomime. I tell you sincerely that Ulster men do not regard it as a pantomime or, a game of bluff. Ulster men would not drill ankl train night after night, and initiate themselves in the art of war ii it were so. Ulster has never bluffed.

A VOICE : It means "nowt." (Laughter.) Mr. SMITH: Do you, men of Warrington, really believe that 480,000 Uister people would take this solemn covenant as a sort of pantomime? Mr. Churchill will never suggest Ulster is 'indulging in a game of bluff, and I ask you to judge between what now say, and what he will say. A VOICE: He went to .South Africa. (Ap- plause.) ' Mr. SMITH: Yes, pay my tribute to.. him, because he was a gallant and brave man. A VOICE: Why didn't you let him speak in Ulster? - - _ -

div.head: CAN THE POWERS BE REVIVED 7
div.p: CAN THE POWERS BE REVIVED 7
Should Warrington become a port? Would it be possible to make it a rival to Manchester? were the topics discussed at the Council meet- ing on Tuesday.
Aldormaa Bennett argued that the proposal to fill in the old river-bed at Wilderspool would make the promised dock impossible.
It was his opinion that, given a dock, Warring- ton would become a suitable port of call for many of the ocean-going steamers which passed its dock.
The Clerk explained that the powers for making a dock had lapsed, and the work could only be done by securing a new Act of Parliament.
Councillor Roberts showed that the traders, through using the river, got preferential treatment they would not get if a dock existed.
Allegations were made by Councillor Pemberton that Warrington had been "sold " in the matter. The subject will come before the General Purposes Committee shortly.
A vision of Warrington becoming a port was held forth at the meeting of the Borough Coun- cil on Tuesday evening, and, unlike most visions, this led to a long, and, at some stages, lively discussion.

The topic arose upon a paragraph "in the re- port of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, which stated: The Borough Surveyor reported that lie had, in accordance 'with instructions, interviewed the engineer of the Manchester Ship Canal Company with reference to the proposal by this committee to build a river wall, for the purpose of strengthening the roadway along the old river bed t the southern end of River-road, and that he had been informed that the com- pany would shortly be filling in the old bed of the river, thus doing 'away with the necessity of this committee's Proposal.

it not possible to induce them to view the mat- ter in that • spirit? If they failed the result would be absolutely calamitous to the town. He did not think that any other side of the town would be half as suitable as the site which had been named, but if it was covered with great mountains of soil they might say "good- bye" for ever to the dock. Ile refused to con- template such a state of things, and they ought never to close their 'eyes to the possibilities of the borough in the time to come. They had their water facilities, and if on the top of them they were able tO say there was the possibility of making a dock, it would help the town to develop, and what it might be in the future he could not conceive. It should be re- membered that the river bed was in existence, and so much of the excavation was done, and they could make a dock to erve their immediate purpose without incurring an extravagant ex- penditure. Here they had one of the 'finest of _waterways, with ships sailing Up continually to Manchester, and yet they had not a single facility for any one of them stopping at War- rington. -
• Councillor ROBERTS: Oh, yes, we have. Alderman BENNETT : The lay-by, which is a mile off.

Alderman Bennett added that they should rise to the spirit of the opportunity. lam quite sure, he said, if we do not, we are going to make a great mistake. The first mistake was Crewe—Crewe ought to have been here to-day.

div.head: "OF TREMENDOUS IMPOP.TANCE."
div.p: "OF TREMENDOUS IMPOP.TANCE."

This is a matter of tremendous importance, said Alderman BENNETT, who raised the subject. I cannot, however, move an amendment. • This proposal seems a simple and easy matter, but I venture to say with a full sense of responsi- bility that it will not be long before you regret taking such a step. It practically means, if the matter is allowed to proceed, the chance, which all public-spirited Warringtonians have been looking forward to, the chance of making War- rington a port will be for ever gone. Alderman Bennett said he would give the history of the matter so vitally important to Warrington. According to the Ship Canal Act the company agreed to make a dock at Warring- ton at their own expense on the Wilderspool site, hut they had many difficulties to contend' with, and asked to be allowed to open the canal before they carried out their obligation. In its anxiety to assist them, the Council consented and it was then 'understood that the company would construct the dock •within three years. That they failed to do; but agreed to transfer their powers to the Warrington Corporation for a further period of seven years, to grant the land free of cost, to connect the dock with their railways, and to afford the Corporation every reasonable facility for working it. That was thought a very reasonable arrangement, and the Council had hoped to have carried it out. He suvposed the Canal Company thought that the Council would recoup themselves for construct- ing the dock out of the revenues chargeable, and once repaid the dock would go,to the Ship Canal Company. The seven yearn .went by and tho time lapsed.

div.head: "OUT OF ORDER."
div.p: "OUT OF ORDER."

The MAyoR : I am afraid, this is out of order. The powers have lapsed in regard to this, Alderman BENNETT : Yes, but I will explain. Alderman .TINNIOX : What can we do? Alderman BENNETT : .We can do a lot. Councillor . JENraxs : The 'committee feel we are compelled to accept this as the final answer. Alderman BF:NNETT : It is not too late. The. Tows CLERK: The powers to construct a dock has lapsed.

Alderman BENNETT : If so, you, can have a new •Act of Parliament to secure new powers. The CLERK: We should have applied for that before the powers lapsed., Councillor ROBERTS: The pewers conferred on the .Corporation were conferred by agreement and not by statute—a different thing. The CLERK: So far as the company is con- cerned.

div.head: NO LOCUS STAND!.
div.p: NO LOCUS STAND!.

F i Councillor I:tow:Ras : When the Corporation ' took over from the Ship Canal Company by agreement the powers to construct a dock and did not carry out the work, the powers reverted to the Manchester Corporation, and that .being so an application for renewal of the powers would rest on the Ship Canal Company, and not upon us, as we have no locus standi at all. • Alderman BEN;IETT, continuing, said that at .one time there was consiOerable fear that the Canal Company would utilise the Site as a tip for ,the spoil which They .were dredging from the river, and in order to avoid that being done the Rivers Committee appointed a deputation, consisting of Councillor • Fulton-Smith and hirdelf, to wait upon the directors of the com- pany and ask them whether they could see their way to retain the site for the original purpose, in the hope that either the Corporation or the company might eventually be able to make use of it.

The directors met them in a most courteous manner, and he was pleased to say that they acceded to their request, and nothing had been done in the meantime to interfere with the old river bed or the land immediately adjoining it. however, the Corroration had made no move in the meantime, the Canal CoMpany appar- ently now intended to revert to their original intention, and to cover the site with-mud, which' they were dredging from the river., That would, as the Council would see, render it practically impossible to construct a dock. in that position, or, at. any rate, would greatly increase the expense of so doing, and lie re- garded the matter as of such vital importance that fie thought the company ought to - be ap- proached again and an endeavour made to induce them to reconsider the matter.

div.head: M!GHT CONSTRUCT.
div.p: M!GHT CONSTRUCT.
He thought they might point out that sonic day the Corporation hoped to make a dock. War

div.head: WANT OF PATRIOTISM.
div.p: WANT OF PATRIOTISM.
Councillor BROADHURST : The Council is not at fault for that.
Councillor ROBERTS: It was want of patriotism.

Alderman BENNETT : Crewe should have been here, and so should Port Sunlight, and the dock, which should have been here, is not here, al- though 20 Years have gone. I want to prevent this great mistake from becoming irretrievable. (Applause.) • Councillor ROBERTS said Alderman Bennett's remarks showed how unacquainted he was with modern dock construction. A great deal was said by gentlemen who looked at matters from the inside of their offices, and who did not con- sider it necessary to ascertain the full facts, to the effect that Warrington had, unfortunately, in its history got a great many lost opportunities to account for.

The only obstacle to the settlement of the large industrial concerns Of Crewe and Port Sunlight in Warrington was the policy of the landowners of that period, and certainly not the policy of the Corporation. As long as the land laws re- mained in their present form and conferred a monopoly upon those who owned land, they must expect that kind of treatment. They had ac- commodation at Walton lay-by for ocean-going steamers for a great many years. If there were any substantial justification for the suggestion that cargoes in bulk could be used in Warring- ton: and were required by the manufacturers, the lay-by would have been used to a much greater extent.
Alderman BENNETT : It iS a mile away. . • Councillor ROBERTS: That is quite true, but the proposed dock would not be nearer the centre of the town.

div.head: TOLLS CHARGEABLE.
div.p: THE TOLLS CHARGEABLE.

Councillor ROBERTS added that Alderman Ben-. nett- had not taken into consideration the fact that a toll was . chargeable upon vessels discharging at that lay-by, which would also apply to vessels discharging in the proposed docks, and which was much heavier than people had any idea of until they came to take it into calculation. The reason why• the manufacturers of Warrington in a great mea- sure found it desirable to tranship in Liverpool was because of the enormous advantage they had with regard to the rates charged on the Ship Canal for traffic passing through Walton locks into the river.

Warrington had a preferential position, worth thou Sands and thousands a year to the manufacturers and rateptlyers of the town—a nosition which, if they were negotiating with the Ship Canal CompanY to-clay, they would never obtain on anything like the present terms and which, entitled the Corporation of that day to permanent credit.

Warrington had facilities such as no other town on the Ship Canal possessed, "and-the dis- advantages of not having a .dock constructed were more imaginary than real. The terms upon which the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany allowed their powers to be transferred temporarily to the Corporation, under which the Corporation were to take all the risk of finding the capital, and of carrying on the docks until they had. recouPed themselves for prin- cipal and interest, and then that they should have no further interest in the product of the docks, were a little toe -one-sided for any busi- ness ,Corporation ultimately to pursue. Tho manufacturers Who transhipped their goods at Liverpool had got financial reasons for doing it.

div.head: WAS WARRINGTON SOLD
div.p: WAS WARRINGTON SOLD

Councillor PEMBERTON : Warrington was sold in this matter. The town didn't insist upon it, as Councillor Roberts has led us to believe. ()Punchier ROBERTS: They didn't? Councillor PEMBERTON : No, or they would have insisted on the dock. Councillor-Roeums : They could not. Councillor PEMBERTON : It should have been made. The. ratepayers of Warrington were sacrificed. Councillor ROBERTS: They were not.

Councillor PEMBERTON added that whelyver a dock was made, trade followed. An important question, however, was whether the tolls would rlampensate for the enormous cost of the pro- ject. The dock would be no use to manufac- turers unless it were available at .a cheap rate. Tt was a fact that spoil. Could be removed at a unall cost, but the question that would then Arise was: Where could they remove it to, once they had allowed it to be deposited on the river bed? He was afraid the dock proposal had been allowed to hang fire too long.
WHY NOT CREWE? -

COMI6IIOr BROADHURST explained why the London and North-Western works were not at Warrington. His father was one who helped to excavate for the foundations of the steam hammer, but there were no foundations on which it could be erected. The consequence was that the works- were,taken to Crewe.

Councillor ROBERTS: That explanation has the harm of novelty. I have not heard it befcre. (Laughter) ' Councillor WirslNsox.: Why do the canal people want to fill this up? Councillor JENKINS : The whole thing is out of Irder.
Councillor 'Mimi:sox added that his impres-
MUD-THROWING 'BUSES.

div.head: Ways in which Motor 'Buses may be Improved.
div.p: Ways in which Motor 'Buses may be Improved.
TRADESMEN COMPLAIN.
" EXAMINER" SPECIAL.

A kindly hint from a fellow pedestrian on Monday saved me from being mud bespattered from head to foot. It was a 'drab, dreary, wet and mtidd.y clay, and the tumble of one of the motor 'buses readied my ears as I took my well- wisher's hint and got as .near to the wall at the lower end of Sankey-street as I could. I was only just in time, for with a bump, the heavy .'bus. splashed into a large puddle and sent the dirt flying in all directions. Some of the Mud fell within an inch of where we were standing, and I thanked My friend most warmly for his timely advice. I thought probably his -pre- cautionary methods were born of a mudbath he might haVe had as a 'bus had passed him; but such was not the case. He informed me that he had seen a young lady with a light mackin- tosh on, endeavouring, with the aid of a small needlework handkerchief, to clean herself up before turning in at the office for business. I noticed that several of the shop windows in the town were So splashed that the goods in them were scarcely perceivable. One tradesman felt very sorely on the matter, as it had been his arduous task only a few hours previously to clean his large plate-glass window, which was now in such a horrible statb. Throughout the day I heard several complaints, and having heard of other .Irge. centres introducing remedial measures, I was ,anxious toiknow if .something was going to be done to protect pedestrians and the business premises of the town.

div.head: SPLASH BOARDS.
div.p: SPLASH BOARDS.

From good authority I gleaned the informa- tion that Messrs. Tilling, the makers of the Warrington ','buses, have arranged to have patent splash boardS fitted to all their vehicles. These are boards eighteen inches in length and twelve inches wide, which are fixed on. to the axle of the 'bus and secured to the hub. A number of metal links are introduced,. which gives sufficient flexibility to. the guard as to prevent it interfering with the running of the 'bus. These Patent guards, I understand, are an effective protection from the discomfiture which some citizens have experienced recently. There is also another capital device which it is understood is equally if not more effective. It is in the nature of a large rubber ring, which will entirely cover the outer edge of the tyre and overlap sufficiently as to catch the mud or throw it in a straight spurt behind into the ordinary metal semi-circular guard. This disc is fastened to the rim of the wheel and will be very durable.

There is no doubt that in the near future the Corporation will have some sort of protective. 'arraxigement fixed up, and it is more than likely that the latter guard will be instituted, for, in addition to keeping the mud off the side walks, and the shop windows, it is no way unsightly. If such a step is decided upon, the Tramways Committee will have the thanks of the whole community. The other heavy motor traffic thrOugh the tovn is also a nuisance in this direction, but 'lcharity begins at home," and the ratepayers of the. town want protection, if it can: be afforded, from their own Corporation systems, at least.. . f Probably some steps will be taken in the matter at the next committee meeting; for, we understand, that complaints have been made in official quarters.

div.head: PUBLIC BOON-.
div.p: A PUBLIC BOON-.

Since the 'buses- first ran in Warrington in July they have proved a great boon to the dis- tricts served, and from then until recently the weather has not been sufficiently bad enough to give rise to such a state of things which has raised the ire of tradesmen and others during the past few days.

div.head: SMEj.L.
div.p: THE SMEj.L.

A frequent rider in the 'bus edmplained to me of the ofMnsive smell which he stated arose from the engine. He had, he said, sat 6.t the far end of the. Illis near the driver, and the smell made him feel ill. I cannot say that I confirm this statement, for beyond a somewhat uncomfortable warmness in summer, I have found the 'buses cosy and convenient. But, then, so long as optimists exist there will also be pessimists, and it is only natural that when any section of the community enjoy a benefit from a municipal project, there are others who deery the innovation—perhaps for jealousy, for it was a He6lhen who complained of the smell. The mild-splashing danger, however, needs remedying, and, we shall all be delighted when the Corporation soe fit to protect the ratepaVers of the borough and endeavour to aid the trades- men to keep their shop fronts as attractive as possible.

div.head: WARRINGTON AS A PORT—cont.
div.p: WARRINGTON AS A PORT—cont.

sion was that the Corporation approached them • with a view to erecting a river wall to save the bank. Init their reply- was : "We won't build a wall. but we will fill up the bed." If the cor- poration asked them not .to fill up the bed, the probability was that the company would accede to the request.. Counctllor Ossor.st agreed that something ought to be done, if possible, to prevent the un- • necessary filling up of the old river bed. Sooner or later it would be of some advantage to the town_to have a dock. If the Corporation could assist the Canal Company by erecting the wall themselves, it might obviate the filling up of the bed. The facilities for the constrUction of a dock must have .been considered -valuable at the time they were obtained, and it would not
be wise to allow them to lapse. It would be a great Mistake to let the facilities drop. Alderman TINNION explained that the Council had no power to prevent the company doing what they chose.
The minutes were adopted, although there is a probability that the question will be raised at the General Purposes Committee.

div.head: NEW ROADWAY.
div.p: NEW ROADWAY.
Proposal to Remove a Death Trap near the New Bridge.

There was some discussion at the Warrington Borough Council on Tuesday over the resolu- tion of the Street Improvement, • Committee.: "That the Borough Surveyor be instructed to report upon the proposed new roadway from Warrington Bridge, crossing the line of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and joining Wilderspool Causeway, near St. James' Church, and that he be authorised to have a model of , the proposed roadway pre* pared."

Alderman BENNETT expressed his strong dissent to the'proposal.fle thought they should proceed with the larger scheme proposed. no suggested scheme would .not improve the diffi- culty much, and it might mean that it mould be years 'before They got the more comprehen- sive -scheme. They ought to- end the existing 'death trap. He Would not he surprised to learn of more faialitieS at the point. The MAYOR thought the larger scheme was worth .consideration, but . the alterations. now proposed would make the death trap at least a bit more safe.

div.head: SPENDING OF THOUSANDS.
div.p: SPENDING OF THOUSANDS.

Councillor PEMBERTON thought it was no um doing a little bit and spending thousands pf pounds on work that would ultimately be thrown away. He was surprised at the com- mittee advising such a thing. CouncilJor ROBERTS 7 thought whatever the larger scheme would be—none of them might see that mature—they should go-on-with the suggested work. The carrying out of the larger scheme would enhance the value of the land adjacent, and he thought it-would be better for the. Corporation to purchase the necessary Pro- perty than to allow the present opportunity to pass.
Alderman BENNErr said he had many com- plaints from people about the inconvenience caused. -
After some further discussion the'reeoni- mendation was adopted.

tut site. He was looking to the day when the citizens would follow in the footsteps of Alder- man Bennett and seek to make the town more beautiful. Alderman BENNETT moved that the matter be taken back, and Councillor Broadhurst sec- onded.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
The Vagrancy Question.

div.head: 'SOME SUGGESTIONS.
div.p: 'SOME SUGGESTIONS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday, Mr. J. L. Jones (vice-chairman) presiding. On the recommendation of the Visiting Com- mittee, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mrs. Hayward, " Greenbank," Whitley Superior, for her gifts to the inmates.

div.head: Children's Home Committee.
div.p: Children's Home Committee.

The Children's Home Committee recommended that the question of boot repairing be left over for the present, and that the Superintendent be instructed to straighten up the garden. That the Superintendent arrange and provide a suit- able dinner for the children attending the Aston Council School. That the makers of the electric light be communicated with in regard to the defective dynamo. - The minutes were confirmed.
Uniformity Needed.

Mr. Spruce and Mr. Pilling gave their report of a meeting to discuss vagrancy, held at Crewe. Mr. Spruce said that it was decided that the co-operation of the police should be requisitioned in order that they might expect to have some better results. The question of providing a mid-day meal, consisting of eight ounces of bread and two ounces of cheese was also raised. They in Dutton were 14 miles from Chester, and the question would arise as to where the 'mid-day meal station would be set up. In regard to indiscriminate alms-giving, the meeting recommended that the county be -well covered with literature, urging those who had been in the habit of supporting vagrants withdraw the giving of alms to those applicants on the ground that they were provided with a mid-day meal. With regard to detention, it was recommended that where practicable vagrants he detained for two nights at their particular task. It was considered that the estimated cost for the meal stations would be one-hundredth part of a penny on the assessable value of the Unions. As far as possible, they ought to dis- criminate between the deserving and the pro- fessional tramp, and, where possible, give them better quarters and discharge them early. Mr. Pilling said that amongst the several questions left to the Executive were uniformity of tasks, way tickets, the publishing of litera- ture, and dietary. The whole idea was to get uniformity.

div.head: Giving of Aims.
div.p: The Giving of Aims.

Mr. Lister-Kaye: With regard to alms-giving, I say that half the People who asked for alms are not workhouse people at all. . Mr. Pilling: We are speaking of workhouse people. Mr. Lister-Kaye: There are lots of it. , Mr. Spruce: With the co-operation of the police it may mean some diminution in the class with which we are trying to deal. Mr. Woodward said that unless they had power to impose the scheme on all -Unions it would be vitiKted. _ _

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
AN ASSAULT ON THE POLICE.
Hugh Mitchell, Water-street, and Margaret Walton, Water-street, were charged at Widnes on Monday with assaulting Sergeant Waterson, in Water-street.

Sergeant Waterson stated that he saw an- other prisoner behaving in a disorderly manner and went to quieten him. He met with a Stub- born refusal. Mitchell and Walton tried to get the prisoner away. The sergeant was knocked over, struck, and kicked. A hostile crowd gathered and for a time the officer was in peril. Defendants were fined 40s. and costs each, or a month in default.
SHOCKING NEGLECT BY A MOTHER. A revolting story of child neglect was told, on Monday,. at Runcorn, in the case of James and Isabella Moore, charged with neglecting their two children.

Mr. W. E. Hough,. who prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., said the case had been under the observation of the society for the last three years. On September 10th, Inspector Evans visited the home in Robert-street, and in conse- quence of the conditions under which the chil- dren existed an order was made for their imme- diate removal to the workhouse. The house was in a shockingly filthy state. The children were fairly well clothed, but poorly nourished. The children's clothing was dirty, and they were literally swarming with vermin.
In view of the evidence the Bench decided to dismiss the charge against the male defendant. The woman, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to six months' hard labour.

div.head: DETECTIVE'S LAST CAPTURE.
div.p: THE DETECTIVE'S LAST CAPTURE.

A good story is told of the last capture made by the detective Calchas, who died on Saturday in Paris. M. Calchas had been to the theatre to see Mistinguett in a new piece, "En Touce." Be- tween the acts he went to her dressing-room. Mistinguett had a letter in her hand, written in very faulty French. It was an offer of service. The applicant, a young woman, would not be denied.
"Every night," said liistinguett, "she comes to me. She kisses my feet, and says she spends every penny in buying seats to see me. I shall have to take her as second femme de chambre."

"Who is she?" asked M. calchas, after he had watched the suppliant. "Oh, I don't know. Some poor girl." "Come here," said Calchas to the girl. "What is that jingling in sour pocket?" and he began to search her. From her pocket he took four bunches of keys, an electric lamp and a bijou jemmy. A couple of minutes later the girl was being bundied down the stairs,
