div.head: Alderman James Evans Replies to the Disclosures of the Smoke Abatement League.
div.p: Alderman James Evans Replies to the Disclosures of the Smoke Abatement League.
COUNCILLOR BROADHURST COMPLIMENTS THE 'EXAMINER'

Smoke was discussed at length at the meeting of the Warrington Town Cduncil on Tuisthky evening, and the caso for the dame was opened by Alderman James Evans. Alderman Eibnnett asked the Chairman of the Health Committee if he had read the article on the smoke question in "The Examiner," and Atderman Evans admitted that he had.
Alderman James Evans gave a mass of figures to show that the smoke was not so black as it v4i4 ,painted, and said that many of the smoky cchimneys were exempt from prosecu- tion.
Another smoke defender said that he knew one of the " greater '' shopkeepers who was never so happy as when the chimney stacks were belching forth black smoke.
The discussion did not lift the serious question any nearer a solution, and the subject was dropped after several had aired their views on smoke.

A discussion on smoke was started in the Warrington. Town Council on Tuesday evening by Alderman Bennett putting: the following question to Alderman James Evans, the chair- man of the Health Committee : Whether his attention had been called to an article on the smoke queftion in the "Warrington Examiner" on tlie 13th Sep- tember, from which it appears that one of the Inspectors of the Smoke Abatement League has recently visited the town and taken careful observations of twenty-three chimneys; that only three of them kept within the time limit prescribed by the Cor- poration; and that nine of them emitted dense black smoke for from 12 to 181. min_ utes per half-hour ; and what steps the com- mittee propose to take to ensure respect for their own regulations and conipliance with

_ the provisions of the Public Health 'Act. Alderman JAMES EVANS : My answer to the first portion is Yes !" It seems to me there is an impression abroad that the smoke ques- tion is one of those questions that can easily be dealt with at once all a person has to do is just to ,take out his watch, take observations, and if he finds the time limit exceeded, he thinks it is the duty of the Health Committee to immediately summon the culprits, and deal with them accordingly. The question is a most difficult one, and hence I propose to say one or two pointed things about it, so far as Warringtqn is congerned.

smako Ciliation. They made 456 observations in 1912. In Warrington in 1912, although we have no inspectors specially set aside for the work, we took 237 observations. (Counallor PEMBERTON : Hear, hear.) I think I have said sufficient on that aspect. I turn to a more vital side—the health work of the borough. Everyone admits that smoke may not be very nice so far as its appearance is concerned. I wish to say at this point that our experience has convinced us that the manu- facturers of this town are not wilfully and wantonly disfiguring the town by smoke. They are doing their best to minimise it. (Hear, hear.) One of the largest firms are putting up a new 'kind of boiler, in which they expect to get complete combustion and bring the smoke nuisance down to nothing. I mention that, as I know there are manufacturers who do not delight in making a smoke nuisance, and it is only bare justice that this phase of the question should be mentioned.

div.head: CHIMNEYS THAT ARE EXEMPT.
div.p: CHIMNEYS THAT ARE EXEMPT.

lace I should like to point out to Bennett that, to all intents and pur- poses, rtSection 334 of the Public Health Alderman the under 1 ifi dreßsenP Act of 1875, a large portion of the chimneys in this borough are exempt. (Councillor PEMBER- TON : Hear, hear.) So far as we are concerned, that ends that particular section of the matter. In the second place, the Act specially men- tions black smoke. I may say, for the informa- tion of those who have not read the Act—for such there may be in the Council—that this dense. specially to This is a black lac Act only applies to Ireland, England and Wales. The smoke question cannot be dealt with on the lines it is dealt with in Scotland. In Scotland it can be dealt with according to the volume of smoke, be it what colour it may. In our pylieedene point I would like you to note—the great smoke not the not Act merely difficulties we have in dealing with the matter. Notices must be served, and before proceedings can be instituted, a second offence must have been committed within six months of the notice. Well, notice what that means. When notifica- tion is made, the utmost the Health Committee can do is to notify the offenders. If a second offence is committed within six months of the giving of the statutory notice, we can proceed.

div.head: THERE ARE 222 CHIMNEYS.
div.p: THERE ARE 222 CHIMNEYS.

I had better draw your attentiOn to the num- ber of chimneys in the town. The total number in connection with works is 222, and, to all intents and purposes, the number of chimneys exempt from Section 91 of the Public Health Act is 87. The chimneys that are constantly under the observation of the inspector are 135. Fancy if you could have the 87 connected with the smelting trade eliminated, and the 135, about which there is not much complaint, left, what would Warrington be like? I think if such a condition of things obtained my friend, Alder- man Bennett, would think the millennium had come. (Laughter.) :In the list given by the Manchester inspector in the " Examiner " there are four firms, the majority of whose chimneys are entirely out- side the Act, and are exempt from observation. The Manchester inspector's figures do not com- pare with our observations. Our figures show a shorter period of black smoke, a longer period of moderate smoke, and a shorter period of no smoke at all.

div.head: NOT ONE DAY'S OBSERVATION.
div.p: NOT ONE DAY'S OBSERVATION.

That is not the observation of one day, or of a particular day, but is the result of a long series of observations 'taken from our books. Alderman Bennett makes the statement that the chimneys observed emitted dense smoke from 12 to-181 niinutes. On examination I find that of those chimneys only two came under our jurisdiction, and, those two belong to one firm. The majority of the chimneys that emitted black .smoke are 'not under the control of the Health Committee. Of the two chimneys that are under our control 'there were, in 1912, some 11 observations made, and on no occasion was the five minutes' limit exceeded. On one occasion, in 1913, the maximum was exceeded .and notice was immediately served. Since then three observations have been taken by our inspectors, and no offence has been com- mitted by those two chimneys. (Councillor PEMBERTON : Hear, hear.) That is, so far a„s we have been able to detect; we do not say that possibly there has been no offence, hut we have not been able to detect it. I think I can justify the lines of our procedure later on.

div.head: "CAREFUL OBSERVATION."
div.p: "CAREFUL OBSERVATION."

With regard to the phrasing of the report— this is rather important, if, we are to take this opinion seriously; I think we ought to do, as it is a serious ma,tter—with regard to the phrase in the " Examiner " report about "careful observation "—that is the word used—we find on looking over the records, given to the "Examiner," that our •friend from Manchester was taking observations of three chimneys at one time. (Laughter) If that is an indication, and we must accept it as such, of the careful manner in which the observations were taken with regard to the remaining chimneys, then we know the value to place upon that report. (Councillor PEMBER- TON : Hear, hear! Hear, hear!) We have nobody on our staff who can take observations of three chimneys at one time. Councillor PEMBERTON : Yours is only a War- rington man, and not from Manchester. . Alderman JAMES EVANS : I am glad 1 come from Warrington. I am. asked What steps the committee propose to take. I think I may venture to say the committee intend to pursue the steady course they have pursued in the past in regard to this question. ,

div.head: MANY OBSERVATIONS MADE
div.p: MANY OBSERVATIONS MADE
I find, on looking at the Manchester Corpora- tion report, that there are in Manchester five inspectors specially appointed to deal with the

div.head: SMOKE NOT INJURIOUS.
div.p: SMOKE NOT INJURIOUS.

It has never been proved—my friend,' Alder- man Bennett, will .not agree with me here—that smoke is particularly injurious to health. We have to consider that if any organs of the body suffer from smoke they are the respiratory' organs or lungs. Take our mortality from these diseases and compare it with the other towns referred to by the Smoke Abatement Associa- tion. I do not think Warrington will be found the black spot.

Compare it with Manchester, and you will find that in 1912 our death-rate from all causes was 14.5, and Manchester had 16.18. Our infan- tile mortality was 92, compared with, 122 in Manchester, and at the same time that index of prosperity, the birth-rate, in this town was 28.3, compared with 25.9 in Manchester. (Coun- cillor PEMBERTON : Hear, hear! Hear, hear!) If there are further questions to ask I shall be happy to answer them, as I consider the subject of great importance to the health and well-being of our town. (Applause.)

div.head: ALDERMAN BENNETT PRECLUDED.
div.p: ALDERMAN BENNETT PRECLUDED.

Alderman BENNETT : I should like to say some- thing, but I am precluded. The MAYOR: And I am precluded also. Alderman BENNETT expressed his thanks to Alderman Evans for his lengthy reply. There are, he, said, some points I would have taken particular pleasure in repudiating, but I must reserve that pleasure for another occasion. A great thing has been achieved if only a wide- Spread public interest is aroused. If there is a feeling that this is a serious question, we should advance steadily in the matter.

My friend has said that smoke was not proved to be injuriqus. I am not going to admit that, but I am not goiUg to, enter into a discussion upon it now. Is it not quite enough to say that it ie exceedingly unpleasant and unsightly, and it has eaused.so much ruin to buildings and so much trouble to people who wish to keep their houses clean? It also involves a great deal of monetary waste. Even the extra wash- ing it entails is quite a formidable figure. (Laughter.) NOT TO BE TAUGHT.

Councillor BROADHURST : I do not think we can be taught much by any man from Manchester; the men of Manchester cannot teach the town of Warrington anything. (Councillor PEMBER- TON : Hear, hear! Hear, hear! and laughter.) I was on a deputation some years ago to make an extenAive examination of the ,sanitary con- ditions of Manchester, and I came back with the report that Manchester could teach War- rington nothing. (Hear, hear.) As regards the smoke nuisance, Councillor Broadhurst went on, he thought they should support the Chairman of the Health Committee in what had been done. At the same time, he agreed that further progress Might be made in tackling the smoke nuisance. It was not suffi- cient that the Town Clerk or his deputy should simply serve statutory notices upon offending firms. They found that the same firm was re- Peatedly guilty of emitting black Smoke, but no strong actimt was taken. If the Council could not deal with offenders from the legal standpoint, they should endea- vour to bring moral suasion to bear. He ob- jected to the names of the firms upon whom notices were served appearing only on the private agenda, as the public ought to know who was responsible for the nuisance. He hoped something would be .done to make these matters more public. I do not think, added the Councillor, that the smoke complaints should be put on the private agenda. I hope the Council will publish the whole of the minutes of this description, and not place them in a confidential report. They should print the whole, so that the Press, and the " Examiner " in particular, which has 'taken such a strong attitude on the question, should let the public of Warrington know.

div.head: MAYOR'S VIEWS.
div.p: THE MAYOR'S VIEWS.

The MAYort. said: There is an old saying that a certain person is not so black as he is painted. In my Opinion that remark applies to smoke. What has given black smoke so bad a reputation is,because a great many noxious vapours are got rid of under-the cover of the black smoke. The tables to which Alderman Evans . has called attention give proof that although black smoke is ugly it might possibly be beneficial:. (Coun- cillor PEMBERTON : Hear, hear.) If all the pros and cons of the case are balanced up Carefully it is doubtful how far the germs of- pneumonia and tuberculosis might be rendered inert through being brought into contact and enveloped in black smoke. There is another point of view, and it is in regard to the domestic smoke. gore than one eminent -authority has held that more than half, if not two-thirds, of the smoke emitted is given off from house chimneys, and we should consider its influence.

I do not know the law with regard to Scot- land, but it strikes me as a very wise law. The smoke should he judged by volume rather than by colour, because many of the dangerous, irri- tating fumes which cause dangerous inflamma- tions of the respiratory organs are colourless.

div.head: 12,000 HOUSE FIRES.
div.p: 12,000 HOUSE FIRES.

Councillor PEMBERTON said he was going to deal. with the question of the house fires. There were 12,000 fires burning daily in private houses in Warrington, and the emission of smoke from chimneys which were only -one-fourth the height of factory chimneys must have a great effect on the atmosphere.

The Manchester inspector condemned himself by his own language, for, referring to the atmos- phere in Warrington, he stated that "it was so dense that it was like looking into the darkness of night." (Laughter.) A man who made such obviously untrue statements was not worth taking notice of. The Health Committee had ' attached too much importance to the whole thing. What he would like to see was a great many more chinineys. He wanted to know if the Health Committee, in accepting tenders for grates for the Aiken- street. Hospital, had made arrangements to con- sume the smoke. Councillor BIRTLES said that the black smoke was a great annoyance i and they knew the damage it did in their parks. He thought the house fires caused a lot of the smoke. Sir Wil- liam Richmond had said that by the adoption of the gas fires in London, a great deal had been done to 'remove fogs. Councillor ARCJIEII said a special committee

div.head: "ABOMINABLE NUISANCE."
div.p: "ABOMINABLE NUISANCE."
An Attempt to Abate the Smoke
Nuisance 76 Years Ago.

div.head: LOCAL MAN'S METHOD.
div.p: A LOCAL MAN'S METHOD.
" EXAMINER " SPECIAL.

Men may come and men may go, but the smoke nuisance' goes on for ever.. The cam- paign against this pest of ciVilisation, which the " Examiner " has been so vigorously wag- ing, and which Alderman Bennett has almost made his pet theme, is of no mushroom growth. It may Surprise some to learn that our fore- fathers waged a War against smoke, but, de- spite their efforts, we still have it--smoke. As far back as 1793 an anti-smoke campaign was initiated by an esay' writer, and he wrote most vehemently Of the then nuisance. . If he ablet d ion. fiNnVdarrilnapggtojragteo characterise what. exists: He was e.: man of genius; and suggested that common salt should be mixed with the coal, and thus prevent smoke arising. Benjamin • Franklin, about the same -day hee.r.: enough to. t 'night not be time, entered into the question, but, great writer and agitator as be was, Franklin failed to find a satisfactory solution for the problem.

div.head: WARRINGTON 76 YEARS AGO.
div.p: WARRINGTON 76 YEARS AGO.

‘l73ictor9act°h ascended The subject was fully discussed in a maga- zine baedr' 1837, or to the throne. The writer make § the statement that the smoke nuisance was then very pro. flounced article ispaufbtleirshQeudeoen n 13th nounced at Liverpool, Warrington, St. Helens, . &e., and, in fact, it was so in all the district lying • between Liverpool and Manchester. - "There is," he wrote, "a great nuisance to the public by' the dense smoke that is pouring out of the chimney stacks of the manufactories. ~

"An interesting experiment," the writer in the magazine adds, "has just been Made in these districts to see the practicability of at length gettipg entirely rid Of the abominable nuisance occasioned. by the volumes of smoke which is vomited fokh from our chimneys in such quantities.

"A Mr. Coad, of Liverpool, and Warrington, has invented a method to get rid of the nuis- the smoke in furnaces with the quan- ance. The new method of Mr. Coad consists of supplying' tity of heat that is necessary for perfect com- bustion, and that is effected in a very simple and ingenious manner.

div.head: THEN IDEA OF PREVENTION.
div.p: THE THEN IDEA OF PREVENTION.

"The apparatus (continued the writer of 76 years ago) consists of a series of small tubes or ithambers, so constructed as to expose a large surface to the Action of the heat, and is placed in the lower part of the chimney beyond the boiler. One end of the series communicates by an open orifice with the external air, 'while the other opens into a slit in the bridge of the furnace.

"That was the whole contrivance, and it acts thus: The . superfluous heat in tfle chimney raises the temperature of the iron tubegto a high degree, and the draught in the chimney causes a current of air to pass into the fire

_ through the other aperture, and consequently through the hot tubes. 'A current of hot air is thus thrown into the flame, and the effect is that a decomposition is promoted, and the flame and heat of the fire are much increased, and not ,a particle of smoke escapes from the top Of the stack." 'Whether the method was a success, is not known, and the editor of the magazine,. com- nienting upon the matter, makes the following cryptic remark: "It seems too good news to be true." The inventor and the inveniion have van- ished, arid we seem no nearer a solution qf the smoke probiern than they Were in 1837.

div.head: TRAIN ON FIRE RACE.
div.p: A TRAIN ON FIRE RACE.

. . While a goods train was proceeding Ifrom the Burnley district to Smithy Bridge on Sunday, the driver noticed as he was passing through Summit tunnel that a large , waggon, carrying about 200 empty skips, was on fire. He detached the waggon and drove it with all speed to Littleborough Station, a mile and-a half away. . The skips were then blazing fiercely, and the lire lit up the whole district. , The driver obtained assistance and the fire was extinguished; but not before considerable damage had been done.

COUNCILLORS' OBJECTIONS.
There was an interesting discussion on the new Town Hall scheme at a meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday night.

The Town Hall Committee recommended that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to prepare specifications and estimates for the extension ,of the Town Hall, by the erection of 'wings on the east and West sides'respectively, and also for a complete sCheme for municipal offices to embrace all departments of the Corporation, on the land behind Bank House, and the buildings occupied by the Health Department and the Education Committee. Councillor PEMBERTON .moved that it be re- ferred back. , It ought to have more careful consideration.

Councillor GOUGH seconded. Ho objected to no details being provided, and he did not know what it was intended to do with the sites in Sankey-street, which were valuable, tie thought the, resolution premature. The Chair- man of the committee was not present, but he hoped the members would agree to reconsider the matter and give the Council an opportunity of discussing it at a meeting of the Genent Purposes Committee.

div.head: TOO FOND OF MAKING WORK.
div.p: TOO FOND OF MAKING WORK.

Alderman TINNION thought some committees were too fond of throwing useless work on the Borough Surveyor's department, which had enough to do' of useful work. There were schemes which wei.e" pressing, but to ask for an extension of such importance in the manner Proposed was utterly ridiculous. This was a matter, which should nor be dealt with by a small committee. (Hear, hear.)

The MAYOR : • The matter has teen hanging fire for two years. Councillor BIRTLES thought the matter had been under the consideration of the Council for a long time, and nothing had been done. It was discussed as far back as the year 1892. He hoped the Council would take the matter in hand seriously, on account of the staff that was employed at the Town Hall. The rooms were too small to work in.

div.head: GAME OF SHUTTLECOCK.
div.p: GAME OF SHUTTLECOCK.

It was their duty, added Councillor Birtles, to look ahead. They wanted accommodation, and the Council should take the matter in hand seriously, and not tamper with it as they had been doing for so many years. If the Council had to consider the matter, let them do it in a large and far-seeing manner. Councillor DICKENSON : I thought the matter had been before the General Purposes Corn-

mittee. I learn that it has not been, and I, -therefore, prefer to withdraw the resolution. The MAYOR said the question would be re- ferred to. the General Purposes Committee. Councillor HENSHALL : That was done a year ago. • It is a game of shuttlecock. Alderman BEi+iNETT said a little delay was not much in a :scheme of such magnitude as that suggested. The Board of Guardians were talk- ing about building new central premises, and in connection with that scheme it might be pos- . , sible to aeconhnodate them and get them to share the expense. They had also heard rumours of the National Insurance Offices being transferred from Warrington because sufficient accommodation could not be found here, and he regarded the continuance of, these offices as of great benefit to the town. The MAYOR: That is not a municipal matter. Aldernian BENNETT : It might be possible to consider the three questiens together. The matter, was withdrawn.
New Version of Genesis.

A tablet dug up in the Nippur some years ago, has just been translated by Dr. Arno Pochel, of Pennsylvania University, who be- lie-es that he has unveiled the oldest story so far known of the creation. The tablet dates tack to ,the reign of Hammurabi, about 7,000 B.c. The record reads like a new version of Genesis, with this important difference, the creator of the world is described as a 'goddess and not a god. Dr. Poebel is engaged in check- ing his translation. He says the tablet depicts a goddess quite clearly, and speaks orf two male gods .as relatively unimportant. The tablet, we are assured, .givesiprobably the first, story of the world's creation,' and also the most won- derful accounts of civilisation in 7.100 B.C.

div.head: How large is a Raindrop?
div.p: How large is a Raindrop?

It. j not easy to determine the size of rain- drops on account of their wide variety. • The finest, are a verY small fraction of an inch in diameter, while the largest, as found in tropical countries, maybe .14 of an inch in diameter. Raindrops gre usually larger in summer than in winter, and for the same 'reason are larger in warm climates than in cold. The cause is plain. At the instant when watery vapour con- denses, small drops very close together aro formed, and under the influence Of gravity they fall. Yielding at the same time to molecular attraction, they come together as they fall, so that when they read' the .earth their size is in proportion to the distance they have fallen.

div.head: MR. LOMAX PREDICTS SUCCESS.
div.p: MR. LOMAX PREDICTS SUCCESS.
Eome Old Warrington Favouiites'

div.head: Favourites in the Making.
div.p: Favourites in the Making.
GREAT EXPECTATIONS.

Mr. Watford, Lomax, the producer and stage manager, who is occupying this important position for the Warrington Society for the fourth time, in an interview with an "Examiner" representative this week, dis- played the utmost confidence as to the outcome of his training. In the course of a large and varied experience, Mr. Lomax has managed, locally, "Tom Jones," "San Toy," and "Dorothy," and those who remember the suc- cess which attended those efforts will know not only that "Miss Hook" is in capable hands, but that the forecast of still higher triumphs for the Opera Section of the Musical Society, made by Mr. Lomax, may be accepted without reserve.
An early question on this point drew from Mr. Lomax the _emphatic statement:

"The company, as a whole, are improving year by year, and I havQ the utmost confidence in saying that all will do their best and will give a most pleasurable performance." "And what of the principals this year?" "Well," replied Mr. Lomax, "We have some well-tried Warrington favourites and :some new faces, with one, Miss Nellie Anderton, who returns, much to the general delight. Miss Anderton, who last appeared in -Warrington as Queen Elizabeth in "Merrie England," takes the title-role of Miss Hook, and her beautiful voice will be heard to great advantage in sev- eral delightful songs she sings during the opera."

It should be specially noted that Miss Ander- ton, though understood to be contralto, has been deliberately introduced in sing the part of the principal soprano. Experts declare that the beautiful effects of her voice in the upper register have been a revelation to all, including herself.

Mr. Lomax spoke with equal enthusiasm of the promised work of Miss Nellie Muffins. "Miss Mullins may always be relied upon to give an attractive performance, and for the part of Mina, upon whom falls a good propor- tion of the comedy of the play, she seems to be particularly well suited and will undoubtedly strengthen her hold upon Warrington audi- ences as the week proceeds." Mr. Fred Fieldhouse, Mr. Rabbitt and Mr. Bibby are others among the goodly company, classed, truly by Mr. Lomax, as•" old favour- ites."

"Mr. Babbitt," he remarked, " has the attractive part of the bandmaster, Van Vuyt, and he and Miss Anderton have some delightful duets. His song with the " Tra-la-la " refrain and chorus is sure to be one of the features of the first act."

Mr. Bibby. the dashing Captain Paap, has built up such a reputation in corresponding parts that his portrayal of this particular char- acter may be safely voted a succe§s in advance. Memories of his singing of such a song as -"I mean to introduce it into China" will induce a feeling of pleasurable anticipation of his singing next week of "Soldiers of the Nether- lands."
Mr. Fieldhouse as .Mr. Hook is, on the authority of Mr. Lomax, parlicularly well fitted for the part, and experience has taught' us to expect a perfect treat from Mr. Ficldhouse when this is so.

. Mr. Lomax has high, hopes respecting the newer principals—Mr. Davis, as Slinks ; Mr. S. L.. Partridge, as Schnapps; Mr. Hannan, as Van Eck; Miss Blackburn, as Freda Voos ; Miss L. Duckworth, a& tiara Voos ; and Miss-B. D. Bond, as Gretchen.

Mr. Davis, a well-known member of Cros- field's Opera Company, is regarded as a very welcome recruit by Mr. Lomax.. He takes the place of the humorous Mr. George Smith, and, Mr. Partridge assisting, and Mr. Hannan sup- porting, will ensure that the comic element sustains no loss.
Mr. Hannan, who plays the part of a mule. Win Eck, and acts by Means of facial expres- sion, is held to be the right man in the right place.

div.head: TIIE CHORUS.
div.p: TIIE CHORUS.

"Needless to say," was Mr. Lomax's verdict on the work of the chorus, "I consider the chorus vocally is much better than ever. They do the stage business, which is probably more elaboraie than anything they have been called upon to do before, with a briskness and ease that is really very highly commendable."

div.head: SCENERY AND COSTUMES.
div.p: SCENERY AND COSTUMES.

The country is Holland, sleepy Holland, with its miles of tulip fields and innumerable wind- mills. The first act is in the cheese market at Arndyk, and some delightful and characteristic specimens of Dutch landscape and architecture are presented. There will be a brilliant scene when the curtain goes up, for the .old Market Place is peopled by dozens of Dutch girls and men in the picturesque costume of the country. These are from the eminent firm of B. J. Simmons and Co., Covent Garden, London. The second act reveals the interior of Mr. livoles distillery at Amsterdam, .and a pro- minent feature is a great display of bottles of the celebrated liqueur, "Cream of the Sky," the recipe for which is lost and restored u9der the most humorous circumstances of the opera. The scenery has been painted by Messrs. Rbbinson, of the Ark, Liver Pool, and Mr. Lomax says prettier, more 'attractive or com- plete pictures have never been staged in War- rington. Mr: Lomax paid a tribute to the work of Mr. Crossley, the musical director, and Mr. War- , burton, the acting manager of the theatre, who, as usual, has given freely of his invaluable assistance.

Who spoke in London about Warrington Women Tariff Reform Leaguers, 6,000 strong, preparing to receive into their homes the women and children of Ulster, while their. men folk were engaged defending their liberty—and so on, and so on, in a rather monotonous manner? Who was it came down to Walton Hall and repeated
the same curious suggestion in the friendly
surroundings of a garden party given in honour of , the same Women Tariff Reformers? And

Wfio has been in Warrington for a long week- end and has refrained from saying one word on the subject to the men folk, whoswould have to pay the cost of finding the accommodation if it were ever needed? If the suggestions about Ulster have been laughed out of:court, at all events those who have been made to
laugh must not be blamed.
But to returi to serious politics. Mr. SAME concentrated on Home Rule; he wishes to con- centrate on Home Rule at the next General

Election. He asks Mr. CROSFIELD to eliminate 1 other questions, and to fight on. the Irish question alone. Tariff Reform, like all 'else, goes by the board. Poor .Tariff Refarm! On Home Rule Mr. SAIMI will fight until " the. last vote is dropped in the ballot box." in War- rington. That, at any rate, is nicer than fighting till the last .man is dropped in the last ditch in Ulster. • Poor Tariff Reform, that was
-to save the country from itself !- It was. in a

poor way when it was shipped, to the Colonies.; it must" be in a worse plight when, in War- rington, with its ruined industries doing record trade and paying record dividends, the Member deems it vie to offer to throw it overboard altogether.
i-iMERICAN DEMOCRATS AND FREE TRADE.

Tariff Reformers persistently deny that the revised American tariff is- in any sense a Free Trade measure. They are better informed, it would seem, than Americans themselves. -The following ,is an extract from the "Pittsburgh Chronicle," of September 10th, a strong Repub- lican journal :

Its characterisation as a Free Trade measure is legitimate, inasmuch as, in the first place, the free list is extended as far as the law-makers dare extend it; and, s,..,condly, its framers make no secret of their purpose of making this measure an entering wedge with a view to bringing about Abso- lute Free Trade in the sequel in case the country stands for the Democratic policies.

The "American Economist," the organ of the American Protective Tariff League, speaks in ~an exactly similar strain. On every page it insistently asserts that the new'tariff is nothing else than Free Trade in its beginning. The following extract, taken from the issue of September 19th, is typical

The final passage of the Bill as amended in the Senate is now a foregone conclusion. Some minor changes will be agreed upon in the Conference Committee, but the radical Free Trade character of the Bill will remain unchanged as it reaches the President and receives his signature.

Naturally, to the British . Tariff Reformer, Inconvenient quotations, like inconvenient statistics, are " untrustworthy," but to the average individual the opinion of Americans themselves will be conclusive. •

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 11, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 11, 1913.
TH PASSING tE' K.
THE SMOKE QUESTION.

We are pleased to think that the Town Coun- cil on 'Tuesday night recognised the importance of the smoke problem so much that the mem- bers, by the kindly consideration. of the Mayor, indulged in a: brief discussion upon a question which, according to the Standing Orders, ought to stand undiscussed. It was clear by what was said that the question is attracting atten- tion in official quarters, as it undoubtedly is in unofficial circles. It' was alsO clear, however, that some people are incapable of 'seeing the difference between retaining trade in the town with a minimum of smoke, and giving our- selves up helplessly in the presence of a reck- less maximum output. "We must have the smoke or ruin the town," is an attitude that will in time give waS- before knowledge. .For our part we have no other desire than to see the industries of the town thrive. We, how- ever, do not wish to see the inhabitants of the place living in a poisoned atmosphere; and, being in possession of facts which prove in- contestably that much of the smoke from which we suffer is not only unnecessary, but a waste to the manufacturer who turns it out, we say that , some systematic effort should be made to bring about the desired improvement. There are firms in town who are making real and sub- stantial efforts to redrire their output of smoke,l and we. are sure they will receive the' utmost consideration not only from the Health Corn- ' mittee, but from that public opiniOn which will sooner or later cOndemn the real culprits with emphasis and effect. Some conflict appears. to .exist between the smoke reformers and the authorities as to those upon whom the Onus of proof falls in respect Of the' places that may claim exemption from the operation of the Public Health Act. Do the manufacturers have to prove that they cannot reduce their smoke without damaging their business, or- do the authorities have to prove that they can? It is a small matter that would easily be settletl when once we got to business in earnest. Here is an expert opinion upon 'one ;TAT point, at all events, given by Mr. William Nicholson, chief smoke inspector to the city of Sheffield:— There is a general impression abroad that • all kinds of furnaces are exempted in the Public Health Act. Some. go further and say emphatically that the municipal author- ity has no power over them', or as they often say, cannot touch them. . As a matter of fact, the Act does deal with the matter, and the authorities have power to control furnaces the same as boilers.

Early yesterday morning the keystone of the centre arch, that was laid with so much pomp and Masonic cere- monial in 1836, as described in "The Examiner" of the periodPtetililr 27th, was removed An account of hsays that the stone, which weighed 12 cwt., had a space in its side, inki which was placed a glass box, containing gold, silver and copper coins of that and the previous reign, and a Masonic medal. The cavity was secured with cement. The cement was left untouched yesterday and the stone was carefully stored at the Town Hall _intact. It is the intention of the Mayor to have the seal broken this morn- ing in the presence of a company interested in the bridge. The Mayor has invited the Wor- shipful Masters of the five local Masonic lodges to witness the ceremony. In the course of putting in( le foundation of the second section of the new bridge, a buttress of the bridge of 1495—the original Warrington Bridge, built by the th-e—n Earl of Derby—has been exposed. It is in an exceptionally good state of preservation.

'HEAVY MOTOR TRAFFIC. When the motor car begun to assert itself, and make itself into a nuisance, it fell to the lot of the writer, along with others, to protest against the use to which our roads were being put. For ir time opposition to ttle motor car cad some effect, but eventually interests pre- vailed, and the motor car monopolised the land and roads It contains. How completely the road hogs have .possession of the road p now can be seen during the holiday season, when ordinaq pedestrians can be seen crouching in hedge backs that skirt the main roads in, say, North Wales, while these lords on wheels dash by, leaving dust and smell—and curses—in their wake. Now we have advanced a step, ana the recent strike has brought heavy motors with train loads behind them, which have shaken our houses to their foundations, and further reducaL the value of Properly. Councillor Locker drew attention to the frightful infliction from which we are suffering, and are likely to suffer. In fact, the question arises, Where are these vehicles to draw the line? Is there even worse to follow? We are afraid there is. The suggestion made is that new roads should be made,' specially suited for this dangerous, un- pleasant traffic. Perhaps the owners of motors will suggest that we should leave them the old roaas, and make new ones for 'ourselves. The existilg roads 'really belong to the motors.
A HYMN OF CONCILIATION.
By permission of the Daily News."

Lord of the world,' Who didst beget This maiden sister of the sea, Lone Erin, mid Thy ocean set, And born, like ocean, fiercely free, Who bast preserved her wondrous chaste, And' not less lovely for her woes,— Au, bast Thou milled that she should taste Of all things save repose?

We cannot live for evermore With nought but " Nay " upon our tongue, And ever hear a voice imnlorev And ever vaunt a heart unwrung. She cries aloud and will not cease; She bids us blush for all the past. If what she craws can bring her peace, Oh, be it hers at last.

No matter by what name 'tis called, If it be sire of nobler days. Perhaps too long we shrank appalled And fled in terror from a phrase. Thou know est all Thy daughter's breast, And all its inmost dreams dost know. If what she craves can bring her rest, Lord, help us to bestow! WILLIAM WATSON.

div.head: WORKERS AND EDUCATION.
div.p: WORKERS AND EDUCATION.

It is pleasing to learn that the local branch of the Workers' Educational Association has been formed in circumstances which .are ex- ceedingly promising.. The, formalities were gone through on Thursday, ad last flight the first meeting of the tutorial .class that is to gather every Friday night at .the Technical In- stitute, under the direction of Mr. .1. U. Nlphol- son, a Liverpool University „tutor, was held. There were 47 candidates fOr. the 32 places. Other practical work has also been acCom: plished. For instance, Dr. Stanley Mellor has arranged to conduct a philosophy class at Cairo-street School; fortnightly. from October 15th. "The Republic of Plato" is his text bbok, aria fhb lecture will be followed by discussion and essays. A reading circle on the subject of the living wage and the cost of living is to be held at the offices of the Guild of Help.

div.head: TO-NIGHT'S INFIRMARY CONCERT.
div.p: TO-NIGHT'S INFIRMARY CONCERT.

To-night the. 'Working Men's Infirmary Com- mittee open, as they usually do, the concert season at Parr Hall. A remarkably fine pro- gramme has been arranged, and the concert, NV/licit will be under the patronage of tlie Mayor, the President. of the Institution. (Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart.), the Board of Manage- ment, and other friends of the Infirmary, will be the all-round success it generally is. Mr. T. J. Down's orchestra • will appear in aid of the committee's funds for the 25th consecutive time, a fine record of good deeds that have brought the best of results. 'Last year the concert Pro- duced '£37 155., against £33 the previous year. We hope there will be another advance this evening.

War Frees Turkish Women.

Women in Turkey are fast becoming eman- cipated from their slave-like existence of cen- turies. The spread of education and the war between Turkey and the allies have opened new avenues of employment to women through the loss of thousands of men; and the Turkish women of to-day enjoy far greater freedom than they did five years ago. HEARTBREAK. Fie, for shame! To curse all women Just because one broke your heart! Would you go and drop to nothing? Still there's life, and work, and art.
Pluck up courage, give up grieving, Come and join the world of men. Somewhere there's another waiting Who will break your heart again!
FROM BENCH TO PULPIT.
The Rev. Frank Melville was on Saturday inducted as vicar of High Crompton, .near Old- ham.

The'Vicar has had an interesting career, hav- ing risen from the engineering bench to the pulpit. He was' apprenticed to the engineering trade as a youth, working at the bench, and on the various machines in the fitting room, and afterwards in the moulding department knd in the pattern room. Whilst at work he studied fiard and fitted himself to go to Oxford, where he took his M.A. degree, and was ordained in 1894.
Mr. Henry Frederick Beaumont, a former Yorkshire M.P., and a landowner in the Hud- dersfield district, died at his Tetworth residence, Ascot, aged 80.
Two hundred girls escaped by an emergency exit and fire escape from the printing works of Messrs. Keene and Co., Hull, which were totally destroyed by fire.
The rumour connecting the name of Mr. Lloyd George with the Mayoralty of-Carnarvon for the coming year, is, according to a •Carnarvon cor- respondent, without foundation.

div.p: HEAVY MOTOR TRAFFIC.
The Mayor's House Shaken as by an Earthquake.

div.head: UNIVERSAL COMPLAINTS.
div.p: UNIVERSAL COMPLAINTS.
Demand for a Special Road to
Spare the Town.

The motor plague, which seems to affect Warrington more than most towns, through it being on the main road between Liverpool and Manchester, was discussed at a meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday. The matter arose through a report that the Paving and Sewerage Committee had consid- ered the great damage being done to the roads, and stated that they recommended that the Borough Surveyor prepare a report 01-1 the matter, with a view to application being made Lo the Boat! Board for a 'special granti-and that the Chairman, the Borough Surveyor and the Town Clerk be empowered to,wait upon the Board with regard thereto. Councillor LOCKER, in supporting this, said that in the vicinity of Manchester-road he had found the heavy motor traill6 passing to be a serious mailer ; it was so serious as to consti- tute a pest. It was time the Corporation took action. There' was an almost continuous stream of motor tratc, day and night, and the inhabit- ants along the line of route from the Cemetery to the Sankey Bridges Must have some very Un- pleasant hours. Seeing that they had an Act of Parliament which was supposed to proVide money for new roadS, the Corporation had 'splendid grounds on which to approach the Roads Board. He hoped that at an early date they wohld consider the possibilities of a scheme for diverting the main-road traffic so that it would not pass through Warrington. Recently he was in a house in Manchester-road•wheA a heavy motor , vehicle passed, and, although the property 'was soundly built,, the vibration was so severe that he would not care to live in it.

div.head: MAYOR'S INVITATION.
div.p: THE MAYOR'S INVITATION.
The MAYOR: I am afr.aid I shall be wanting a new house soon. I should like a deputation to come and spend the night with me.

• Alderman TINNION : I propose that we accept the invitation for to-night. (Laughter.) The MAYOR: Nearly every flight my house is shaken as if by an earthquake through the passing of so many heavy motor vehicles. . Councillor LOCKER: The vibration is terrible. Councillor OSBORNE said something ought to be done. He had a similar 'experience as the Mayor. The people who fived in Arpley-Street were also, complainipg bitterly of the diversion of traffic down that thoroughfare.

Something should be done as suggested by Councillor Locker, in the same way. that the Cheshire Lines Committee diverted part of their railway traffic from Manchester to Liverpool, so ns to miss Warrington. It was .not right that. Warrington should be saddled with the expense of ' maintaining the rOads, and 4t‘ the same time have to tolerate such -a 'nuisance. COuncillor HAWTHORN said a great deal of heavy motor- trafii was recently occasioned by the Ship Canal str 'e at Manchester. . . Councillor LOCKE : But it is continuous be- sides that. ,

Councillor PEMBERTON .thought the remedy was for the Town Planning Committee -to pre- pare a scheme for a new road that would miss Warrington altogether. Alderman TINNION said neither the roads nor the sewers were constructed with a view to such heavy traffic passing over them-; in fact, it was never dreamed of when these were made. The suggestion was adopted.

div.head: MR. PARKER'S SUGGESTION.
div.p: MR. PARKER'S SUGGESTION.
How the Town Might be Avoided by Means of a New Road.

Sir —I wish, through the Press, to bring be- fore the people of Warrington a subject which I deem to be of great and growing importance. I refer to the question of the through-road traffic. With the growing increase of touring cars and heavy motor traffic the congestion in our main streets is becoming very Marked. The through heavy motor traffic, both by day and night, is steadily on the increase. This heavy motor traffic is a source of considerable dan- ger, delay, and inconvenience. The damage by vibration to all the property in the streetS through which it passes is considerable. At present all the through 'traffic between Liver- pool and the Manchester district comes right through the heart of Warrington, to the incon- venience, loss and expense of the town. The idea I wish to bring before your readers is surely one that has occurred to many, but if it has been publicly mentioned and discussed it has escaped my notice. My proposal is so self-evident that it is surprising that it has not as far as I know, received public consideration. It is simply this: that just as the Cheshire Lines Railway Company, while serving 'the town by its loop line through ,the Central Station, have constructed a straight line outside the town for its through traffic, in like manner, while allow- ing the road through Sankey Bridges, Sankey- street, Buttermarket-street, Church-street, &c., to serve the town, a new road on the northern boundary should. be constructed to take the through traffic. What Course such a road should follow is a question for engineers, but one natural course would seem to me that the road on the west should begin at the Penketh- lane Ends ;this would serve any traffic from Wid- nes and Runcorn Bridge. It would then make, for Folly-lane Bridge, to get across the L. and N.-W. Railway. It would approaCh this bridge by joining the road at the point where the Cheshire Lines cross over Folly-lane. Affer crossing the bridge it could use the present road in front of the Barracks, and join the Alanchester-road somewhere in Padgate. An- other, and as it seems to be a bolder and better, plan would be to leave the main Liver-. pool-road before it crosses the Cheshire Lines Railway near Sankey Station, and follow the straight course alongside the railway, crossing the L. and N.-W. Railway by Folly-lane Bridge, and instead of bending towards the Barracks keep straight on, on the north side of the Cheshire Lines, and join the Manchester-road. beyond Padgate. Both routes suggested .would be shorter than the present road, the. latter decidedly shorter. But it is unnecessary at such a stage to enter into details. The desira- bility ,of such a road must' be obvious to all, and it ought to receive the consideration of the Town Council, Chamber of Commerce, Rural District Council, and • similar bodies, and be urged upon the- Road Development Board. The danger to foot passengers is an impor- tant consideration. Last week we had the record of three children killed by road convey- ances. It is true these were not in the route referred to, ,but wherever there is much road traffic the danger exists, and anything that will lessen the number of road vehicles passing through thickly, populated areas lessens the danger. A .pedestrian can avoid a single Vehicle, but' accidents generally occur when the attention is confused with two vehicles, or one overtaking another. L trust the matter will receive the atteAtion it deserves, as I feel sure if not tackled speedily the diflicultieS will increase every week. Pro- perty,is• probably being built on some land where the road would be constructed, which. ever course it took, and this is increasing the cost of the land required. CHATILE E. PARKER.
,Penlceth, October 7th; 1013. • •• P.S.--.Since writing the above, I hear that the, question has occupied the attention of the Council, on the initiative of Councillor Locker.

div.head: Health Committee's Duties and Maniacturers' Duties.
div.p: Health Committee's Duties and Maniacturers' Duties.
ALDERMAN EVANS CONFOUNDS
THE TWO.
Legal Ot
A discussion upon the smoke question, c. 3 raised In the columns of "The Examiner," took place in the Council on Tuesday night.
Alderman James Evans entered upon a defence of the Health' Committee, but, as will ba seen by our article below, his arguments were not convincing.

•Mr. Alderman James Evans, chairman of the Health Committee, begins his defence for ex- cessive smoke by assuring the Council that the question is a most difficult one. We agree. So is the question of tuberculosis and several others, which his own committee are energetic- ally tackling. It has its difficulties, but, as far as the Health Committee is concerned, their task is simple, viz., to protect tile public by the faithful administration of the Public Health Act of 1875, which says:

Any chimney (not being the chimney of a private dwelling-house) sending forth black smoke in such quantity as to be a nuisance, shall be deernv obe nuisances liable to be dealt with summarily in manner provided by this Act.

The Health Committee's duty is to trie public. Why should its Chairman burden himself with the difficulties of manufacturers? It is with the manufacturers that these rest, not with the Health Committee. There is no difficulty in a manufacturer equipping his plant ta produce power .ecenomically, and the best evidende of his success is that it does not produce black smoke. *o far so good. The difficulties arise when manufacturer S want more power than their boilers can produce economically; hence overworked boilers and black smoke.' A fur- ther dillichlty arises from a too prevalent idea that any sort, of a labourer can economically fire a boiler ;, the rate of remuneration is often .too low to command the intelligence required to fire economically, which means a minimum of black smoke. Further causes of black smoke emission might be mentioned, but all are within the province of the, manufacturer, and outside that, of the Chairman of the Health Committee. If Alderman Evans would give more considera- tion to the difficulties and hardships which the householder has to endure from unnecessary* smoke, and leave the manufacturers to tackle their own difficulties, he would better fulfil the trust' which he has voluntarily taken up on behalf of the public. •

div.head: BLACK SMOKE.
div.p: BLACK SMOKE.

The Chairman goes on to say that the Act speaks of black smoke, "it must be black, and not merely dense." There can be no dense smoke that is not black. The black constitu- ency of smoke is unburnt carbon. When the carbon is burnt (as it ought to be if full heat value is to be got from the coal heat), what is left in the 'form of brown smoke is not denk, it is thin, can almost always be seen through; and varies in its shades .of brown according to its constituents. There is no prac- tical means known by which this brown smoke can be altogether prevented, and it is not classed as a nuisance under the Act.

. The Alderman then proceeds to give the num- ber of chimneys, which, he says, are, " to all intents and purposes, exempt from Section 91 in the Public Health Act." We have already given the main feature of Section 91 of this Adt, which begins with "Any chimney," &c. Instead of laying emphasis on the main section, the Alderman lays his emphasis on the exception, which is as follows :-

That where a person is summoned before any Court in respect of a nuisance arising from a fireplace or furnace, which does not consume the smoke arising from the com- bustible used in such fireplace or furnace, THE COURT shall hold that no nuisance Is created within the meaning of this Act, and dismiss the complaint, if IT IS SATIS- FIED that such fireplace or furnace is con- structed in such manner as to consume as far as practicable, having regard to the nature of the manufacture or trade, all smoke arising therefrom, and that such fire- place or furnace has been carefully attendcd to by the person having the charge thereof.

div.head: SPECIAL CONSIDERATION: COMMITTEE OR
div.p: SPECIAL CONSIDERATION: COMMITTEE OR
COURT?

It will be seen that before any manufacturer can claim consideration he has to prove before a Court that he has done all that is practicable, and the Court has to be satisfied before it. dis- misses the complaint. Now what has our War- rington Health Committee done? It has assumed the duties of the Court, has, on its own Initiative, without any inquiry (except possibly the opinion of certain members of the Health Committee), with one clean sweep put beyond Its control 87 of (he Warrington chimneys, the very chimneys which create most of the smoke. The Alderman also makes reference to Section 334, which defines the special trades to which a hard and fast time limit shall not apply, if by such application the efficient working in these trades is ob- structed. The two. sections may be taken together. The main section provides that the public (in this case through the Health Com- mittee) can exercise control over all chimneys other than domestic, and Sub-section 91 and Section 334, which provides that certain'indus- tries can get special consideration riy proving before a Court that their t ades cannot be satis- factorily carried on witho it this consideration. The Warrington Health Committee, in altering the venue from the Court to themselves, have adopted a course which was never intended, or provided for, by the Act, awl has not been fol- lowed by other towns, unless they have a back- ward authority. In regard to the 87 chimneys excluded, we are under the impression if this figure were checked by those acquainted with the law, the number would be considerably reduced. ,

It may be contended that it is useless for the committee to bring before the .Courts cases in which the manufacturers would be Ole to prove they are entitled to special consideration. This may be true in some cases, but the authority are .not justified in taking for granted in the wholesale manner they I-lave adopted, noi are they justified in assuming' that it is impossible for these manufacturers to abate the smoke by intelligent investigation, and at the instiga- tion ,and with the. co-operation of the Health Committee. We deprecate legal action • unless, absolutely necessary, but it is folly to act and talk as if you had not the power. Even if unable to bring the black smoke down to the general Council limit, this is no reason why the Health Committee should ignore such an important tutor in' smoke pro- duction. For example, if in some works it were impossible to conform to the five min- utes' limit; there is no reason \illy, say, ten minutes' should not be thefr limit. How ridicu- lous is the position created by the Health Corn- rittee. Here is a law designed for, and impable of, protecting the public' from air Pol- lution by excessive smoke, every work's boiler fire and furnace is under the law, special con- sideration may be claimed in the case of 'certain furnaces. This .last has been seized upon by our local authority, and used as a means of de- feating the main object of the Act. They have voluntarily surrendered' their powers, adopted a limitation of their authority never intended, and for which there is no sanction in the Act. They Continued in next column

div.head: Diarrhoea Decreasing.
div.p: Diarrhoea Decreasing.

With the departure of the warm weather the deaths from diarrhcea are decreasing in Warrington, and only one was recorded last week. The deaths numbered 18, of which seven were males and 11 females. The rate was 12.6, compared with 9.9 i the same week last year.

div.head: Parr Hall Organ Tenders.
div.p: Parr Hall Organ Tenders.

The Parr Hall Committee of the Corporation yesterday afterneon, received the report of Mr. W. H. Payton on the 22 tenders for the new organ. They selected .a tender to be submitted to the General Purposes Committee on Mon- day. The estimate of .21,500 is not likely to be exceeded.

A Well-known Antiquary. A well-known local antiquary in the person of Mr. Thomas May, of Walton-road, Stockton Heath, is leaving town next Tuesday for Creif, Perthshire. Mr. May was formerly an Inland Revenue superviser, and has accomplished a great deal in excavating the old Roman remains in Wilderspool-causeway, specimens of which are to, be seen in the Museum.

Increased Rate of Insurance Benefit. The National Health Insurance Commission ask the " Examiner " to draw attention to the fact that, under the National Insurance Act, the rate of sickness benefit for insured persons who have entered insurance between the ages of 50 and 70 is raised, as from October 13th, to the same full rate as for younger persons, viz., 10s. a week for men, and 7s. 6d. for women.

div.head: Warrington Leather Trade.
div.p: Warrington Leather Trade.

The trade during the week; says "The Leather World," was of _ very fair dimensions, and of all-round character, and contract deliveries, which have tended to get into arrears for long past, absorbed much of the . production. At the same time the amount of new business offer- ing is 'rather disappointing, and is not develop- ing at the. rate One 'expects in the 'autumn.

div.head: Lapsed Commitmeiit Order.
div.p: A Lapsed Commitmeiit Order.

A question of a lapsed commitment order was raised in Warrington County Court on Wed- nesday. It was staled that the order had lapsed without the debtor having gone to prison. Mr. White asked for a pronouncement as to whether the lapsing of the order prevented the issue of a fresh judgment summons, and applied for a , fresh summons. This Judge Stanger granted, on the condition that it did not establish a precedent.

• Labourer's Claim Fails. Peter Newton (60), labourer, 14, NOrman- stneet, sought, at Warrington County, Court. on Thursday, compensation for injurieS he alleged he had met with in the warehouse of the Bishop Wharf Carrying Co.-, He averred that in ware- housing some boxes he received a rupture and was unable to work. Defendants pleaded that they were not advised of the accident within the legal .limit of time, and on that ground Judge Stanger gave judgment to the employers.

div.head: " What Man May Be."
div.p: " What Man May Be."

Under the ausp-ices of the New Church the Rev. T. howartii, Bolton, commenced a series of lectures in the Masonic Hall on Tuesday night. The subject was "What man is; what he may be." In every sphere of life, he said, they were asking for what purpose they were and for what did they exist? Scientists, philo- sophers and great thinkers had striven to tell what man is. Their answers were lofty, pro- found and suggestive, but did not solve the solution. Man. was much more than a material structure. In him was a type of all that had preceded him in the order of the creation. Man was a living soul, attached for the time to a material body, fitting him to inhabit a material world. It was because of that the Lord showed such merciful care and faithful guardianship of man.
United Kingdom Band of Hope Union.

The 45th Autumnal Convention has been held at Dover, when over 900 delegates, appointed by the various Band of Hope Unions through- out the country, have been assembled.. The proceedings opened by a large demonstration of children of the Kent Union in Connaught Park, followed by a civic reception of the dele- gates by the Mayor of Dover in the Town Hall. On Sunday special services were held in all places of worship in the Kent -Union area. Mr. Lionel Mundy, chairman of the U.K.8.H.U., pre- sided at the first conference, and spoke of the progress of the movement during the past year, the Band of Hope members now numbering close on •four millions, embodied in the 33,324 societies.

div.head: Working Men's Mission Women's Bible Class.
div.p: Working Men's Mission Women's Bible Class.

The members of the class celebrated their eighth anniversary on Wednesday evening. About 100 sat down to tea, after which a con- cert was. held. Mrs. Owen, of Penketh, •pre- sided, in the unavoidable absence of Mrs. and Miss Crosfield, president and vice-president. The minstrel troupe, consisting of eight members in fancy attire, made much merriment. by their humorous songs and recitations, and were re- called. .Mrs. Owen delighted all with two readings, one tragic and the other humorous. Mrs. Beadow gave a laughable recitation on husband and wife doing each other's work for .a day.. Mrs. Moore read the annual report, which was very. cheering. ..Much has been accomplished during the year by the sick and absentee visitors, and the class has encouraged the , leader by their regular attendance, the Feb Band of Hope, members now numbering close -On • four millions,, embodied in the presiding.
Workers' Educational Association.

A keener interest which is being taken in the Workers' Educational Association, War- rington 'Branch, was manifested on Thursday evening, at a meeting held at the Town Hall. Mr. 3. Men were outside more and got more news, hut she urged wOmen to read educational books. The, W.E.A. offered ,them ample facilities for in- creasing their education.

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS%
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS%
-- ROYAL COURT THEN). RE.
"WHEN KNIGHTS WERE BOLD."

'Despondency cannot rule when this great farce is about, and "When Knights NN ere Bold," at the -Court Theatre this week,, is u liner anti- dote for melancholia Man all medicine can pre- 'scribe. In the farce' line it is a masterpiece— one long laugh from start to finish. Bored with accounts of what his noble ancestors did, Sir Guy. De Vere sleeps and dreams. in dream- land he goes back, to Norman times,' meets his retainers, Ifights a battle,' and generally does things which keeps the audience under the spell of merriment for a couple of hours. James! Welch's famous farce has been con- densed to meet the requirements of the two

houses a night system, find the condensation is an+ improvement. The fun is fast and furious. As Sir Guy, Mr. Arthur Stanley shows himself a born humorist, and is a, most able successor to Mr. James Welch, the /Creator of the part. Miss Isla Glyn is a graceful Lady flowenia, and all the other parts are in capable hands.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODIMME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODIMME.

nighter, and the mind-reading, duck adds to a .ighly diverting turn. Gray and White have ~number of new gags, whilst the'Schellot Bros.

perform clever acr;b7atics—itc-`;S—li-a.d—o-w—land—;.; Wyllie the. trzinip musician, makes a welcome reappearance. Jeannie Pullin, as a droll contedian,, is a huge .success. Rosie Pink cap- tivates with her breezy songs,. and indeed the whole show is exceedingly good.. •

div.p: THE ADULT SCHOOLS.
Interesting Address on the History of Trade Unionism.

At the Academy-street Men's School on Sun- day morning Dr. Stanley Mellor gave a lectur- ette on "Science and Religion." Dr. Mellor demonstrated that science and religiOn are not so antagonistic as is generally accepted.

div.head: BENoiSEY MEN'S.
div.p: BENoiSEY MEN'S.

• The Social Club was opened for the season on Saturday night by a billiard handicap. There were several exciting and keenly con- tested games, the victory eventually resting with John Bennett, who beat Fred. Hinchcliffe in the final.

On Sunday the school welcomed a visit of Mr. Taylor, of the Higher Openshaw, School, Manchester. The subject in the morning was on "Child Life." In the afternoon Mr. Taylor addressed. the Women's School.

div.head: SANKEY BRIDGES MEN'S.
div.p: SANKEY BRIDGES MEN'S.

Mr. Jos. Elwell gave the first of a series of lecturettes on "The History of Trade Union- ism." Trade unions existed, said the speater, in the Roman Empire. The earliest record we have in English history of men binding them- selves together for the protection of common interests was in the time of Alfred the Great. Mr. Elwell traced briefly the part played by the CraftS Guilds, describing the Black Death and its effects on wages, land laws and social life generally. The speaker gave a brief refer- ence to the chartists, ancl:'„ the growth ' Of the Trades Congress movement, mentioning. the interesting fact that Warrington was: repre- sented at the first Trades Congress by a Mr. Ashton.

An interesting discussion followed, in which the President said that the real spirit of the solidarity and fraternity in the trade unions was not to be learned from the party news- paper; one had to ,be a member to understand that there is a power much stronger than party politics amongst the workers.
