div.p: STOCKTON HEATH WOMEN'S.

The Sewing Class was held on Monday even- ing. Mrs. F. Cox, of Mersey-street, is conduct- ing a fancy sewing class this winter, which is well attended and much appreciated. On Thursday evening the usual Bible lesson was taken by Mrs. W. H. Sherburn.

div.head: NOVA SCOTIA'S COAL INDUSTRY.
div.p: NOVA SCOTIA'S COAL INDUSTRY.

With the immediate expenditure of a large sum of money for the further development of the valuable coal areas owned by the Maritime Coal Railway and Power Company at Joggins and Chignecto, Nova Scotia, it is stated officially that the new machinery and plant which are being installed will cause the output of the mines to be more than doubled and the cot of production to be greatly reduced.

div.head: MAYOR-ELECT.
div.p: THE MAYOR-ELECT.
Councillor Peter Peacock's Friendly Society Work.
CORDIAL RECOGNITI ON.

'1 he high esteem in which the Mayor-elect (Coundillor Peacock) is held by members of Warrington friendly societies was illustrated at the annual bowling prize distribution of the Loyal Ancient Order of Shepherds at the Blue Bell Hotel on Wednesday evening. Councillor Peacock was most enthusiastically received, the members joining lustily in sing- ing. "For he's a jolly good fellow." Major Potter, who' presided, said they, were all pleased to have the Mayor-elect With [hem. (Applause.) They heartily welcomed Councillor Peacock as a member of friendly societies. He (the speaker) thought that was the first public function Councillor Peacock had attended since he had' been selected as the Mayor. (Applause.) They could depend on men like - their Mayor- elect.

div.head: COUNCILLOR PEACOCK'S INTERESTING
div.p: COUNCILLOR PEACOCK'S INTERESTING
RETROSPECT.

Councillor Peacock said he owed almost everything to friendly society work, which he joined when he was 1.6: He was the first Mayor-elect of Warrington who was actually a benefit member of a friendly society. (Applause.) If he \V as off ill whilst he was in the Mayoral chair he, could„ go to the Foresters and the other societies • and claim his -10 s. or 18s.- per week. (I,aughtee.) The friendly Society people had enabled him to win one or two municipal elections, for he had always had' the hearty support of the bulk of friendly society -members in the wards in which he had contested.
The Future.
Now_ he was being raised to the _position of

liief Magistrate or the town, ad he could assure them that he would .endeavour to be a credit and a pride to Trie societies. He was glad to know that the Loyal Ancient Order of Shepherds had been able to withstand
the heavy strain during the year, for he under- stood that notwithstanding the excessive claims they had had they were still thriving,' 'and he hoped it would continue in. that direc-

ion in the future., Social affairs like that fos- ;ered a better feeling aniongst the members. IC was one of the first in the Warrington Dis- xict of -Foresters to institute an annual bowi- ng main, and this year two ,bowling mains lad been played successfully. (Applause.) fie horoUghly appreciated the remarks of Major Potter: (Renewed applause and prolonged. theers.).

Mr. J. Fulton-Smith said they saw Councillor Peacock about to occupy the highest, position in the town. (Applause.) He felt sure that the honourable career their worthy brother had had in the past with friendly societies had been a steppingstone to that grand appointment.

div.head: MAYOR'S SUNDAY SUGGESTION.
div.p: A MAYOR'S SUNDAY SUGGESTION.

In seconding a vote of thanks, Bro.'F. S. Massey said he put his Politics on one side that night. On the 10th November Bro. Peacock would have attained the highest Position in the town. Following that there would be the church parade. What Could be nicer than that everyone present that night should go and ask their brethren in the other lodges tO fall in in ic Mayoral Procession with one of those who had done as they had done. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Councillor Peacock joined the friendly society very young, and had helped largely to raise friendly societies to the Standard they were to-clay. It was such brothers as the Mayor-elect who brought out the highest. ideals and aspirations of the friendly society move- ment. He sincerely hoped the idea he had mentioned would be enthusiastically taken up. Counpillor Peacock said before a month was out he hoped to be a member of the mother lodge of that Order---(applause)—not in order to get another 'los., 'but he was going to be a member and would cpme amongst them occa- sionally. It would give him great pleasure when he joined the society. (Prolonged cheers.)

div.head: WORKHOUSE BREAD.
div.p: WORKHOUSE BREAD.
Flour Nine Months Old Used for Baking Purposes. ,
THE GUARDIANS' EXPLANATION.

The question of the inferior condition of 1 ite bread supplied to the Workhouse inmates one day in September was referred to at a meeting of the Warrington Guardians, on Wednesday, over Which Mr. E. L. Bent presided.
The Rev. A. M. Mitchell said: There is noth- ing in the minutes about the bread?
The Chairman :.The minutes are passed. Mr. Mitchell: I know, but there is nothing mentioned about the bread.
The Chairman: If you raise that question at the end of the meeting we will discuss it. At the end Of the meeting Mr. Mitchell said he would like to refer to .the question of the bread.

Mr. Garnett: I have seen the baker and he was upset at seeing the report that his bread was not up to the standard. It has been ex- plained before that the fault does not lie with the baker, the ovens, or any machinery, but in the fact that we had flour in excess something like nine months old. There has been about six sacks lying against the wall, and the baker has had to be very careful in the sifting of the flour to get the bread anything like what it is. It has taken the baker longer to mix his bread than if he had been getting the flour once a month.
Mr. Mitchell: I said it was the flOur at last meeting. Mr. Mather Exdctly, we all knew that; then why bring it up here?

div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.
LATCHFORD'S FINE WIN.

Weaste were the visitors to Latchford on Sat- urday, and the home team were victorious by four goals to two. Only one goal was scored in the first half, and that by a good shot from the Waste inside right, which lead they retained until the interval, although the home forwards had very hard lines on several occasions. In the second half Latchford seemed.to settle down and, scored four times, Pearson being responsible for three and Dale for one, which were only replied to by one from the visitors. The Latch- ford team gave an improved, display all round. The feature of the game was the shooting of Pearson, who played a fine game. Fletcher and Billington played well at back, while the halves were strengthened by the return of Wil- kinson at centre.

The second eleven were at Bowdon and en- joyed a keen and vigorous game, finishing up with a score of 3-3, which, against a team of Bowdon's calibre, ought to be considered a very good performance. Furness scored twice and Fletcher once for Latchford. TEAMS FOR TO-DAY.

To-day the first eleven, are at home to Win- nington, with the following team :—J. Bruhl ; W. Fletcher, C. Millington; F. W. Isherwood, J. B. Wilkinson, A: Knight, R. A. Dale, D. Travis, J. E. Pearson, W. H. Minards, H. It Colton. Bully-off 3 p.m. Umpire, Mr. F. Grounds.

Second Eleven vi Winnington 2nd :—T. F. Dixon; W. T. Eccles, C. Newbold; A. E. Brad- shaw, F. C. Newbold, T. Banks; A. B. Starkey, V. H. Fletcher, W. S. Furness, A. G. Marsden, D. Holt. 'Bus leaves Bridge Foot at 1.30 p.m. Umpire, Mr. H. Eccles.

div.head: CO-OPERATIVE EMPLOYES.
div.p: CO-OPERATIVE EMPLOYES.
An Effort to Organise Effectively
the store Workers.
A WOMAN'S CASE.

An important effort is being made to get all the workers connected with the Warrington Co-operative Store organised, and a special function was held, under the auspices of the local branch of the Amalgamated Union of Co- operative Employes, in the Co-operative Hall on Wednesday evening. The annual meeting was made a business one, combined with a social evening.

• Mr. H. BILLINGRAM, who presided, -as president of the local branch of the union, said there was one thing about the union that was a fault. When they called a general meeting they got a poor gathering, but when the first spark of in- justice comes along they were there as one man. (Applause.) He was glad to find the better class of employes with them that night, and that augured well for what they were going to do during the ensuing year. (Applause.) Mr. A. MORRIS, the secretary, submitted his annual report, which stated that the branch had concluded a very successful year's work, both from the social and the trade union point of view.

div.head: Busy as Trade Unionists.
div.p: Busy as Trade Unionists.

On the trade union side, he continued, we have been very busy. A reduction of one and a half hours in our working week has been ob- tained;- also an increase 'in wages, and a week's holiday with .Pay has been Secured for the coal carters.; (Applause.) All female eniplpyes haVe been put on the A.U.C.E. scale, as. well as the male apprentices, which means substantial increases in wage to all. Our soCiety are still retaining the. 28:3. at 21 years, which. makes our. minimum 4s. per week more than the -A.UX.E, scale at present for that age. For these con- cessions, I am sure, we are all grateful to the Committee of Management, and we trust there is more to follow. (Applause.) We have been' greatly surprised at the solid- arity of our members when the occasion re- quired it, such as during the dis7)ute in May last. We trust the same unity will be shown in all we undertako. as it is only by unity that we shall make headway.

div.head: Increased Membership.
div.p: Increased Membership.

We. have again to report large increase in membership. We commenced the year with 126 members; 56 new members have joined,, 18 have left the society, leaving a membership at pre- sent of 165, a net increase of 38 during the year. (Applause.) The accounts showed expenditure of ...t127 on the central fund, and on the branch fund, leaving a satisfactory balance. It was decided to join the Liverpool and Dis- trict Federation of Co-operative Employes, in order- to strengthen their position as a branch. . .

The officers elected were: President. H. Bil- lingham ; ;secretary, A. Morris; treasurer, J. Benion ; committee, W. Bottomley, G. Brown- hill, T. Hardman, P. Thomason and J. Lord; sick visitors, male, J. Kennington and J. Bailey; sick visitor, female, Miss. E. Benion; auditor, P. Johnson.

div.head: Goaded to Act.
div.p: Goaded to Act.

Mr. E. E. DALE, Pendleton, a Member of the Executive of ' the Union, in the course of a rousing address, said since the national pro- posals had been enunciated the pace of the union had become quicker, and the societies had taken fright and. alarm. Since then there had come into being District Wages Boards. These Boards were not established to protect societies against the assumptions of the em- ployes, but to advise societies. The union looked with askance at these Wages Boards, one of, which met in Warrington last week. They did not intend .to recognise them for anything different than ,the minimum scale of wages. They had been goaded •on to action by the way Co-operative Societies had dealt With their employes. Since the national policy was proclaimed the Warrington branch had got a 521 hours week. lie did not think it would be difficult to go on to negotiate for a 48-hour Week by mutual arrangement. , It did not mean to close the shops on a 48-hour week. There would be no violent interruption in the method of conducting business in the shops. It meant only a 48-hour week for each man. Conditions were still bad. The fault of the past had been to make dividend instead of carrying out the co-operative spirit. (Applause.)

div.head: No Non-Unionists.
div.p: No Non-Unionists.

In Warrington, he said, you are not touched with that little disease—non-union labour. Some of these men not in the union are the best paid employes, and it is most discouraging to find men in receipt of good wages, whose conditions would not be touched by the operations of trade union- ism, refusing to get their hands down for a few, pence to help the poorer workers. I want you in Warrington to raise one point in the Congress scale for women, which stop at 20 years, although a woman's age does not stop at that. Try to get from the committee of your Co-operative Society that the wage be 21s. per week for a woman at 21 years. They cannot refuse 21s. for women when they give 28s. per week to a man at 21 years. (Applause.)

div.head: Trade Unionism in Warrington.
div.p: Trade Unionism in Warrington.

Mr. C. DUKES, secretary of the Warrington Trades Council, also addressed the meeting. He said that the co-operative movement in War- rington would undoubtedly join in the future in the uplifting of the workers. There would be a closer alliance between it and trade unionism. There was a great growth in the trade union movement in Warrington, and noW they had 9,000 organised workers. The result of that•had been not only an in- crease in wages, but better working agreements and conditions. It had also meant that when the workers had become organised they had not been so much subjected to the petty tyranny of overseers as formerly. He could mention cases where women were in Warrington afraid to go to work for fear of being fined. and if they stayed away they were fined. In some trades they were getting 7s. and Bs. below the rates in neighbouring towns. Organisation would, and did, end all that.

div.head: DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: THE DEBATING SOCIETY.
System of Discussion Altered and the
Institution Continued.
LADY SPEAKERS ADMITTED.

There were divers opinions expressed at a meeting .held in the Town Hail on Wednesday night, when the, future of the Warrington Par- liamentary Debating Society was under con- sideration, but 'happily there-. were. none so sceptical as to propose its entire disbandon- ment, arid the society will continue. The Mayor -presided, and said it would be a great disaster if the society fell -into disuse, because they were looking out for young men of the town to be successors to those at present responsible for the municipal government of the district, and it was most imporiant that they should have such experience as they could :)htain from being members of a well-conducted society. M. A. White said it was a great pity that a society of that nature should entirely cease, but he recognised last season, as he did then, that if the society was to continue, they must have a greater influx of young men. - The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton said he would not like to see a society capable of such a work abandoned because there were not a hundred members, and he thought they ought to get a sufficient number to carry on. Under new con- ditions they might get better attendances. . _

Alderman Bennett thought they ought to have a wider scope of subjects than the limitations which were necessarily associated with Par- liamentary form. He proposed that ladies be invited to join—a proposal which was carried unanimously. It was also decided that in future the party element should be dropped, and that tlie meetings be held fortnightly.

div.head: STRIKING CHAPEL SCENES! THE COU NT RYSI DE
div.p: STRIKING CHAPEL SCENES! THE COU NT RYSI DE
How Warrington Wesleyans Cele- brated the Missionary Centenary.
REMARKABLE SERVICES.
" EX %MINER " SPECIAL.

There were remarkable and impressive scenes in the Wesleyan Churches in Warrißg- ton and district on Sunday evening. The centenary of the inauguration of foreign mis- sions fell due on that day, and our local Wesleyans, like their brothers and sisters', all over the world, found a unique way of cele- brating the deeply interesting event. The preachers at the morning .services made special reference to the great event in the history of the Connexion, and in other churches, both Nonconformist and Established, some passing comment was made to the celebration. It was at the evening services, however, that the centenary was chiefly celebrated.

When the hour of seven drew near the usual service was departed from, and for some minutes .the congregations, and pastors engaged in silent prayer, to give thanks for a hundred years of profitable labour in the foreign field, and ,to invoke blessings upon the work in the future. The solemn silence which prevailed for these few minutes was most impressive; in fact, it was the most 'remarkable scene ever, perhaps, witnessed in any of the Warrington churches. •
ENTHUSIASTIC SINGING.
Worked to a high pitch of fervent excitement,
the congregations then rendered the well- known and popular hymn, "All hail the power

of Jesu's Name." The hymn has been rendered hundreds of times in Wesleyan churches in Warrington, but, according to old members, it was never sung before with the fervour and enthusiasm which marked the rendition. of it on Sunday evening. "We have often been told," said an aged Wesleyan, "that we modern Wesleyans cannot sing as did our forefathers, who took a pride in their hymn vocalisation, but the way 'All hail the power of Jesu's Name' was sung dis- poses of that story., Methodists of the past
could not have rendered it with greater enthu- siasm and joy than did our great congrega- tions in Warrington on Sabbath night. It was good to live to participate in such a joyful sen- sation."

The sermons also were appropriate and deeply interesting, and they dealt with a record of the great work the Wesleyan Church had accomplished in the wide field over which their foreign mission cause. is to be found in opera- tion. It was a .striking act of triumphant faith that renewed dedication.
HOW THE CAUSE STARTED. N

It was in 1813 that khe Wesleyan Missionary Society was founded, but prior to that "Wesley 'Preachers," as -the didciples of John Wesley were known, were at work in the British posses- sions in America, where Wesley himself paid a visit. It was in Liverpool that -the- society got its first great shirt. The inanwho effected the launch of the imissionary ship was Dr. Coße, who, it is believed,\ preached more than once in Warrington. He 'insisted, ..at that memorable conference of 100 years ago, that the time had come when the Christian Gospel should be givOn to the heathen hordes in India. The minutes of the conference tersely puts the matter thus—

"What is the judgment of the conference concerning the proposal of a Methodist Mission to the East?"—Answer: "The conference authorises and appoints Dr. Coke to undertake a mission to Ceylon .and Java, and allows him. to take with him six preachers lor that purpose exclusively of one for the Cape of Good Hope." The men who volunteered to accompany Dr. Coke, and who thus became the founders of the Wesleyan Missions in the East, were Revs. William Ault, • James Lynch, George Erskine, William M. Harvard, Thomas Squance and Benjamin Clough. Delighted at: the opportunity to begin 'a work he felt wheaven-sent call to perform, 'Dr. Coke started on the voyage to the East. It was not givo him to even start the work, for one morn- ing he was found dead on the cabin floor of the ship in which he was making the voyage.

div.head: REMARKABLE MAN.
div.p: A REMARKABLE MAN.

Dr. Coke was a remarkable man. He was a Welshman, the only 'son of a surgeon, and, born in 1747. He took the degebe of Doctor\ of Civil Laws at Oxford, arid received episcopal ordination, but became impatient because he was for several years without preferment. He accepted the first opening that presented itself, which was a curacy at South Petherton, in Somersetshire, where his vigorous ministry filled the church, and as the parishioners would not provide additional accommodation, he did so at his own expense, and erected a gallery, which is still part of the fabric and is asso- ciated with his name:

Though popular with the people, he was not with the officials and in the end he was rung out of the parish. He then, sought out John Wesley and became the general superintendent of the foreign mission department of Wesley's evangelistic movement. It was this that secured for him the title of "The Father of Wes- leyan Missions." Starting 100 years ago with :IV mission stations and 1,725 members, the society. ha§. pow in Europe, India, Ceylon, Africa, . China, and the West Indies c. membership! Of 129,323, with 32,793 on trial. It has also 123.358 schol- ars in the Sunday schools and 116,429 in the day schools.

In addition, it has a vast number Of adherents who have no place in the tabulated returns of the society. The work was never more flour- ishing lhan it: is to-day, and the opportunities of evangelisation are recognised as pressing and numerous.
The foundation stones of a new Sunday school for the ,Miller-street Primitive, Methodist hureli,.Heywood, .Were laid on Saturday by a number of "..new and old" Sunday • school scholars. ,

There are IS3 applications for the position of salesman at the showrooms which are being opened by the Rochdale ,Corporation 'Gas com- mittee for the display of stoves and other gas- heating appliances.
Giving evidence at the inquest on her husband at Hull'on Saturday, a woman named Barbron said he had been drunk every day during the past week. A verdict of " Suicide" was re- turned.

At a Rochdale inquest on Zachariah Ash- worth, of Bacup, it was stated that owing to the snapping of a hook eleven tubs of coal ran back into a pit at Troughgate and dashed into Ashworth, who was fatally injured.

At a mass meeting of the Amalgamated Car- ters, Lurrymen and Motormen's Union, held at Farnworth, near Bolton, a resolution was passed asking the executive to obtain an advance of wages on behalf of the members.

Sergeant-Major Jepson, of Whaley Bridge, who is nearly 80 years of age, has received a letter Atating.that the King has granted him an annuity of .„tlO, together with a silver medal, as a reward for his long and meritorious service, which _includes the Indian Mutiny.

div.head: Modern Inventors that have Robbed Harvest-Time of its Glamour.
div.p: Modern Inventors that have Robbed Harvest-Time of its Glamour.
THE FALL OF THE YEAR,

It was only the other day that we had the golden, 'y:,ellow, waving corn still swaying with the winti, and the -sun scintil.lating its gleaming shafts of light o'er the ripened crops. Then came the lanour-saving combinec-i reaping and binding machine, looking very light as it made its rectangular journeys round the field, reduc- ing the standing stalks into sheaves at one operation. The progress of man's invention in his conquest of Nature is really marvellous when one thinks of the past for a moment.. It seems but yesterday, when, as a boy, I used. to watch with juvenile interest the operations. of the harvestmen hooking down the corn with the sickle Then came the'men from the sister isle across the Irish Sea with his .scythe.. Now the advent of the •American reaping machines has robbed us of much of the glamour of the old , rural scenes. Things have progressed, and perhaps improved; yes, but corn is , just as dear! It is fascinating, if one , be in , the mood, to lean over the gate. and spend a quiet half-hotir watching

the wonderful machine with its saw-like blade shaving the ground -like a safety razor, the big six-armed wheel throwing the corn across to meet the knife with every. revolution. The sheaves and the shocks are all built into stacks now, and nothing is left :of the golden beauty but. short earth-brown stubble. • - '
Seedtime. and Harvest.

Strictly speaking, harvest, or, rather, seed time, begins in the late spring months, for the early spring flowers are running to seed long before the latecomers have opened their blos- soms. Seed-time and harvest then proceed-all through the summer and autumn, even some- times, when October and November are mild, prolonging into early winter. The Marsh, Marigold or the Sweet Violet will have shed their seeds in May, but the beech and the oak may wait 'till late October before their lhower of " mast" and acorns begin. September is the real month for wild fruits in hedgerows and cOpse. It is then that the feast of scarlet berries, of .haws. and hips, rowans, guelder rose is spread o'er the trees. flight well, too, the birds know when the sugar is mature in the bit,terest fruits. Young sparrows and finches who have never seen a cherry in their life before, receive it* some occult hint when the fruit is at its best,

and the merry thrushes, young and old, will strip the rowan berries from the tree at the ripe moment. The deep-red haws are usually left till the last, and this autumn they are very scarce. There is hardly a cluster to be seen where they are usually abundant. The colour of ,the woodland fruits is often very Conspicuous, and contrasts very distinctly with that. of the foliage. There is a very good and distinct reason for this. All fleshy fruits are intended to be eaten by animals which are supposed to carry them off and drop the seeds at• a distance from the parent plant., A black- bird eating the fruit of the,Dog. Bose pecks at the fleshy part, and in the course of its meal scatters the stony seeds over a considerable space, the stiff, elastic hairs of the,latter assist- ing in the precess of dispersal. It therefore appears that the colours, sugars, and fruitjellies, which involve a great sacrifice of material on the part of the plant, are produced for the sake of colonisation. The colour is not developed till the fruit is ripe. Young fruits are green and not easily distinguished from the leaves, but when mature the fruit is conspicuous. Both colour and the sweet taste .appear together.

Versatility of Nature. Nature in her care for the continuity of species does not confine herself to one sole method. They are infinite in their variety. Every wild plant in its own peculiar distribution of it seed adapts itself , to circumstances. Were seeds simply dropped to the ground the seedlings would have little chance to escape being over- • crowded and overshadowed. There is there- fore' some, active contrivance for getting the seeds distributed to a distaiice. Sometimes the seed-vessels show exceeding ingenuity, like the Broom, whose dry, parchment-like pods curl up suddenly with a loud crack, discharging the black pellet-like seeds to a considerable distance. The small boatishaped valves of the violet burst open with a loud report, sending its little bullet seeds in all directions. In most of the great and numerous family of composites, the air is the chief agent of distribution. The seeds them- selves are light and usually have a feathery or parachute appendages, which act as wings for the play of the wind. Examine and watch when „liberated the " pappus " of a Dandelion, or the beautiful parachute of the Goat's Beard, and its exquisite adaptability for long-distance traffic will need no explanation. Many fruits like the Teasal, Burdock and Agrimony shed their seeds by the :help of animals, who, passing to and fro, come in contact with the spines and hooks of the seeds and drag them away—a process which is anything but to the comfort nf the animals concerned. Plants growing in water, and often those growing on the edge of water, have seeds with a hard and impervious outer covering, and a cushion of air inside to give buoyancy when floating down stream. There are seeds again which so resemble ants' cocoons that the ants are deceived and convey 'them into the fastnesses of their subterranean rizsts. Seedtime and harvest are full of infinite sug- gestiviness to those who care to use their eyes when taking walks by hedgerow and green

Extraordinary Phenomena. Towards the close of August a most unusual occurrence took place in the Dutton and Preston Diook district. One morning, after a day anti night of continuous and excessively heavy rain, the fields, pavements, roads and the roofs of the houses were seen to be covered with elongate globules of jelly. The jelly mass was so thick in some places that it was reported that pedes- trians could with difficulty walk on the side- walks. .An area of one and a half square miles was coVered in this way. A friend told me he counted thirty-six of .the globules in a space of six square inches. An examination of a single jelly mass under the microscope revealed a very compli- cated structure. They were elongate, oval cells,, lined with an epithelial ,layer, and the rest r the space, occupied with spherical globules. The. various cell i were 'arranged in a spiral manner and involved completely in a mass of mucus. At first it was thought that they were stages of

some fungus, the -spores of which had been carried from a distance in an upper current uf air, and brought to earth by the rain. . But it was eventually seen that they were of an animal maize. Several of the jelly masses were sub- mitted to the authorities at the. British Museum, who identified • them as the egg-masses of some . species of chironoinus (midges). The eggs of midges. are usually deposited in water, and their occurrence in the situation described is very remarkable. The only possible explanation seems to be that the egg-masses have been drawn up from sOme pond by a water-spout, and subsequently showered on the Dutton dis- trict during the heavy rain. An alternative explanation, which seems less likely, is that the midges mistook the grasS and roofs for water, but it is very improbable that this would 'happen on so large a scale. • No jelly masses were found under open sheds, or in the open goods station at Preston Brook; they all occurred in the open. Ist October, 1913.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
RAID ON A GARDEN.

Four young men, Edward,Holden, John Duffy, James Baines and James Burns, of Gerards Bridge, were fined N. each at St. Helens, for stealing a quantity of garden produce from the garden of Thomas Webster, of Haresfinch.

div.head: STRANDED BY A STRIKE.
div.p: STRANDED BY A STRIKE.

Simon Bennett and William Plant, of Burn- ley, were charged at St. Helens on Monday with frequenting Church-street with intent to com- mit a felony.—Both said that they went to Man- chester to take ship, but, the strike itiid the ship .up and they had to go on to Liverpool, where they were stranded.--The Bench said that if they were willing to work the men would be allowed to go.

div.head: ILL-HEALTH AND SUICIDE
div.p: ILL-HEALTH AND SUICIDE

An inquest on Richard Henry Dagnall (42), glassblower, 166, Boundary-road, qt. Helens,,was held on Monday by Coroner Brighouse. Mrs, Dagnall said her husband on Friday night was-very -depressed, . He had a walk, and on returning .eat with his head itt his hands and said the pain was 'very- severe. She went..-.to bed, and about 'midnight Was aroused and told that deceased was hanging in the 'stable. _ _ _ _

James Wilkinson, deceased's -- brother-in-14'W, said the stable was used as a coal-place. 'He found Da.gnall in the stable in a sitting position. A rope was tied tightly round his neck; and he was quite dead. A verdict of" Suicide while of unsound mind" was returned.

div.head: BARONET AS THE MAYOR
div.p: BARONET AS THE MAYOR

Sir David Gamble, Bart., has agreed to be Mayor of St. Helens during the coming year. Sir David resides at Windlehurst, St. Helens, the residence which was built by his grand- father. He is the third baronet, and his grand- father, Sir David Gamble, K.C.8., received the title in 1897. In February, 1907, Sir David was .succeeded by Sir Josiah •Christopher 'Gamble, whose health gave way, and he died in Septem- ber, 1908. The first baronet was the first Mayor of the town when it was irtorporated, and, held the office from 1868 till 1870, 1882-3, and 1886-7. Sir Christopher was also a member of the Coun- cil for a very long period, and Mayor in 1888. The Mayor-Elect, who is thirty-seven years of age, was, some years ago, a councillor for South Windle Ward.

div.head: ALLEGED SUSPICIOUS HUSBAND.
div.p: ALLEGED SUSPICIOUS HUSBAND.

Albert Edward Smith, 4, Peel-street, was charged on remand at St. Helens on Monday ..,with wounding his wife. The" Chief Constable said that the circum- stances were of a very painful nature. Thirteen years ago he was detained in Whiston Work, house on amount of the state of his mind. For Ame time he had appeared to be jealous of his wife, and accused her of bringing men to the house. tOn Wednesday afternoon. September 2ith, prisoner was ill and went to bed. He slept in the back bedroom with his sons. and, the wife slept in the front room with her datigh- tors, About two o'clock on Thursday morning she was awakened by her .daughter, Susan, tell- ing her that prisoner was coming into the room. Ife was fully dressed, and, taking hold of his wife's ,hand, he said, "Come on, I want you!" He dragged her to the landing and ten tripped her up and said, "Are you not goi4g to admit it was Joe you had in the house on Sunday night?" She replied that that was not so. The prisoner then struck her several times with a knife. She tried to take the knife from him, aftd in doing so received a cut across her hand, cutting the muscles in two. Mrs. Smith said she had a large family that she brought up respectably, and her husband's accusations against her were all false, due to his fancies. The prisoner was committed for trial.

div.head: HATTON.
div.p: HATTON.

Parish Church Festival—Harvest thanksgiv- ing services were held at the Daresbury Parish Church on Sunday. In the morning the preaoher was the Rev. A. N. Perrin, vicar of Runcorn. In the afternoon there was a chil- deen's service. The preacher at the evening service was the Rev. U. L. Johnstone, vicar of Aston. The ilev. gentleman kook as his text, P.n.s harvest is the end of the world." The anthem was from that grand old harireSt. hymn, "Come,. ye thankful people, come." •Mr. Albert Deprez was responsible for the bass solo, and acquitted himself in a creditable manner. Mr. John Wright presided at the organ. The church at the evening service was crowded.' The ancient edifice was tastefully decorated with a profusion of choice flowers and fruits.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER 11, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER 11, 1913.
PRIZE DAY AT LYMM.
An Interesting Time at the Local Grammar School.
A HEADMASTER'S ADVICE.

An eagerly anticipated event in the school year at the Lymm Grammar hichool is prize day, which took place this year on Saturday. There was.a large .attendance, over which the Rev. G. B. Thurston presided. Amongst those present were the Rev. H. P. Wethered, Mr.' G.-L. Wel- ford, Mr. and Mrs. T. J. Ridgway, Mr. Willson (headmaster), Mr. J. L. Paten (headmaster, Manchester Grammar School, who Afterwards distributed the prizes and gave an interesting address), and Mr. Callender. A part-song, "A song of the sea," excellently rendered by the school choii) commenced the pince°di!le- _ _ _

- The Chairman called upon the Headmaster to read his report. Mr. Willson said that the year just oompleted represented the first complete year under the new and, improved conditions, and the record of results in the various examinations, which was the best they had had for some years past,' fur- nished sufficient evidence that the improved conditions were beginning to bear fruit. This year, for the first time, two candidates from the school competed for county intermediate scholarships, both of whom were successful. Ada Joynson distinguished herself in particu- lar by obtaining the fifth place in the county. (Applause.) Walter - Jones was successful in obtaining a boy clerkship in the Civil Service, in open competition, securing the 87th place on the list. He was subsequently appointed to a clerkship in the Lancashire Insurance Company. (Applause.) In the annual examinations of the Northern Universities Joint Board three out of four can- didates were successful in obtaining certificates. Ada Joynsou obtained a senior school certificate, which was also a matriculation certificate, though very mud' below the average age for the examination. In this examination excellent results were obtained in mathematics, French, science and geography, but the results in Eng- lish and history were somewhat disappointing. The examiner's report stated that the work of both candidates showed that the teaching had been careful and sound. In the school certificate examination, in which the papers were taken by all Form V., Ruth Willan and John Broadbent. were success- ful in obtaining certificates, and William Barker qualified by marks for a certificate. The examiner's report stated that the average mark ;in the different subjects was very fair, though often spoilt by the very weak work of one or two individuals.

A Record in Drawing. In the annual examination of the Royal Drawing Society the school obtained 50 certifi- cates out of a possible 53, of which 34 were I honours certificates, a record well in advance of tile average percentage throughout the United Kingdom. Special credit was due to C. Nuttall, who obtained a pass in Division VI., the highest division of the examination, and to H. Atkin- son, C. ,Nuttall and W. Barker, who obtained honours in Division V. He (Mr. Willson) trusted that these results would furnish suffi- cient evidence that while there was still plenty of room for improvement, the work of the school was steadily progressing, and was characterised both by seriousness and strenuousness. In common with all secondary schools of their type, they had to face the serious difficulty of the leaving age problem, more espeeially in the case of the boys, but he had reason to hope that as the result of very special efforts with the parents, they would have a larger matriculation form this term, and that the average age of the top form- will be well in advance ,of that of .preceding years. (Applause.) It was also hoped that it would be possible to strengthen somewhat the staff of the kindergarten depart- ment this term, to meet the increasing num- bers. During the year an important inquiry had been held with regard to the occupations and welfare of about 200 old scholars who have left the school during the past six years. It was extremely satisfactory to be able to report that, almost without exception, they were occupying useful positions and appear likely to do well. Several notable distinctions had been won by old .scholars, who had recently left the school during the year. 0. De Jong obtained distinc- tion in forensic medicine at the third M.E. examination at Manchester University. R Odlin, who recently matriculated at London University, had giuccessf ally palAt.l. the Inter- mediate B.Sc. examination. R. Wilks had passed, the London Institute of Bankers' pre- liminary examination, W. Langford had ob- tained first-class certificates in plant, model and freehand drawing at the Manchester 5( boo! of Art, and T. Parr had passed the second M.B. examination at St. Andrew's Univereity. (Ap- plause.) Games and Physical Culture. The usual keenness had been displayed in con- nection with the games. The football team won most of their matches, and it was satis- factory to note that the Old Boys' football team had been revived and promised to do well dur- ing the coming season. In cricket they had not done quite so well as in previous years. The girls had played basket ball, hockey and tennis with vigour and success. They had to thank very heartily those ladies who had kindly pre- sented cups for tennis and hockey house com- petitions among the girls. The gymnasium classes had been reorganised and placed on a better footing, and the effect of the improved conditions and teaching was already beginning to manifest itself in the physical development of a considerable number of the boys and girls.

div.head: Social Life.
div.p: Social Life.

The usual features of the social life of the school had been supported more heartily than ever. The lantern lectures given included, some of the best yet given to the schooL The second manual wiork exhibition took place at the end of the spring term, and the display of work attracted much interest and attention. The Inter-form singing shield was won by Forms V. and IVa. It was here suggested that a similar shield for competition in ordinary school work between the forms might prove a valuable in- centive. Such a plan had been tried with suc- cess in a number of schools.

div.head: Staff.
div.p: Staff.

She would be much missed, especially in connec- tion with the drawing, in which she secured such excellent results, and the girls', games. She was succeeded -by Miss M. Adams, who came to them with excellent qualifications from Tadcaster Grawmar School. The qualifica- tions and work ,of the staff were spoken of with commendation in the recent Board of Education report, and he could not speak too highly of the loyal and unselfish manner in which the staff had co-operated with him, both in and out of school. on behalf of what they. conceived to be the highest interests of the children. (Ap- plause.)

div.head: General.
div.p: General.

The health of the school had been uniformly good throughout the year. There had been a very satisfactory increase in the numbers at the right end of the school, and last term there were over. 140 pupils in-the school. There had been" another -'large entry this term, and the numbers had risen to 150. The improvement obtained in the matter of early entry was com- mented on in the recent report. The material at the disposal 'of the school, if not of a high order, was, on the whole, more promising than for some time, past. A new and more ser- viceable school prospectus had been issued during the year. Such , Specific suggestions as were embodied in , the recent Board of Educa- tion report were already being 'Tut into force as .far as 'possible, hut doubtless something in the nature of a united conference between parents, teachers, inspectors and governors would be of immense Value, with a view to securing a better mutual understanding on various points.

div.head: Serious Life.
div.p: A Serious Life.

In conclusion he said that they wanted mutual intercourse between the parents. When the time arrived for the scholar entering, upon a serious business of life they wished the parents to co-operate with them in the best interests of the children. Parents must trust in the school to which they sent their children, and give the teachers a free hand. When - the seed time came, parents and teachers co-operated in the interests of the scholars. They had yet an immense amount to learn from America, where they had Parents' Associations, which we could equal or match in this country. There were organisations of parents and teachers, and they were bound together in the common interests of the children and of the community. He asked that parents who .vanted assistance or advice should send a message to the school, and the teachers would do their• best for them; indeed, they were only anxious and wishful to do it. (Applause.) After congratulating Mr. Willson on his report the Rev. G. B. Thurston said he congratulated the headmaster and the staff for the work they did in a most difficult school., for in a place the size of Lymm, with its peculiar situation a diffi- culty had to be faced. He would be strongly
in favour of such a Parents' Association men- tioned by Mr. Willson. (Applause.)

div.head: VIEWS OF AN EXPERT.
div.p: THE VIEWS OF AN EXPERT.

Education After the Age of 14. Mr. Paton then delivered nus address and said that the extension of that school showed that the work which was being done was appre- ciated more and more by tile people in the district which the school served. fie was sure the governors of the school, the headmaster and teachers must feel that encouragement which came to all of them every September, when the entry was a large one. At that school they were more than maintaining, they were enhancing the confidences which they had commanded in the past. The prizes he had just awarded would be a stimulus.- They were struggling to retain boys up to 14 years•o! age, and he iciund that-in matters of education English people were purely impassive and inert, and one had to show a thing before the people knew what one was talking about. (Hear, hear.) He thought that the thing they had to do now in all secondary schools in Eng- land was to persuade parents that when the boy came tithe age of 15 years that he might be able to command ss. per week, but it was the best thing for him to be kept on at school, so that he could be trained more fully. Speaking generally, it was a foolish investment for a parent to send a boy to a secondary school un- less he was prepared to send the lad through the whole course. The best secondary school edu- 'Cation yielded a late crop, but yet it was a crop that was well worth gathering. On ecoriomic grounds the crop was worth waiting for and worth the sacrifices made to enable the scholar to stay at school till he was 17 or 18 years of age. Need for Higher Education.

Speaking on higher education, Mr. Paton said that if they had thought of the word at all, they had thought about something which lifted scholars up out of the low rucks of life, physically, morally, and mentally; lifted out of the low level to which so many lads who were not edu- cated went. The boy at a secondary school saw that this kind of education meant calling on several minor sacrifices. They should recog- nise that they were out for a high object and filled with such high ambitions, and therefore their evenings should be given to home work. Those who did not enjoy that were not out for higher education. They, in the secondary 'schools, were expected to attain . accu- racy and thoroughness, which was not expected ' of those whose ambitions were fixed ' on some lower objects, such as football, &c. The former were expected .not to have everything minced up, so that they could not chew it, and everything brought in a silver spoon. They were •expected to have a higher idea of attention and' a 'joy to master the difficulties: which had nearly mastered them. In a prize-giving, as they knew, there were certain favoured individuals who got a number of prizes. Then there was the school life. The hea•imaster, in his report, did not lay so much stress on the single successes, but spoke of col- lective life; of the physical ;development as a whole; of work in the forms and the interest taken in games. Those proceedings ha.si been opened with a bit of social life, when the choir gang the song so well.

div.head: Co-operative Effort.
div.p: Co-operative Effort.

When out for higher education they must have co-operative effort. He could walk along the road alone, but if he and they wanted to climb the Matterhorn they would have to rope thempelves-to .others. It was the same in higher- education. 'lndividual effort was a diffi- cult thing. -and--what they needed in every secondary school was 'a spirit of shoulder-to- shoulder comradeship. They wanted the spirit of comradeship in the moral life of the school, if there was to be honesty, transparent honesty, and purity that would tolerate no dirty word, thought, deed, or picture. (Hear, hear.) They wanted some- thing more than masters and mistresses, and monitors and monitresses; each single member of the rank and file must have a burning enthu- siasm for the things that were considered neces- sary in,highereducation. Every little fellow in that school could do something to heln the spirit of learning in the school. (Hear, hear.) They were now beginning to look at things; to have visions of what the future might he, and they saw that the future would not bring things to us, but that we must get them ourselves. They had plenty of critical thinkers, but very few possessed constructive .ideas. To accom- plish these dreams of nrogress they must he prepared to make sacrifices and support the snirit of co-operation, which would help those of the future to bridge the difficulties by a long 11,111, a strong pull, and a pull all together. (Applause.)

The season seems topsy-turvy. Laburmun trees are again in bloom. Gorse is also in full flower.. Snowdrops have likewise appeared. A " Heathen " has gathered strawberries. Verily, which season are we in? The harvest .festivals are in full swing. We are still awaiting the largest vegetable marrow. Is it to be seen at a festival this season? The parish meeting ,takes place fzin Monday. What will the burning questions he Is it .time a Warrington :councillor, is con..ing With a sheafful of questions to ask. The local men may have a hot time. Street improvements may be hie question. There are some who think £2,520 too much. There are others who do not, and there you are. " Bulbosis".is a new local disease. It is the latest term for bulb ptaTit:rg A few of our gardeners have got Vie disease badly.
They expect to have a record show in lhc spring. Still they have not yet got the black tulip. in two hours ten pounds of blackberries Were gathered in the vicinity of Stockton Heath. -
The 'gatherer would, have done for an official at a negro's funeral. , He seems to have been particularly good at "black-burying." The Parochial Committee meet, on Tuesday.

Evidently they are not alarmed at the Parish Meeting. A little servant maid was sent to the chemist. Her mission was to procure a I.d. worth of pumice stone. The 'girl gave the man of drugs a rude shock. She asked for "a id. worth of the best tomb- stone." Heathens think " Whon Knights Were Bold" great. They have flocked to the theatre during the week. "Miss Hook of Holland ", promises to get a great reception. The Heathens are to be there in their strong- est numbers. -- We like comedy and music, do we Heathens.

Held Up.—The Ship Canal was extremely busy yesterday, and much inconvenience was caused to Heathens going to and coming from War- rington. The tram traffic was considerably dis- organised. more particularly in the morning, and one traveller averred that he was delayed as much as 25 minutes.

Offer Declined.—The Warrington Fire Bri- gade Committee reported to the Town Council on Tuesday night that a letter had been received stating that the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee are not at the present time prepared ~to accept the terms oflered%by the Corporation. for the services of the Fire Brigade in.„Stockton Heath.--The matter passed without comment.

The Parish Meeting.—Councillor Whitley, the chairman of the Stockton Heath Parish Coun- cil, has summoned ~the half-yearly parish meet- ing for Monday night at the Assembly Rooms. It is expected he will preside. There -are no important questions for the parishioners, but doubtless the usual crop of gtievances will he there. A proposal may be made to hold the meeting once, instead Of twice a year.

Fell in the 'Canal.--While some boys Were " larking " on .the cane:l bank, between Stockton Heath and Walton on Sunday, one overbalanced diid fell into the water. Canal boat was passing at the time and one of the bargemen promptly fished the youngster out with a boat hook. The boy suffered from nothing but a drenching. .

Foreign Mission Centenary.—ln common with even, church in the connexion, the centenary of the starting of the foreign mission scheme was celebrated at the Stockton Heath Wesleyan Church on Sunday, when good congregations attended. Both at the morning and evening 'service reference was made to the great event in the history of the Wesleyan Church. At seven o'clock in the evening the service was inter- rupted, the congregation briefly engaged ill .silent prayer, and then heartily sang "All hail the power of Jesu's Name." At the same hour all over the world a similar incident, occurred in every Wesleyan Church.

Coming-of-Age Party.—A pleasing event took place on Thursday evening, when Mr. and Mrs. S. Brocklehurst, ef Moss House, Stocktqn Heath, gave a supper and dance at AtkinsOn's 'Cafe, Bridge-street, Warrington, to celebrate the com- ing of age of their eldest son, Sydney. Invita- tions had been extended to over sixty rela- tives and friends, several coming from distances outside Warrington. Amongst the number was noticed the Mayor-elect, Mr. Peacock, who is a near relative of the family. A dainty supper was, served, after which speeches were given. acknowledging the occasion, by Mr. Brockle- karst and Mr. Peacock, being responded to by Mr.,Brocklehurst. jun. Prizes for whist were presented by Mrs. Peacock, Mayoress-elect.

St. Thomas' Festiva—The harvest festival was celebrated at the St. Thomas' Church, Stockton Heath during last week-end. The church was tastefully, if not elaborately, decor- ated by the lady members of the congregation, chrysanthemums and lilies playing a large part in the scheme. The choir rendered special harvest music, and Mr. F. Rose played suitable selections on the organ. On Friday evening the first service was held, and at this the Rev. G. Vale-Owen, vicar of Orford, was the preacher. There were largo congregations at the Sunday services, more particularly at that in the evening, when the edifice was crowded. In the morning the Rev. Canon Morley Steven- son, the Principal of the Warrington Training College, was the preacher. In the evening a very appropriate harvest discourse was preached by the Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth.

Popular Singer's Death.—A popular singer, who had done much to enliven the life of the district with his fine tenor voico, has passed away, in the person, of Mr. Edward Reddish. The death occurred at his residence in War- burton-street, Stockton Heath, where he had lain some time through a severe illness, which culminated in death from heart failure. Mr. Reddish was well known and highly esteemed in the district, and while in health he was a popu- lar personage at many social functions. He was a most capable tenor vocalist and possessed a voice of fine range and quality. For a long number of years he was actively associated with the•choir of St. Thomas' Church, and had taken a prominent part in most of the special musical services given by the choir. He was 58 ,years of age. The funeral took place on Tuesday and it was attended by the choir, who took part in the service at the church. There were a number of wreaths, including one from the choir.

Tragedy of Human Lofe."—The first of a series of united services under the auspices of the Free Church Council was held at the Bap- tist Church, Higher-lane, on Wednesday night, when the Rev. E. E. Lovell was the preacher. Taking Psalm ciii.. 15,16 and 17, as his:teat, the preacher spoke of the. "Brevity, beauty and tragedy of human life." Speaking of the brevity he said that -1,5.0 should all aim .to' live the best we can in the little time we have. Though brief, life was full of beauty, as illustrated in the freshness -of the green grass and the glory of the flower.. That life was full of tragedies was demonstrated daily in the newspapers, and we are only able to bear up by the gleams of hope and the mercy of God. After dwelling on the everlasting quality of God's mercy, he said that his audience Must not be disheartened, but look away to 06 time when all the tragedies will vanish and the glory remftins.

This he made at the Rural District Council. Polly, the local parrot, made a daring escape. She took up a position on a large tree. A man tried'to get at Polly, but she was a flirt. '
She led the mere male on from branch to branch.

"Now I've got you!" said the man, making a grab- " I don't think so!" screeched. Poll, as she flew higher. The chase lasted for a considelible time. Then the cage was placed on the lawn; Poll hopped in. • She had an enjoyable little trip and was now satisfied. The streets and roads are being named. The houses are Aot to he numbered. • Each abode has a characteristic title of its own. It is quite an aristocratic fashion, donl-cher- know..

div.head: YOUNG GIRL'S TRAGIC DEATH.
div.p: YOUNG GIRL'S TRAGIC DEATH.

Fatal Play With Matches. Phyllis Nicholls (11), Sycamore Cottage, Grap- penhall, was burning leaves in the garden on Thursday week, and in the absence of her mother she would appear to have secured paper and matches, and endeavoured to keep a "big blaze." Her clothing caught fire; and she was burned to death.

Coroner Brighouse held the inquest at Wax:- eington on Saturday morning, and he described the case as a very sad one: Mrs. Nicholls said she was the wife of Henry T. Nicholls, tannery manager. On Tuesday and Wednesday she had made fires in the garden at the rear of the house for disposing of all the dried leaves and rubbish. About 1.45 on Thurs- day she heard screams and ran downstairs, to see her daughter enveloped in flames. She covered the child with a sack and two aprons, and endeavoured to extinguish the flames. As one flame was put out another seemed to come into existence. All the child's clothes were burned off her body. She burned herself, and shouted for assistance. Neighbours came, and the child was removed to the Infirmary. When she (witness) looked round she found eight or hine matches in a box, burned paper and several used matches. The whole of the child's cloth- ing was of cotton.

The Coroner said that probably the mother did not know that the best thing to do was to put the child on the floor at once. A verdict of "Accidental death" was re- turned, and the jury expressed their sympathy with the rOatives.

div.head: "SEWAGE SCHEME TOO COSTLY." Mr. Lister Kaye Makes a Protest at the
div.p: "SEWAGE SCHEME TOO COSTLY." Mr. Lister Kaye Makes a Protest at the
Iriu-ncorn Council.
TOO LATE TO STOP THE WORK.

The discussion of Grappenhall matters took UP a large amount of the time at the fort- nightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council. Mr. c. E. Linaker presided. The Local Government Board wrote to the `Council giving the sanction to the borrowing by the Council of the sum of £1,924 for the making of Victoria-avenue, Albert-road, and York-drive, Grappenhall., under the Private Street Works Aet.
In answer to Mr. Lister. Kaye, the Chairman said that the tenders varied between £1,600 and A:1,900.
Mr. Lister Kayo's Protest.

The Clerk reported tat a meeting of the Grappenhalr, Latchford Without and Thelwall Sewerage Committee•was held on the akth ult., when the clerk read replies he had received from owners of property in answer to the Goun- cil's inquiry as to whether they would be pre- pared to sell a piece of land for sewage outfall works; from owners of land adjoining the sites suggested, as to whether they would oppoie the acquisition of such sites for the purpose of sewerage outfall works. The Clerk also produced the engineer's esti- mate of the cost, in the event of the site offered by Lord Barrymore being adopted, from which it appeared that -there would be the following saving to the parishes of Grappenhall and Latchford Without; Grappenhall, a capital sum of £976, annual payment £54, rate in the 1d; Latchford Without, capital sum £522, annual payment .229, rate in the .2 lid. It was resolved, with Mr. Lister Kaye dis- senting, that the Chairman of the committee and the Clerk attend before the Local Govern- ment Board, and after laying all the• corre- spondence before them; aseertain whether they would be prepared to approve an outfall site on Lord Barrvmore's land in the parish of Grap- penhall. That, with the view of 'obtaining a Provisional Order for the next session of Parlia- ment, in the event of Lord Barryniore's land not being approved, the necessary steps be taken at once for the compulsory acquisition of the land belonging to Admiral Jones Parry. in the parish of Thelwall (which was submitted to the Local Government Board as the site of out- fall works in the original scheme, together with the right of way thereto, belonging to the Seaton estate).
_ • Mr., Pilling proposed the adontion of the re- pct, and Mr. Hallows seconded.

To Pay Two-thirds. Mr. Lister Kaye said he was going to object to the resolution. Just now the Chairman had Raid that the tenders for the new streets varied between £1,600 and £1,900, and that was lust his argument. He represented Grappenhall, which would pay two-thirds of the scheme.
