div.head: HOLY ISLAPD OF LINDISFARNE,
div.p: THE HOLY ISLAPD OF LINDISFARNE,
The Home of Saint Cuthbert and a Place of Pilgrimage for a Thousand Years.

div.head: LEGEND, HISTORY ARID ADVENTURE.
div.p: LEGEND, HISTORY ARID ADVENTURE.

At the extreme northerly tip of England a little wind-swept island stands cold and lonely in the North Sea. Though bleak and compara- tively barren, it has associations which Mive made it dear and memorable, and the charm of its history draws visitors from far and near. Its familiar name to the Englishman is "Holy Island." To the Scot it is "The 'Other 4.101 y Island," for the Scot, with true knowledge, claims that THE Holy Island is his own lona, and must be for ever. We notice that the makers of the map keep clear of criticism by giving the sounding title "The Holy Island of Lindisfarne," and in the .title of our :article we have been at pains to copy their shrewdness.

This bit of land, two miles long and two miles wide, lifting itself about fifty feet out of the water, part sand hills and haunted by rabbits,: would never by its own charms, attract a pil- grim from the mainland.
ling's •black bonnet is preserved in a local museum.. _
THE ABBEY.

Lindisfarne has a capital little harbour, over which the Castle towers upon a piece of steep rock . Here We land, and choosing the biggest -thing first, Make our way to the ruins of the priory: This monastic building, beautiful in its decay, is the oldest in Northumberland. It was founded in A.D. 1093, by the Benedictine Monks. of Durham, and in general design is very much like Durham Cathedral. But the red sandstone, carted slowly across the channel by the monks, has not proved strong enough to resist the fierce weather of the North Sea, and it:is- badly time-eaten. The Priory has suffered too at the hands of the spoiler. It shared the wholesale plunder under Henry VIII., of famous Reformation memory, and in 1613 received the final humiliation from Lord Walden, who car- ried away the lead roof and bells and what- ever else seemed worth the theft. The vessel that bore this load foundered, and the metal has rested for three centuries in. the. ocean sand. The record which tells' the story says: "The Ship, with manic persons therein, was drowned, and sonke into the sea, even. soone after their goeinge from the island." Stripped •of its lead, the roof perished, and left gaunt walls to tell of comer glories. The ruin is now under the care of the Crown.

div.head: STORY OF ST. CUTHBERT.
div.p: THE STORY OF ST. CUTHBERT.

The interest is historical, and we had, there- fore, better first tell our story of Saint Cuthbert' before giving Our impressions of his home. It is the ypar..6sl A.D., and the saintly, Aldan, Bishop of Lindisfarne, has just i)dsged- away. A shepherd lad' tending sheep in Lauderdale sees a strange vision in which angels bear the soul of the good Bishop to heaven. There were few Christians then, but perhaps the lad's par- ents were among them. At any rate, the way is opened, and the young shepherd becomes a shepherd of men. He became an ardent monk

div.head: SEVENTH CENTURY CHURCH. Going back to a period much earlier than
div.p: A SEVENTH CENTURY CHURCH. Going back to a period much earlier than

div.head: LINDISFARNE ABBEY.
div.p: LINDISFARNE ABBEY.

in the Monastery of Melrose, and the name of Cuthbert became familiar and famous among the Ecclesiastics of the day. After some useful years at Melrose and liipOn, he followed his old friend and master, St. Eata, to Lindisfarne, for St. Eata had become its Abbot. But life in Lindisfarne, quiet as it_must have been, was too cheerful for the austere Cuth- bert. The call to holiness led him along paths which modern piety selcrom feels impelled to tread J „ excelled all his brethren in devo- Lion, giving himself to heavenly contemplation, and becoming (so, the ancient chroniclers say) more angel than man.". That .he might give himself wholly to heavenly thoughts he trav- elled to one of the Fame Islands, where, with his own hands, assisted.(again we quote the old ehronieles) by angels, he built a rude cirCular it was partly unroofed, and sunken in the rock, .which he excavated, so that, looking up hence, he could see only the sky overhead, and be thus guarded 'against distraction and wan- dering thoughts. 7 Barley crops, which he contrived to grow, provided food, and .the sea birds were his friends. So great was his influence upon his favourite eider ducks, that the tribe .aa. ,-e ,r.-e was cured' of pilfering and strife, and • has been, famous for its quiet habits ever since. If the legend speaks true, this was a triumph indeed. . Only for two years did Cuthbert live here. Ile died in his cell and was- buried in Lindis- farne. With most mortals, burial is the last chapter, and it might reasonably be supposed that his history would end here, but it fell to the lot of the quiet Cuthbert to have a post- mortem biographti7 far. more - exciting and curious than anything that happened to him: during. his lifetime. It was the last thing he would. have desired, tut strange things have happened in this world, especially the bones of .the saints. If our readers ask for it we will tell the story.• For the present we are to'see Lindisfarne and its relies.

the priory, we must recall that., a church stood here long before these strong columns were built. The original cnurch ox the Bishop of Lindisfarne was limit of split oak, and thatched with the coarse rushes that grow on the sand hills. Tins lasted till atiout 680 A.D.„ when Bishop Eauberi substituted a roof of lead. The late of the little structure was very sad. 'lov- ing Danes landed and ravaged the island, cruelly treated the monks, and destroyed the -churcii.l,-;But Lindisfarne was holy ground even then. The monks took courage to return, and remained on the unprotected island until 875 A.n.

Driven away again by the fear of the Dimes, they croAsed to the mainland, carrying with them the body' of St. Cuthbert across the flood. For nearly two hundred years the island lay desolate. But it was holy, if lonely, ground, and dear to the religious heart. Hence, when circumstances permitted, the building of the great priory, VII massive lofty -arches that stand out so grandly even yet against the sky. About fifty years after the priory there rose the Parish Church of St. Mary, of which there is still something left to attract us. Its archi- Lecture, is partly Norman, Partly early English, but; alas! it has been restored, and the floor has been so laid that the bases of the fine pillars' are buried.

div.head: AN AIIPMBIOUS PONY.
div.p: AN AIIPMBIOUS PONY.

We alight at the little station of Beal in a mood for adventure'. A trap waits there for pilgrims,. and a substantial pony yoked to a sort of governess car takes us away towards the coast. The pony is a for more attractive. creature than we could at first have guessed. Arrived at tile sea edge he took to the water like a creature amphibious: A few splashes of those sturdy legs. and we are well out into the sea, enjoying .effects of sky and water, yet tugged by a pony who trots cheerily through the waves. . Formidable as the broad water looks, it is quite shallow, and as the tide is re- treating a broad expanse of yellow sand will soon join the island to the Mainland.. We can only cross at low water, and the experience is the most delightful feature of the day. For ages pilorinis have, travelled thus. As Sir Walter Scott has it:

The tide did now its flood mark gain, And girdled in the saints domain; For with the flow and ebh its style Varies from Continent to isle. Dry shod o'er sands, twice a day, The pilgrims "to the shrine find way. Twice every day the waves efface, Of staves and sandalled.feet the trace.

141.1 f a mfie of water blows between Undis- fur e and the mainland, but the day. is 'calm, and we need not be apprehensive. Tall posts mark the safe track. and here and there a plat,-„ form with a ladder has been reared for the ad- vantage of these who may be overtaken by the tide. A different place the channel muSt appear when winter winds and angry waters sweep round holy Island. Grin] tales our driver can, tell of his passages in the dark, but. he has regard for our nerves, and only tells of lostl lives when pressed to do so by. inquisitive pas- sengers. About five Hundred inhabitants live in peace upon lonely Lindisfarne, Silty or sixty of them being fishermen. There are two churches, Episcopal and Presbyterian, two hoteN anti two lifeboats. THE HOME OF GRACE DARLING.

The mention of lifeboats recalls the Ov&- memorablis bravery of Graca Darling. It was tier-, from (ale of the Firne Islands. that she rowed out to the wreck, end the sight of this bleak coast, even though the day is calm, brings hOme the memory with a force we have never known before. Years ago we saw the boat in which she rowed, now we see the lonely coast, and try 10 picture it as it would be upon a stormy night. They tell Us that Grace Dar-

div.head: QI %INT RELIC OF THE PAST.
div.p: A QI %INT RELIC OF THE PAST.
• A memorial inside the altar rails is pointed out to us,. which beats a quaint Latin inscrip- tion: There is/ no medicine in the garden Which, eat, conquer death."

* The-Church is quite close to the priory ruins, and 'between the two st.ands a rude stone 'boulder. It is called the Petting Stone, and as married couples leave the chlirck it is custom- ary for the bride to leap over it. No woman in Lindisfarne would consider she had been pro- .perly, Married- if she had not jumped the stone. old or .'young, active Or shy, she must go ! !trough: the ordeal.. But strong men are there lo- give assistance, and the task is not so hard as migTit appear.

div.head: WONDERFUL MANUSCRIPT.
div.p: A WONDERFUL MANUSCRIPT.

The abbey aisles are now carpeted .:with Mari- golds, and wallflowers grow where once the altar: stood. It is a long time since the walls echoed to the psalms of he monks, but the sparrows do their best, and the graceful gullS add their deeper note. . We must not forget to recall, as we wander over the ground where once these patient men lived, that one of the. most precious writings we possess was written here. . In the British Museum is what is called the Durhan Manu- seripta copy of the Latin Gospels inscribed on vellum, and wondrously ornamented. It is a national possession and proud we may well he to have it. Its writer was Badfrid, who wasl infidel' bishop in A.D. 698; after him came Aethelwald, who did the illuminations in colour ::nd gold, and after him Bilfred the Hermit, who itve a rich cover of silver and gold, inlaid with preeiouS stones. Later on Aidred wrote -between the lines a translation in Dano-Saxon, with marginal notes. For eight hundred years the volume was treasured by the monks, and only left the island when Henry VIII. dissolved the monastery. Remembering all that has hap- pened during the past twelve hundred years, we may be grateful indeed that The old writing has surVived.
THE HOLY ISL AND-OF LINDISFARN E
continued.

div.head: ST. ccTimEtirs BEADS.
div.p: ST. ccTimEtirs BEADS.

There are other things WC' should like to see, but the tide returns. quickly. Two hours or twelve is the inexorable rule for visitors to Lindisfarne, and twelve we cannot afford. We should have liked to go and look for St. Cuth- bert's beads, which are to be found on the sea shore. Of these Curiosities, superstitious .folk will give the explanation, recorded in the "Marmion": St. :Cuthbert •sits and toils to frame The sea-born beads that bear his name,

and will show us the rock he fises for lis anvil as he: toils through the night. The scientist will tell us that they are the joints .Of the stems of fossil stone lilies washed from the fossiliferous rocks by the action of the waves. Some of these are as large as a three- penny Piece, and being naturally .perforated in the centre, can be placed upon a string. In earlier days these were eagerly sought by pil- grims, who made them into rosaries, and we learn that they are still gathered and sold by the native. They also, out of the shells that
(Continued :n next column.)

besprinkle their shores, make shell flowers and butterflies, an industry which Holy Island seems to have all to itself. We learn that when the 'Queen visited the island some years ago, they gave her quite a big basketful of them. There is time to take another glance at the 'abbey, and to recall Sir Walter's lines: . . . the Wasting sea breeze keen Had worn the pillar's carving quaint, And mouldered in his niche the saint, Ana rounded with consuming power, The pointed angles of each tower; Yet still entire the abbey stood, Like veteran worn but unsubdued.

The poet's description of the Vault of Peni- li.)lce, said, to have been Made by King Colwolf, Where in a Secret aisle beneath, Coencil Ntas held of life and death, It was more dark and lone, that vault, •
• : Than the worst dungeon cell; Ls too creepy to be introduced upon, a holiday, but the curious reader will find it in the second Canto of " Marmion."

Again we are in the c'art, and the pony—fit successor surely in all patient and plodding qualities to the monks of Lindisfarne—has begun the homeward splash. To the mild Music of the swish of water and sea birds' cries, we make our jolting way. In half an hour his feet strike flinty stones, and we are in rural roads again.

div.head: TABLE TALK.
div.p: TABLE TALK.
The World's Tribute of Interesting
Items of News.
QUAINT AND AMUSING.

Originally started by Sir Robert Hart as the Customs' Postal Service, the Chinese postal ser- vice has now grown to such proportions that two years ago it was taken from the customs and made an independent organisation, with a Frenchman at its head. The Chinese' are great letter writers, and something over 350,000,000 letters were carried by the Chinese posts last year. It is the most extensive and the cheap- est postal system in the world. The Chinese post will carry a letter to any part of China for about three farthings, whether it is sent by rail, or horse, or foot courier.
France's Leaning Tower:

Pisa is not the only place to possess a leaning tower. There is also a little-known one at Etampes, which dates back to the sixteenth century. Recently it was thought that this tower. was leaning too much, and an expert investigation was ordered. The experts, says "Les Nouvelles," have come to the conclusion that the position of the tower has not altered by a millimetre during the past three centuries. Cardinal Richelieu had the tower examined in 1639, and a comparison of the figures then ar- rived at with those of the present experts shows no differende that can be measured by scientific instruments.
A Chinawoman's Hair.

The only pleasure of a-Chinese wonlan. semis to be in dressing her hair. This, remarks the "Family Doctor," is arranged with.extradrdin- ary care and most elaborately. The hair is always black and very long, and is drawn tightly from the face, stiffened with gum, and then piled in coils, wing, and loops, that re- main in position without the aid of hairpins or any other appliances. Not a single hair is out of the place, and the dressing is done to last a week, when the hair is taken down and re- arranged. To prevent the hair becoming dis- ordered during sleep, the only pillow allowed is a small leather cushion, which tits in at the back of the neck and keeps the head in a settled position. .
Aid for Cured Lunatic.

Still another new form of inuniipal has been 'taken up by the city of Berlin in the shape of a bureau for finding .employment for persons released as cured from public luirtilie asylums. It was found that hundreds of such persons had the Utmost difficulty in re-establilh- ing themselves as self-respecting members of society owing to the prejudice agOnst persons who admitted they had spent moths or years In asylums. A bureau has now been estab- lished for the purpose of aiding these. It gives financial assistance until they become self-sup- porting, and in many cases gives employers medical guarantees as to the responsibility of the persons in question. It is said that with few exceptions they turn out to be exceptionally re- liable and capable employes.
Why. the Train Was Late.

_ An express train leaving Madrid, in which Count Ilomanones, the Spanish Premier, had taken a reserved saloon, -was three-quarters of an hour late in starting. Indignant passengers made fruitless demands to the stationmaster that the train should leave at once. The official replied that he was unable to order the de- parture of the train, for a reason that he would not state. Eventually a breathless .messenger arrived from the Premier's house ..carrying a cardboard box, which, to the obvious. rend of Count Homanones, was installed in the reserved saloon. The stationmaster then explained to the passengers that the Premier :had forgotten his top hat and had refused toi alloWlhe train to start without IL

Building 901 Feet. High. • New York has the tallest habitable building in the world. The structure that bears this dis- tinction, however, will in all probability soon lose it, for there is to be built another that will be all of 150 feet nearer the sky than the pre- sent colussus. Plans for the building, which will rise to a height of 901 feet, should the scheme of the projectors—the Pan-American States Association—be, carried out, have been completed ,by Mi.. F. 11. Kimball, who is re- sponsible already for many lofty buildings, in- cluding the thirty-three storey City Investing building,-the Empire building, Adams Express, of thirty-three storeys, and the Trinity "twins," each twenty storeys. Qf the probable cost, it is said that the new cloud-piercer will, perhaps, reach £1,800,000.
Eat Cheese for Meat.
A London physician Claims that cheese is a most important element in the food Of the work- men of that great city. For centuries English- men .have been great beef eaters, and as a con-

sequence their systems have developed a great need for meaty (proteid) foods. .Meat is becom- ing higher in price everyday, and the poor man, finds himself with the meat appetite, but not a meat pocketbook. The only way he can save himself is by taking to cheese. It is claimed that, there is as large an amount of proteid in a half-pound of cheese as there is in a pound of meat, and it costs less than one-fourth as much. In addition to the proteid matter in cheese, there is- a large amount of fat in it, so here .the working man has an excellent substitute for meat, and at a lower cost.
Reviving Animals Nine Minutes Dead.

Dr. A. L. Soresi. of New York, demonstrated at trig recent Medical Congress how the heart's action and respiration had .been restarted in animals after all signs of life had disappeared. He had devised a new method of direct trans- fusion of blood by which he inner lining of the blood vessels of donor and cipient were brought into perfect contact and formed a continuous blood vessel. Animals were bled to death, and when all heart beating had stopped -direct transfusion of blood was resorted to. Heart beating and life had been restored up to seven minutes, after heart heating had - completely stopped. In other cases, where the method was varied, similar results had been maintained nine minutes after heart beating, respiration and any other sign of life had completely dis- appeared.

div.head: WORLD OF LETTERS.
div.p: THE WORLD OF LETTERS.
Literary Gleanings.

LORD LISTER'S LIFE AND WORK. In a beautiful sonnet—called " The chief " W. E. Henley, who was Lord Lister's patient in the first weeks of his Edinburgh professorship, gave a perfect picture in miniature of the great- est healer of our time. Now there is published a full-length portrait of the man in a study of his life and work by Dr. G. T. Wrench. Written in an admirable. style with profound sympathy and ap glowing enthusiasm, Dr. Wrench's life of Lister is a worthy monument to a great man. Here is a personal 'sketcri_ that could- not well 1)4 excelled :

" His-appearance at once impressed those who saw him for the first time with the feeling that they were in the presence of a great man. He was a little above the medium height, was slen- der, and excellently proportioned. He carried himself with singular grace, and every move- ment 'was frauglii, with the ease and control that are the qualities of dignity. • PHs face was one that, without disparagement to his man- hood, could be called beautiful. It had the high thoughtfulness, the unlived nobility, the. evi- dent detachment from momentary matters and absorption in matters that are rooted in eternal truth, which gave to Lister's,more, I think, than to any other English face the wonderful medita- tive serenity and power that- forms the exalted aim of Oriental wisdom."

His equable temper served in Lister to put a just valuation on the bitter attacks which he, as a discoverer, received at the hands of preju- dice, antL. ignorance., Meanwhile Lister- was founding-modern surgery and ,solving the:pro- blem why putrefaction. should follow: the-hr6,..ak- ing. of- the human_ skin. Lister .found - the- -ho9l-- tals- veritable hells. upon earth.. -As. a result of his labours he lest Them comparative. heavens.

div.head: IN A DARK ROOM WITH A KEIIALT.
div.p: IN A DARK ROOM WITH A KEIIALT.
Mr. H. D. Couzens, a civil engineer, whose work has taken him all over the world, tells the following story of what was to him a thrilling experience.

I had retired one niglit in Bombay in a native hotel. The heat had been oppressive, and although I was dog-fired I tossed for hours before I got to sleep. A native hotel in Bom- bay is not the most engaging hostelry, and the weird noises of the night were not conducive to .sound slumber.

About 2 o'clock in the morning I was awak- ened by a queer noise in my room. The night was not so dark but that I could make out some of the objects near my bed. On a chair near to the window was a black snake—a kerait—sway- ing back and forth.

The cold perspiration broke out all over my body. I knew one bite from a kerait would kill. me. The deadly reptile was only three feet away. I. gave a scream for help sand fainted. A few minutes 'later my room Was filled with excited natives. When they revived ine,. I told them about the snake, and a search .was made for the reptile. ' Before the search had •progressed •far I dis- covered what had happened. A stocking tying on a chair by the window had been blown abobt by the wind. In the darkness I had mistaken it for t kerait.
But the thrill was just as terrifying as if the deadly snake were before me. It was the worst fright I ever had.
PERILOUS DUCKING IN A CROCODILE POOL.

Captain Dingle, a soldier, has fought Chinese river pirates and was in the Boer War, has taken part in three expeditions in search of buried treasure, one of which was successful. •There are • few lands in- which he has not ex- perienced thrills; He . writes:— It happened in Calcutta nearly a dozen years ago. I had Missed the tender which was to Lake me back to my ship anchored in the Iloogly river, as the mouth of the Ganges is called. It was long after midnight. There was no way out of, my predicament except. to .take a native loat and row to' my ship, three 'miles down stream. I found two boatmen, and em- barked in their frail craft, which was little more. than two logs bent into the shape of a boat. There was a heavy fog on the river, and we ran aground several times. On one occasion it was ndcessary for one of them to use his feet in pushing off. Almost the very instant that he placed his foot in the water we heard the click of a croco- dile's jaws. In the excitement to escape from the huge reptile the native boatmen upset us. I was thrown into the Water, which was teem- ing with crqcodiles. I could hear their jaws snapping, and every moment I expected to be eaten-alive.

The two natives cried out loudly, and tho shallow waters were lashed into fury by the crocodiles, who fled in all directions. I did not know that crocodiles were arrant cowards, and until we righted out boat and were safe aboard her I passed as thrilling moments as one could ask for.

div.head: FIGIITING THE • QUICK S; iNDS. A Terrible Experience.
div.p: FIGIITING THE • QUICK S; iNDS. A Terrible Experience.

Frederick 11. Chase has searched for gold in Alaska and has. hunted big game in. the Cana- dian North-west, and writes in the "New York World Sunday Magazine " :—I Was preparing to go back-into the Alaskan gold fields on spring, when 'an attractive woman who was spending the winter in SeWard asked me if she could join my party. She was tupcious to reach her brother, a good friend of mine, who was in the interior. -I consented, and we set out together. My. companion proved delightful: Before we had travelled together five.days I was head over heels' in love with her.

Our journey Was comparatively easy until we reached the Copper Valley, which was filled with 'quicksand. We had great difficulty in crossing it, and were forced to make rude bridges of logs. My companion, lost her bal- ance.. While crossing one of these and; fell into the treacherous sands.
I reached :out quickly and seized one of her arms. I kept a secure hold on the bridge for, if I slipped, k knew, both of us would be dragged down until the sand .closed over our heads.

Slowly and with tremendous force, like a huge hungry animal, the sands drew in the body of the' one person in the world for whom I cared. Beadily I would have given up my life that she might be saved. But in order that she live, I must live too.

If ever a man worked hard to cave a human life, I did. She held on to my arms and I pulled and struggled for what seemed to be hours. She was perfectlycalni. The horror of the situation can be appreoiated'only.by one who has seen a person die in .quicksand. She sank to her armpits before I could coun- teract the suction of the sands. Then, exerting all my strength, I managed 'to drag her body out only a• few inches. Another tug and she was half a foot further from death. I struggled and struggled, and finally, through some God- given power, I was able to, get her safely back On the log bridge. Then, she fainted and I fell exhausted by my efforts.

div.head: R%ILWAY SUPERSIITIONS.
div.p: R%ILWAY SUPERSIITIONS.

It is asserted, that while a large percentage of railway employes still indulge in the luxury of a pet superstition, the old-time railroader \\TS as "superstitious as a South Sea Islander and as, full of whims as an Old hougewife." Men, it is stated, did, not 'care to run over the road .unless a horseshoe was fastened to some part of the 'woodwork of the locomotive or caboose. There it a well authenticated case of a brake- man who became demented because he failed to find a freight car bearing a certain lucky number. . One driver used to tell how, when working on a night train, at'a lonely spot, 'the wraith of an old track-walker killed there " ap- peared on the track as natural as life, with his maul over his shoulder, arid alter keeping ahead of the train, which was making a good sixty miles an hour, had disappeared in the bushes." Anothef., driver who was not superstitious afterward thought he saw a similar appearance at nearly the same point, but upon investiga- tion found that the dancing shudow on. the track

was made by a wet maple leaf that had become flattened against the head light glass! Work- ing on his engine alone one dark night, a driver was startled to hear the locomotive bell begin to toll in a very deliberate and nerve- racking manner; but ISeing- of a sceptical turn of mind, he discovered a young cleaner at the other end of the line, the remaining end being fastened to the clapper of the bell. A fireman, inclined to be superstitious, was nearly frightened out of his wits in this way. One of the train men fastened a bell cord to the movable sea upon which the fireman was sit- ting. When the locomotive was passing a spot Where an engineer had been killed, the cord was pulled, causing the fireman to fall -off the seat. For some time after he believed that the dead driver was in some way connected with the occurrence. An elderly Irish cleaner was sent to "fire up" an old engine that was said to be haunted, and a young firenian overheard the foreman giving the order. The fireman crawled into the firebox, and when the cleaner threw in a stick of wood, the fireman threw. it. out. • The old man was startled, but when he saw the second stick come out, apparently without hands, he "took to the woods." Thus another " mystery " was added to the growing collection.—" The Railway Magazine."

ANGLO-INDIAN STUDIi.S. There can be no doubt that Mr. ..T. M. Mitra is doing a real service both to Great Britain and to her .premier Dependency, the Indian Empire, by his indefatigable and whole-hearted effort to play the interpreter between the nations. Mr. Mitra is a Hindu, who knows his country well, and loves it passionately. But he has spent a •good part of his life in England,and understands the English attitude to India just as Well as he understands the Indian sentiment towards Eng- land. And the present volume is an attempt to present the Indian psychology with special reference to the relation between the two coun- tries, so that the English public may be the better able to appreciate the importance of India to the Empire, and the problems which are aroused by the necessity of keeping India in d peaceful, placable and governable state of mind.

As Mr. Mitra insists, there is an unfortunate apathy among the general British public towards Indian interests and politics. India, as he points out, .has one quality in common with England, among many that are dissimilar. It is essentially the home of an aristocratic race. And the great cliance for ,England lies in making the best of the Indian aristocracy, and in bringing them into line with British interests. In his own words "The British Government in India have never attempted 'or desired 'to move the masses, and have no means of doing so if they wished. Of power would be but a cold and crude instrument for the purpose; its efficiency would depend entirely on the force of the sanction behind IL ' The Indian princes, on the other hand, can work through religious influences, which operate _speedily and effectively on the minds of the masses; such influences can be put in motion by the priestly class at Me will of an Indian prince. And this might, indeed, be done secretly without the knowledge •of the British Government., who have been before now taken •by surprise.'.' , Mr. Mitra's *gramme, therefore, is designed to utilise the suggested reform of the House of Lords by giving a direct voice in its delibera- tions to a company of those Indian princes who understand India so thoroughly. These Indilin princes would, in Mr. Mitra's judgment, be able to convince the English Parliament of their obligations towards the native race. As things stand at present, the Indian natives, allnough theoretically admitted to the advantages of British • citizenship, have very little real posi- tion or privilege. Hitherto the main policy of British Govern- ment in India has been 'concentrated upon set- ting Hindu over against Moslem. 'There are on an average three Hindus to every Moslem, and the balance of power has not been difficult to maintain. But during the last few years there has .arisen a vigorous "entente cordiale" between the Hindu and Moslenv elements in the comniunity, and through this movement the influence of the democracy has been very Sen- sibly increased. More especially has the Mos- lem noiver been strengthened by the recent re- moval of the capital to Delhi—a step which Mt. Mitra criticises in no half-hearted fashion. If Mr. Mara is to be trusted, the moral effect of this transference' of the capital is enormous. It carries the national imagination back to the years of untrammelled liberty and independ- ence:

"in transferring the capital (says our author) to the old centre of Indian Imperialism, Eng- land has in a flash aroused memories to a de- gree that thousands of demagogues and agita- tors could not have done in a cenlury. Was it wise to awaken .ambitions and sentiments if they cannot be gratified? It should now be. England's policy to 'make the hundreds of mil- lions of her Indian subjects feel that they are not hopelessly sunk beneath, but living up to, the traditions of their distinguished past as represented by Delhi, otherwise they may weigh 'Britain in the balance and find her wanting. Would' it not be a dangerous experiment for a man to take up his abode with his wife in a -house where she had lived prosperously with It former husband, where everyroom, every de- tail of the furniture, Would speak to her in a hundred voices of the past? Or What would be thought of a man who every morning at the breakfast table .insisted on his wife reading over • the love letters whichther first husband penned to her in their happy courting days? Could he reasonably expect her to turn a smiling face to wards him? Something similar is the risk' that England has unwittingly taken in her new khan capital."

div.head: PARTHENON AS IT IS TO-DAY.
div.p: PARTHENON AS IT IS TO-DAY.

What seems a notable description of a famous ‘,liissie in marble is given by Robert Hichins in the "Century Magazine.". Speaking of the Acropolis, he says: - The Parthenon, as it exists to-day, shattered, almost entirely roofless, deprived of its gilding and colour, its glorious statues, its elaborate and wonderful friezes, its lions, its golden oil- jars, its Athene Parthenos of gold and ivory, the mere naked ,shell of what it once was, is stupendous. No memory of the gigantic ruins of Egypt, however familiarly known, can live in, the thought, can make even the puniest fight for existence, before this Doric iront of Pentelic nthrble. simple, even plain, but still in its devas- tation supreme. The size is great, but one has seen far greater ruins. The fluted columns, lifted up on the marble stylobate which has been trodden by the feet of Pericles and Phidias, are huge in girth, and rise to a height of be- tween 30 and 40 feet. The architrave above their plain capitals, with its projecting ,mould- ings, is tremendously massive. The walls of the cellar, or sanctuary of the temple, where they still remain, are immense. But :now, where dimness reigned—for in the days when the temple was complete no light could enter it except through the doorway—the sunlight has full possession. And from what was. once a hidden place Me passing traveller can look out over land and sea.

Sonic learned men have called the Parthenon severe. It is wonderfully simple. so Simple that it is not easy to say exactly why it produces such an oVerpowering impression of sublimity and grandeur. But it is not severe, for in severity there is-something repellant. something that frowns. It seems to me That the impres- stim ereafed by the Parthenon as a building is akin to that created by the Sphinx. as a statue. It. seems actually to send out like an atmos- phere a 'tremendous calm, far beyond the limits of any severity.

div.p: MORE. MEMBERS \VAN-TED.
My dear Children,—

• One nephew has already sent in ht, favourite bit of poetry, and I hope to have some- thing from every member of the "Corner." There is plenty of time, however, as the coin- petition does not close until the 18th October: What I should like most is yam' assistance to get new members. We are steadily grow- ing in number, but not so fast as I would like to see. You can help considerably by telling your school friends 'about the column, which is all your own, and getting them to send in their names.

'lt is very easy to join our club, and if I have any readers who have not yet joined, let me tell you how to do it. Just write your name, address, and date of birthday on a postcard and send it to "Uncle Jack," "Examiner ". Office, Bewsey-street, Warrington. I shall be delighted to do the rest, and you shall see your names printed amongst our new members. I hope to have a big rush of new members during -the next week. Will 'my nephews and. nieces help me to get triem? I should like to have one big book filled with names before Christmas. That reminds rue. I am thinking .out a big competition for Christmas, but have not deckled quite what form it will take. I shall let you know, however, in plenty Of time.. Now, then, boys and girls, let me see which of you will get the Most new members for our club.
Your loving UNCLE JACK.

Corn 'Race.

The leader of this game seleAs a handful of corn from the bin and holds it tight between the palms of his hands, the other players. stand- ing in a, circle around him.. Then, as in the old game of. " ButAn, Button," the leader puts his closed hands inte the open hands of each of the other players in turn, pretending to drop in the corn„ Perhaps the leader will make,' the round of the players twice, but at the last some child receives the corn. This player is then chased ands only saved from being " it " by being able to give the corn back to the leader before he is tagged.

• Paper-bag Games. A small bag inflated and tightly tied makes on excellent airballvto be batted npward with the palm of the hand. When two or three boys and girls try- to bat it before it falls to the floor there is plenty of excitement. .The bag will stand a good deal of batting. A larger bag filled with wool or pieces of soft woollen cloth, and tied tight, serves well for an indoor football and will do no injury. _ A paper bag, the size of the ordinary punch- ing-bag can be stuffed, tied, caw' hung in the doorway just low enough for a youngster to punch.

Paper bags of any and all sizes will give pleasure when the children want to play store, either „in the house, on the piazza or lawn. Smoothed-out paper bags can be used for kites, and will amuse the little tots. The bags should be tied 164 the window-sill outside, and left to flutter against the panes.

Fables at the Zoo: The Giraffes. Many attempts have been made to strike up a friendship with the giraffes, but they hold their heads so high that this is a matter which is next to impossible. The female hippopota- mus, who lives next door to them, and is one of the most respected inhabitants of the Zoo- logical, Gardens, has the poorest possible opinion of them and. can scarcely speak of the male giraffe without a sneer. It all arose out; of certain friendly overtures made by the hip- popotamus (as one of the oldest inhabitants) to the male giraffe, when he was a newcomer. The female hippopotamus .on almost the first day after his arrival asked him to come and call on her—although she had positively not. the smallest .idea what he was lilie—and with the hospitality for ,which the Zoological Gar- dens are famous, provided a handsome _fish supper for him in the adjoining tank. Natur- ally the giraffe could not partake of -these pro- visions, partly because he does hot eat fish, and partly because, though an excellent wader, he cannot dive.

Hoivever, a few days later when he hcd settled down, and the hippopotamus went to return the call, he invited her to share the meal of hv and straw _which is collected in his manger. As the manger is fourteen feet from the floor, and the hippopotamus is constitution- ally Unable to stand on her hind legs, the bad taste of this im)itation does not need enlarging upon. ." I shouldn't have minded the joke sp much," the hippOpotamus was understood. to say, '" if it jtadn't been old. But sk-fmMhing of the same kind happened some two thousand years ago with the fox and the stork, as NV'S admirably. related by Mr. rEsop." The giraffe is said by his detractors to be an Ungraceful animal. They point to his walk, which is certainly a little clumsy. "The truth is," says the hippopotamus, ", that his neck bas outgrown his strength. and .anyone can see .at a glance that he is pigeon-chested." For my Part I believe that the giraffe's awkwardness is due to his anxiety lest he should hit his head against something, though the house in which he lives is constructed so that nothing hut the grossest carelessness could cause him fa fio this. Time hangs rather heavy on the giraffes' necks M the absence of many intimate friends, and they spend most of their time in eating. The trees round their enclosure are railed to the height of leighteen feet. so that the giraffes shall' not eat them, for the keener rays the bark is always the worse for their bite.

div.head: CASE OF OVERCROWDING
div.p: CASE OF OVERCROWDING

An order to abate a nuisance was issued to James Clarke, on Monday, at Runcorn, at, the instance of the Vrban, District Council, ler overcrowding at his residence, 13, Cambridge.- street. Defendant also had to pay costs, which amounted to 13s. 6d.

Mr. Lake, for the prosecution, said there were only two bedrooms at the house, one 10ft. 9in. by 10ft. Gin., and the other lift, by 10ft. 9in., and that accommodation, according to the Local Government Board, was only sufficient for six adults and one infant. When Inspector Per- cival visited the premises in January last he found there were nine adults and seven children there.

The Council passed a formal resolution to abate the nuisance, and that notice had been served by the inspector. The notice was not complied with, and a summons was taken out. There had been repeated adjournments to allow the defendant to try and get a suitable house.
Charged at the Chester Police Court with attempting to commit suicide by jumping ov,:r the old Dee Bridge, James APNeil, an iron- worker, was discharged. It was stated that he was drunk at the time.

Inquest on the Child Killed by a

div.head: "ACCIDENTAL DEATH."
div.p: "ACCIDENTAL DEATH."

Another fatal street accident occurred last week, when Doris Lee (1), 29, Croft, off Cross- ley-street, was knocked down by a bread van And died from her injuries. The inquiry into the circumstances was held by Coroner S. Brighouse at the Warrington Coroner's Court on Saturday. • Mrs. Lee said she was the wife of James Lee, general labourer. About 11 o'clock on the rhussday morning she took her daughter in Crossley-street to see the soldiers, headed by a band, pass along. They went to the house and deceased then ggt her bucket and spade And went to play amongst sand, whilst she (the mbther) did some washing. A few moments later she heard some women screaming, and on vushing into Crossley-street she was informed that her child had been run over. Dr. Geary was passing and pronounced life extinct. Ernest Butthew, insurance agent, 121, Orford- lane, said that about 11.10 he saw the cart, belonging to Millwood and Sons, bakers, pro- eeding up the street on its right side of the mad. The child got. off the footpath, but how n earth it got past the. horse's hind legs Ile 3 ould not say. However, it did, and the horse tripped the child up and it fell down, the wheel A the van going over its forehead. The horse could be travelling at about • four miles per hour.
In answer to the Coroner, witness said that .the horse had got past and the child walked underneath the shafts at the rear of the animal. The driver did all he could-. •
Stanley Robertson, the driver of the van, 33, firecn-street, said that he heard a scream and Felt the right wheel go up He did nat see the which must have run in from the side of the van.
Detectire-Sergeant Holland said there was n'o lugg,e,Stion that the driver was going fast. From 01 accounts he was practically walking at the time.
The Coroner said Ile knew of a ,case where a lad , had rushed into the horse and come out safe at the other side.„

- A verdict of " Accidental death" • was re- turned, and the foreman of the jury said they would like to know if Messrs. Hallwood were prepared to do anything for the parents. The Coroner: I would rather not interfere in that, if you don't mind. Mrs. Lee: The driver never came to sympa- thise with me at.all. No one has been near. Detective-Sergeant Holland: The driver is only a lad, and .you know what lads are.
The Driver: My mother and I were going down last night, but it got too late. Sympathy was expressed with the bereaved 1)3, the jury.

THE SAILOR MEN.
EDEN PHILPOTTS (A.uthor of "The Poacher's Wife," "The' Whirlwind," etc.).

When old Captain Tuckett of the mercan- tile marine died, everybody thought that his daughter, - Mercy Tuckett, would give up Dunnabridge Farm and go away from Dar,- moor; Out she didn't. He took to farming when-he left the sea, though 'twas only just a pastime with him and he didn't make ,much money, if any at all, at Dunnabridge. Bu H t he liked the 'Moor and always said that, after the rolling sea; 'twos the best place he knowed; and so he caine there and spent a bit of his savings and enjoyed his fag end of life. A widower he was. with but one .child, Mercy by name; and when he died, two year short of eighty, Miss Tuckett might have been hovering a year or two over tay per- hap9, though Eh e didn't leek that by five or six year at the least. And I was in the early sixties myself—a widower and a sailor also. I'd sailed as mate, along with Miss Mercy's father and known her ever since she was a young and comely girl; and when my missis died and the days of mourning were passed, I began to hanker after my old skipper's daughter; and I wes hankering yet, though I'd been a wiiew _man fifteen year at the time of this queer tale. You ace I dwelt up to Princetown village and kept a small house of refreshment there; and as Miss Tuckett's farm weren't abeee, five 'mile off, Awes a very common thing, for me to drive over and offer myself in Marriage from 'time to time as the fancy took me. It had get to be a sort of holiday amusemetit for both Of Us you might say; and ttiou. she always refused me, there weren't no stieg to it and I went on trying and feeling that when the right moment came and I catchcd chheranjguest to , n tyhees.Prolpercanni?tods,ayhel was in any no' would great hurry myself. She was a clever farmer and took to it, and she'd got a Dartmcor woman, named A:ice Mumford, for her right hand at Dunne- bridge; and what them two females didn't know about Dartmoor farming weren't worth knowing. The hinds went in terrible fear of Alice, no man nearer than Plymouth was ever known to over-reach her. Spinsters both, but very different, because Miss Tuck- at, while firm was kind and full of the milk of human nature, but Miss Munaford— it is enough to say that her grandfather was hanged for sheep-stealing and her father died just in time to escape the heavy hand of the law. And she WaS a hard case and I never liked and never trusted her neither. There .corned a day—just after Easter Bank Heliday 'twas--when.l left my little ,licensed house to my .potinan and drove over to have a bit of fun with Mercy Tuckett. And she M had news. for me and I felt more pleased than not to know that Alice Mumford was going to leave. So far as love-making went it herself no excited doubt, because ercy found k ore think about anything else but t'other woman. In fact wages, and as e she took it a good bit to heart and dressed down her old friend pretty sharp. In a word eimkingralsoedr motwreie in eighteen Aliceshe 'd was str ads , months a'ready, her missis began to fear .you can pay too dear for anything, and told her she mustn't be so grasping. With that Vother used coarse language and said she was the backbone of Dunnabridge, and as- sured Miss luckett that she'd have the brok- ers in before a twelvemonth was passed if she got rid of her. But my Mercy, SO to call her, had plenty of pluck and she hit out from the shoulder—with her. tongue I mean —and in a word, Alice Mumford had given notice and was going that day month. And go she did; but she didn't go far. There was an empty cottage to Brownberry —a homestead not above half a mile from Dunnabridge, and there went Alice Mumford and lived on her savings, which was account- ed pretty heavy; and she lost no opportunity to say untrue and unkind things of her old mistress. • Her cot stood by the highroad over the Moor, while Dunnabridge hung back a lot and rose up over Dart, where the river runs in a great loop of water full of rocks with fume brakes on the banks. The old farm had been pulled down afore the Tucketts went there and a stout modern house had taken its place; but the fields were the same as ever; and the old tar-pitched bard, with the granite steps still stood there, and the spinneys up over, on the hill top above, were a pretty sure draw for a fox most hunt- ing. days. Dunnabridge used to be all mud and slush and chickees and pigs and ducks in wet weather; and there was an old stone over the water trough, by an aged white- thorn, that haven't been moved' for cen- turies. And you might generally, see a tor- toise-shell cat with a brOken paw -lopping about in the yard or coming down the wocd- en ladder from the loft. It couldn't have been the same cat, for I'd knowed the place twenty year by the time of this tale; but a lame cat have always been part of the furni- ture of the farm, and a bob-tailed, black and • • grey sheep-dog was generally to be seen about also. When next I called on Mercy the inVstery of the sailor men was in full Swing and, as an old sailor man myself, it interested me amazing. I noticed a change in her and was a good deal surprised to find her a thought snappy, which was curious, for a, milder tem- pered woman by nature never drew breath. . Holne Revel 'twas, and I stopped to Dun- nabridge on my way back, to imck a bit of supper with Mercy and give her the news. We talked on general subjects, and then she said, ••y stets ! I never knowed you so dull,. Thomas." • 'Twas a hint and no mistake, for alone, with the revel, and Farmer Redland fallina down in a fit by the steam-roundabout, ana one thing and another, I'd forgot the matter as always passed between me and Mercy when we met after a few menths absence. "Well you may say it," I replied to her. "You might a'most think I was' market-mer- ry t) have forgot ! " •• I wish you • was," she answered. "I'd sooner have you like that than Hien, this. Here be I—a lonely, forgotten worn /h that none ever calls upon, except tramps begging for a meal, and voie---as haven't seen me since Neah's floods4'l should think—can't tell nothing livelier than news of a man I don't know tallinog down in a fit." ," I'm badly to blame," I Gadd. •f.` Never was such a know-nought great zany as me." With that I plunged into the usual thing and offered my heert and hand, and told that I was steadfast as the northern star and true as the needle to the pole, and the rest of it. "Now Alice Mumford be gone," I said, "your state is most forlorn and I wish to God you'd change it. Here be I living a lone- ly life up the hill, and you living a lonely life down the hill, and whf, to goodness you can't see the foolishness She got a lot happier when I struck into the familiar, subject and let ITIQ take heir hand as usual. She put her fine fdce to mine, and blinked her beautiful pale brown eves; and somehow I felt as she was in a more yielding frame of mind than ever I'd known her to .be since her father died. 'Twas the. influence of Alice Mumford gone no doubt, for that whey-faced and cross-eyed creature was always a ferocious man-ater—owina doubtless to the fact that the male sex baa no use for her from her youth V.% She KO that 'twas along of her grand:Lathe,: bent halted V•other side pf the Moor; but 'tyres- el at all; because no fair-minded man would let a little thing like that stand between himself and a nice woman if he loved her. But, Alice was that curst and vinegary end evil-minded that no man ever had offered for her; and now the time was past and she hated 'em all. ,
Her being once wen apay froni Minna- bridge however, a change had clearly come ..)v,r Mercy TzeteLt, ar-d raaa though. I was, the unexpected softnesa of her took me a bit

by surprise bcc you see, never count- ed Iva' it, an i oas ike a bolt from the blue to find, after all this time that she want- ed for me to kisS her—a thin I'd- offered to do for fifteen year ait.,l be-eu re2used. In fact a man bah:Pt screwed up to a feat like that in a minute, and I lost my self-control and held .off. I saw in a twinkle, the case was al- tered and that I Lad but to p in and win; And very well ..plea3ed and nility proud I was; but the c_imax of my love aft'air had come too sudden and startling. - I wanted to think over it all. I'd got. into a. sort cf 'hab- it of paying court and expecting no' for an answer; ana to find Mercy. viii.aclenly altering the run of the game like this here, rather flabbersted mr. u Englisii I wase't sorry when, at the critical there came a loud knock at the Th(T:: was r,_c-2,2 to home but h:r, for h:r men and maid we...-e to Hone Revel, 68 she had to rise up and go; and , while she was away, I steadied myself and resolved that I wouldn't return to the subject of marriage. no more that day, but come to it—in all the solemn pomp such a thing -demanded—some- where about next Michaelmas, if not later. There was a powerful lot to think of, and since we'd been fiddling and philandering for fifteen, year, I felt there Couldn't be no crying need to rush it now at a woman's whim.

She came back crusty as an ill-cooked loaf. "Another of them sailor man," she said. "A plague on 'em. ! They tell each other, .believe, and not a day goes now but one and sometimes two, bain't here. And 'half of 'em be rogues and not sailors at all I'll war- rant."

You see, when her father was dying, he told Mercy never ta turn away an old sailor, and she never did. But now she told me how more and more came, and as by her fa- ther's orders, every such man was to have sixpence and a full meal, the thing got be- yond a joke. "They was a nuisance from the first, and thought myself ill-used," said Mercy Tuck- ett to me as he cut the beggar a lump of bread and cheese and poured him a mug of cider; " but, it have got worse by laaps an bounds of late. half-a-crown the men had out of ma last week, wad this is the second have called since Thursday last."

"And turnpike sailors I'll wager," I an- swered her. You can bring him in here and I'll sit behind this screen and mark him while he eats. You ask him about the sea, and I shall very soon know by his remarks if he can tell a marling-spike from a reefing- block or a boom from a bowsprit." She obeyed me, and I hid and listened to a cockney tramp, who may or may not have seen the mud barges in a canal, but had cer- tainly never met with anything noble: afloat. He guzzled, and tippled, however, and took his tanner, and I secd the back of him as he went off. He was cad in sailor's clothes, and that was all could be said for the man.

When he was gone Mercy cast about how she could manage to escape from her promise to her dead father. " My heart sinks when I see the creatures gaming down the yard," she said. "Some be 'old and some be young; some be ginger and some grey; some go lame and some lack an arm or a hand; but they're all dressal in that horrid blue with them dirty trousers tight to the knee and loose below; and they've all got the sante talp about a ship at Plymouth—except the maimed ones. They mostly say they ha owed money by the State an have to ga to the Docks to g3t it. Ro- gues !' I itch to set the dog on 'em; but suppose father would turn in his grave if I did."

For my part I smelt a fraud from the first and by good chance on that wry day, while yet 'twas broad light, there happened that to make my doubt a certainty. Not an hour after the cockney was gone, another sailor man turned up; and I did as before and told Mercy to ietch him in the kitchen and let him feed, while I listened un- seen. Of course he was np more a sailor than my pot-boy, and when she asked him about the perils of the deep, he told my nautic- al ear in half a minute that he was only a wolf in sheop's3 clothing and knew •nought of the seaman's life. But that didn't astonish me; what did was the squint I got of his back view as he went off. Then I stared in- deed, till my eyes very near bulged out of nri head.
Mercy thought me mad,- for, forgetting my hat and everything, I went cif after the sham sailor and loped along behind a stone wall and kept him in sight unbeknownst to him.

He marched down the road on very good terms with himself, and I saw him as far as Alice Mumford's cottage in the high road. But there he stopped and went in. With that I crept nearer, till I was right abreast of the house; and I squatted under the wall, like a hare in her form. and bided ray time, patient as you please, for I was playing a winning' game and well I. knowed it. In ten minutes a man come out of the cot- tage, but he didn't come alone. Another man .followed him; and the first man was the first sailor as had called at Dunnabridge, and the second man was the second sailor as had done so. They'd doffed their sailors' togs and they walked off in very good humour clad like a pair of scare-crows, after the man- ner of tramps as a rule. "We'll call again some fine day, ma'am," they said to Alice Mumford, who stood at the door to see 'em go; but she didn't answer, because she was counting pennies, as one of the rogues had give her before they set out. Of course I seed the whole wicked trick at a glance; but I was too clever to pounce on the woman at that time. Instead I trotted back to Mercy Tuckett and made a bit of- mystery about it and puzzled her not a little. 'Twas my wish you see, to distract her mind from the subject of matrimony, and I didrilt stop very long then. but got on my horse and galloped away pretty soon. "Fret no more about anything," I told her when she came to see me off in the dimp- sy light. "'Twas rare good fortune . as brought me to you to-day, Mercy Tuckett; because the luck be double-barrelled by the look of it; and I've heard what will be a great source of joy to me, when I've had time to think it oyer; and I've found out what will be a grqiit relief to you presently. But I must go, cautious in both matters and not do nothing rash or reckless. Only this I'll promise you: I've found out where your sailor men come from, and you shan't much longer be troubled with them." She looked at me dangerously and come close and put up her hand to mine as I settled myself on the saddle. "There's one sailor man as would never tie nO trouble to me,". she .said.
" And what might his name be ?" I asked, feeling pretty safe wrclied up on my saddle well out of her reach. "Thomas Sweet's the man's name," she answered. •

'Twas me, of course, and her eyes in the light of the evening very near brought me off my hoss again. But the sudden nature of it had shook me and I felt in justice to myself, as well as the woman, that I must let a few days pass. " ljave no fear for Tom Sweet," I to7d her, guarded like and then I rcde away with plenty to think upon. But, after all, I let another man get the credit for my cleverness. Before a week, but not till I had received a strong letter from Mercy I 'went over to Yr. Byles, at the po- lice-,tat:oir., and toid hiiii of the gr2at mys- tery what I'd found out.

1:i; like-, this here, Constable Byles," I said to the, man. " Mis `Puckett ,dismisse m c‘ that woman,' Alice Muford, from- her ser- vice a while back, and Alice, wirti have got bad blood. in her without 'a doubt, swore to a. revenged upon her for so doing. And she have been revenged, for since she went, there have come.. a proper plague of sailor men to Dunn.abruhre. and owinv to her pro-

Inne to ner (lead father, Mercy Tuczett, have had to suffer 'em. • And, when I was there last, one came and I Watched him- hid- den behind an 'old 'satire: screen that Miss Tuokett have lately bought, to keep the wind out of her back hair on winter nights; and I heard in a jifiev :beat ha was no sailor; and I also noted that .the man had a black patch on his jumper. Away he ,went, and. pre- sently up CO th te another scamp—another sailor if you'll credit it ! Well I watched him, likewise, and I stared I Warn you, for if he hadn't a black patch on his jumper also ! And now you'll do well to send one of "a'our m:n to lie lachint the h:f.e.3 -there. Then. they'll flnl out wlizia a tramp gees by Alice Mumford's cottage or calls at it, .S the case' may be, she has. him in her house, and rigs him up in, a suit of sailor's clothes, and sends him off to Dunnabr:dge, where there's a square meal and a certain sixpence await- ing the thief. Then back he goes to her, and as I saw her ceunting pennies the time I was on the' watch, I make no doubt.' at all that she be very well paid for all her trouble. 'Tis the most barefaced imposition I ever heard' tell about on Dartymoor and you'll do well, Constable Byles, to look in the matter and see it den't happen ne more." . Was a youag officer, with his spurs to win, and he fastened on the job, like a dog to a bone. In fact he took it on himself, and three days later it happened just as I told him it would happen, arid he arrested anether fellow coming gaily off from Dunna- bridge with sixpence in his pocket and a full meal in his belly and a black patch on his juniper. Sc when next I appeared in public 'twas to be a witness against Alice Mumford; and the justices gave her six weeks hard for 'what she'd done; and she swore something sinful in open court and premised to make it hot both for me and Mercy 'Puckett when. she corned out of klink again. . But she never had the chance to do us no more wickedness, for a let may happen in six weeks and before the end of that time, when Alice was let loose on a trusting world once more, I'd taken Mercy's lead and fin. ished our affair out o' hand. I thought it out, you. sce, and my eennnon. sense corned to my rescue, and I said to my- self, ".Thomas Sweet, 'weet, you've been at this here weman to take you for fifteen year. and now, because- she's at Aast ready and willine• to do so, you grow faint about, it, and find yourself in two minds. 'Tis all very well to Eay you're a creature of habit, and that this be a bit of aii upset, by reason of its sudden falling out: but what the mischief would you have ?" Blig, of course, a reasonable man, I aeon rose to the situation, and got ac- cust:med to the idea of Mercy 'Puckett as a wife, and took her for that purpo. In a fortnight from the end of tll,l men, we was tokened; and a month later, with all the dash and fire of yotth, n plunged into matrimony. All Princeton was to the wedding pretty near; and whc that Alice Mumord cama back to I3rownberry n she heard as her old mistress was lifted up to be Mrs. Sweet, and on her honeymoe at that moment.. And she likewise heard that Dun- nal:ridge was to be let or sold; be?eanse mer_ ev had decided to give it up and come to frineetown and throw in her lot with my business. But my little place was far- too small for the likes of her, and 'tis settled that we take " The Snowball Inn." after Christmas. 'Tis a tidy sized place, and the last man worked up a goOd business, so I'm hopeful that us shall do very' clever 'there.

VERDICT OF "lOUND DROWNED."

An hi-quest was held by Coronrig louse, Ber at Warrington on Saturday. morning, body of \\,,illiarn Woolley (34), wire'w 1", the Cartwright-street, who was found drl-eld' in the Sunk 86, Canal the previous Thursdane eY Mrs. Woolley said that her husband had nearly always been a very healthy man, and drng the eleven years she had been married hhn he had not been attended by a doctor until the 23rd of last month. He was then suffering from pneumonia, 'and was attended by Dr. Manson. About 1.0.10, on the previous Wednesday she gave her husband a powder and a tablespoonful of whisky, according to orders. Ile appeared to go to sleep, but about midnight he asked her for a drink, and she gave him milk and soda. They talked for an hour, and lie, then said that he .would like her to go to his Mother's house and bring her back., She (witness) pointed out that his mother could do no good, but he was so persistent that she was obliged to go. His mother's house was a quar- ter of a mile away.

Disappeared from Home. They returned as soon as possible, and imme- diately missed deceased's jacket and vest. On oing • to the bed they discovered that .he had g out. An alarm was, raised, and neigh- h ou rs s Hlcd round about. William Little- ear 78, cartwright-street. yeturned with de- ceased's Gap, which he had found on the bank of the canal. About 7.30 the body was recov- qed from Me canal. In nnswer to the Coroner, witness said that deceased seemed to be quite all right, lie talked quite sensible, and was very quiel. .;he had no suspicion -that he was going to do any- thing to himself. The coroner : Did it make h'..rn light-headed rind talk silly? No. He never talked 'silly, \\lmam Littlefair, geneyal labourer, deposed to finding the cap and afterwards seeing the I,od Vrecovered. The coroner: Detective-Sergeant Holland says that although deceased was not delirions. a medical Mall had expressed the opinion that delirium was corning on, The lucy returned a verdict of " Found „,.,,,yruld." and expressed the sympathy with the relatives.,

div.head: REMARKABLE CONFESSION.
div.p: A REMARKABLE CONFESSION.

An extraordinary story is revealed in, Chicago 'by • the arrest of a man, named Henry .Spencer, on suspicion of shooting and killing Mrs. Mil- dred Rexroat, a dancing teacher, and subse- quently placing the body on the railway track. Spencer is alleged to have coolly confessed to this and 13 other murders, all of which (except two) were committed for the purpose of robbery. The two exceptions were two policemen, whom lie is said to have 'shot twelve years ago when escaping arrest. Ten murders, five of women and five of Men, were committed, it is said, during the past year, some of the victims having been shot and others battered with _a hammer. •

---S-ITencer in his confession is alleged to h:-.Bv(, declared : " I have been a thief all my life t killed women to obtain money. ' That was the easiest way to live." Spencer also admitted that he was an opium fiend: • iThe police, while doubtful as to whatll,:r Spencer is guilty of all the murders, are n- vinced that he committed several of them, anti say that 'be is the most dangerous homicid9.l maniac who has been arrested for years past.

div.head: WATER PLO.
div.p: WATER PLO.
WARRINGTON BEAT CHESTER.

The Water Polo League fixtiftes were com- pleted by Warrington on Monday, when they met Chester at Chester. Warrington defended the deep • end. Turner scored from near goal. Hughes equalised. - Dutton followed with an- other goal for the'holuesters. Peers replied for Warrington. Turner added a further goal. In- terval: Warrington, three goals; Chester, two goals. Chester .attacked, Chadwick. bringing the scores level. Peers scored twice and Turner registered his third goal. Jolley saved cleverly on several occasions. Final: Warrington, six goals; Chester, three -goals.'

div.head: Annual Prize Distribution.
div.p: Annual Prize Distribution.

A succelsful smoking concert was held in tha. Blue Bell Hotel, Horsemarket-street, on Wednesday evening, the occasion - being the annual prize distribution in connection with the Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds (A.U.), Warrington district bowling main. Major A. F. G. Potter presided, and Bro. J. Fulton- Smith presented the prizes. There were also present amongst others Bro. W. E. Clegg; Prov. •Chief Shopherd; Bros. James Parr (district .L.W.-Pomfrey, Py.C.S., T. C. Duck- worth, P.P.C.S., P. L. Edgar (district secre- tary), and P. Peacock (Mayor-elect), district treasurer Ancient Order of Foresters.
The Chairman proposed the toast of the "Duke of Lancaster," and also the toast of the Queen and the Royal Family. The King's toast was accorded musical honours.
Later the Chairman said he had heard that some societies wore in a bad way at the present time, but they hoped for the success of the future. (Applause.) •

Mr., Smith then presented the prizes to the following: Mr. John Warburton ("Greenall" Challenge Shield and marble clock), Bros. J. Atkinson, Harry Higham, Hugh Ratcliffe. C. Crozier, W. Hadcroft. Jos. Massey, Wm. San- ders, Harry .11Iather, W. Ratcliffe, R. Warbur- ton, Harry Carter, Ben Higham, Thos. Potter, Jas. Cart, Jos. Holcroft, W. H. Jackson, Wm. Massey, T. S. Champion, R. H. Halford, H. Lawton, A. Warburton, Fredk. Dale; W. Brace- girdle. E. Jones, Herbert Twiss, Jos. Harding, John Lingard, John Warburton, Jos. W. Porn- frey, IL Johnson and H. Daniels.

Bro. Warburton briefly replied and said he had previously been in the last six, eight and four, • and wast proud to win the trophy that year.. (Applause.) Mr. Smith said that what they required now was to have the society funds in their own hands, and not dissipated by interference from outside. They could perhaps side-track the In- surance Act by promoting some scheme which would help members of a society in times of diStress; perhaps something to educate their children at a higher rate in school,, or even to get an extra suit of clothes per year. ..,(Ap- plause.) Councillor Peacock proposed and Bro. W. E. Clegg seconded, a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Smith. Bro. T. C. Duckworth proposed and Bro. F. S. Massey seconded, a vote of thanks to tile prize donors and artistes, and thanks to the Chairman were awarded, on the oroposition of Bro. J. W.-Pomfrey, seconded by Bro. James Parr.
A talented programme was presented by Mr. W. Whittle, an excentionally clever humorist; Bros. Percy Smith, E. T. Rogers and W. Den- nett.

div.head: TOWN WIPED OUT.
div.p: A TOWN WIPED OUT.

The 'town of Norne, Alaska, has been destroyed by a storm. • Five hundred houses, says a cablegram, were demolished and other are still falling. Men and women are working with icy seas breaking over the town in an endeavour to save their household goods. i The loss is estimated at one and a half ilhion dollars.

div.head: Skeihorn Signs On.
div.p: Skeihorn Signs On.

Skelhorn ought to be an acquisition to the front rank, who just require a hustler of his type to bind the pack together. , lie has got over the difficulties which arose at the commence- ment of the season. Skelhorn attended at the meeting of the committee on Wednesday even- ing, agreed to the terms the committee set forth, and signed on. He is reported to be in condition, and I am hoping to see him give us a taste of his old form.

Harmer, although he did good work on Satur- day, has been relegated to the "A " team, to make way for Skelhorn, but it may not be long before he is back again. Otherwise the side is much the same as Saturday. They will pro- bably come up to the mark as follows

div.head: ENCOURAGING THE PLAYERS,
div.p: ENCOURAGING THE PLAYERS,

The Warrington Committee are doing their best to encourage the players to put their, best foot forward. A scheme for ,furthering foster- ing the players' interest in the winning of matches was adopted at the meeting of the committee. on Wednesday night. The offer is made of .„tlOO to the' first team men if they finish in the first four teams at the top of the League. The money will be divided amongst the men according to the number of matches in which they have participated.
GEORGE ETURNS THANKS. We have received the following from Dicken- son :

should like, through the medium of your columns, to express tmy sincere thanks to the many friends who made my benefit match on Saturday last so great a success. I realise to the full how the committee have laboured hard to ensure its completion, and also pay a high tribute to the splendid way the Press has assisted me. It is due to their co-operation that the financal returns reached such satisfactory dimensions. To the players, both St. Helens and Warrington, my thanks are also due, and in conclusion I hope that I shall be spared for many seasons to maintain the prestige of the club of my native town.—Yours, &c., GEORGE DICKENSON. 101, Winwick-road, • October 20th, 1913.

div.head: FIRST DEFEAT OF THE "A" TEAM.
div.p: FIRST DEFEAT OF THE "A" TEAM.

The " A " team met with their first defeat on Saturday. This happened at St. Helens, where a Stiff game ended in a win for the " Saints " by 21 points to 18. The score fairly represents the general trend of the game, but Warrington had not the luck which came the way .of the home side. If they had had a share of it the score would have been different.

Ruddick played- a capital game at half. The "little 'un" was everywhere when he was needed. Way-well was an active worker in the threequarter line. Cri,tchley and Green were conspicuous in the pack. C. Brown, who was transferred from Leigh, made a good appearance in the thr,eequarter line and played well in conjunction with the others.

div.head: ANOTHER NEW PLAYER.
div.p: ANOTHER NEW PLAYER.

The Warrington "A" team have a stiff journey to go at Wilderspool to-day, when they meet the Oldtaam Reserves. There should be a big gate, as this is one of the reserve matches of the season. Some good play is assured.

Bramhall, Rylarids' full-back, will appear as custodian of the "A" team. His abilities in that position are too well known to enumerate, and Warrington have done a good stroke of business in securing his services. Another League club had an eye upon him, but War- rington have now signed. Bramhall on. It is a bit hard, all the same, on Rylands', who, since last season, ~have lost Bramhall, Hennes-, sey to Salford, and Leah to Swinton. The "A" team will be : Bramhall; Baker, C. Brown, Daintith and Davies; A. Brown and Douglas; Harmer, Nay- lor, Blundell, Bevan, Green and Critchley. The Oldham team will be: Cook; Finnerty, Oliver, Swithenbank and Young; Shannon and White; Metcalf, Groves, Wise, -McCabe, Owens and Liversedge.

div.head: TRAP4TER GOES ON STRIKE.
div.p: TRAP4TER GOES ON STRIKE.

Tranter, who was selected to turn out for the " A " team against St. Helens on Saturday, re- fused to do so almost at the last moment. This the committee look upon_ as a breach of discip- line, and the player was reported to a full meet- ing of the committee held on Wednesday even- ing. , The matter was carefully investigated, arid the committee decided that Tranter should not have acted as he did. They decided to suspend him for two weeks.

div.head: "WIREMEN" STILL WINNING.
div.p: THE "WIREMEN" STILL WINNING.

Cadishead Their Latest Victims. From a spectators' point of view, the game at Gorey-lane between Rylands' Recreation and Cadishead, in -the Manchester League, was not a " great " one. Neither side were at full strength. Sid. Carter was an absentee from the Rylands' team, and this meant a re-shullling of the players, Bramliall playing centre and Warren operating on the wing in place of F. Horrocks, who went full-back. Welsby, one of the reserve forwards, was also brought into the team at the last moment. The Recreation fully deserved 'their victory of 13 points to five. Taken all round, they were a much quicker lot than the Cadishead men, who somehow could do nothing right. The first score came through a beautiful piece of "bluffing" on the part of Warren, who sent Floyd over for a well-earned try. Bramhall, however, failed with the kick. On one occasion Warren most certainly should have scored, hut he was badly obstructed ly a Cadishead player. This glaring offence, how- ever, escaped the notice of the referee, and it was exceedingly hard lines on the "little 'un," who was showing rare resource. Connor re- peatedly broke away for Cadishead, but he lacked support, and Povey .made desperate efforts to break through without success, and at the end Of a rather tame first half Rylands' led by one try to nil. MUCH BETTER FOOTBALL IN SECOND

div.head: HALF.
div.p: HALF.

Immediately on resuming, Cadishead pressed, and were awarded a penalty for obstruction, score for :Hylands', after a splendid dribble, and Warren had no difficulty in adding the extra points. After midfield play; P.ovey gatherect the ball smartly and raced away, scor- ing a very fine try. The same player, however, failed, with the kick. Ryland? were now doing most of the pressing, and from a rush Slater got over. Bramhall landed a beautiful goal. Soon after this the whistle went, the final scores being: 'Rylands' Recreation, 2 goals 3 tries (13 points); Cadishead, 1 goal 1 try (5 points).

div.head: COMMENTS ON THE GAME.
div.p: COMMENTS ON THE GAME.

The. Recreation fully deserved their win. There was little to choose between the teams in the first half, Rylands', however, being much quicker in their movements. After the change of ends there was no doubt 'as to which was the superior side, and the " Wiremen's" stamina seemed to be better than the visitors'. For Rylands', F. Horrocks played a sound game at full-back, and was far ahead of the visiting custodian—Mears—who at times showed, very poor judgment, his kicking being at fault. The threequarters all played well. • Bramhall shaped very well at centre, although we much prefer to see him in the full-hack position. He kicks with rare judgment and is indeed a tower of strength to the " judgment, Warren played brilliantly on the right Wing. and showed good judgment. He is a very tricky player, and a great favourite with the home spectators. Griffiths also . did splendid work on the other wing. Floyd and Gallop played well together at•half-back and made many nice openings. The forwards packed Much better than the opposing sextet, the most noticeable in the loose being Slater and Welsby. Cadishead were best repre- sented in the threequarter line by Povey and Povey, by the way,. is a Warring- ton sprinter, and he showed a rare turn of speed when he scored his try. Connor, at half, played a good game, but he was poorly supported, and much of his dashing work went a-begging. Of -the, ,Cadishead forwards, no one was more in the picture than Harry Forster, the old Warringtonian, who has delighted many ,a Wilderspeol crowd with his dashing displays.'
