div.head: PICKS OUT OF THE SCRUM.
div.p: PICKS OUT OF THE SCRUM.

Pithy Points About the Games. There is still life in the veteran. George played a capital game. His best for a long time, it was. You should have heard the cheer When George made his fine mark. St. Helens came over to win. They were sure, certain, positive. However, they didn't count on George. Dickenson was a thorn in their flesh. "They're too hot stuff for us 1" Such was a " Saint's " remark After his side was nicely beaten.

**** * * ' An "expert" said Turtill was the back. There was no man equal to him. Jolley was not equal. to Turtill. No, for Jolley was his superior. The little 'un was in a merry mood. He simply rollicked in the game. What secret has Jolley in his boots? Some folk would like to know if The -Warrington back has a mascot there. if not, how. does lie get the goals? ' Jolley has a secret, but it's simple. He kicks with sound judgment.

* * * * * * Renwick has scored his first try. It was an exciting moment to him wen he did so. Even for the Moment the referee was affected. That was a testimony to the brilliant try. Renwick ran like a New Zealand deer. We want a lot more of the same kind. Now he has got into form, possibly Renwick will do his best to oblige. . Nicholas was in running form also. He scored a very neat try, indeed. Pope is said to. be the best hooker in the League. Pearnley beat him at that game.

* * * * * * Daintith made a " dainty " re-appearance. • He did his work most skilfully. Some nice runs he inade. Trenwith did not like him at all. Cheshire wished him in Cheshire. Instead of on the Wilderspool pitch. Daintith held up the cracks finely. The two " Saints "Were not•pleased by that. Harmer was a bit of a hammerman. He put every ounce into his work. His presence improved the home pack. Harmer also showed that he can run.

,*** * * * Oldham to-day! What will be our fate? Shall it be a clever win? ' Shall it be a big rout? , If the hustling game is played, There Is a good chance for Warrington. Boys, you will have to go the pace. Jolley, get your sleeves rolled up, You will have your work cut out. Just do as you did at Huddersfield. Worry the life out a them, And perhaps Warrington will win. * * * * * *

Rylands' are still winning. Saturday's victory was a good one. The team was re-shuffled. F. Horrocks played well as custodian. He is a most versatile player. Superior speed did the trick. Warren is a born blnffer.. This trick led to the first score.

div.head: Latchford Secure a Fine Win in Cheshire Cup
div.p: Latchford Secure a Fine Win in Cheshire Cup
at Sale.

div.head: IN TERESTIMG LOCAL LEAGUE MATCHES.
div.p: IN TERESTIMG LOCAL LEAGUE MATCHES.

Of all the matches on Saturday, the one which ap‘pealed most to the supporters of this code in the town was that played at Atkinson- road, Sale, between the Brooklands Club and Latchford, in the Cheshire Amateur Cup-tie, Senior. Competition, and which match was made also interesting to, the Latchford supporters by the fact that the club had the assistance of J. C. Bardsley, the amateur International, who has promised to assist the club whenever his busi- ness will allow him.

The home team were at full strength, but the visitors were minus two of their selected players. Haspill missed his train connections, and Robinson, through some unexpected busi- ness, was unable to make the journey. Happily for the visitors, they had two reliable reserves to fall back upon in Stubbs and Siddall, and both acquitted themselves with credit in their first senior engagement.
By "Linesman."
Referee, Mr. G. Rushton

more effective, and an attack was made on the home goal, only to he driven back by Pemberton. A fine pass by Carter set Taylor going on the left. He sent across a fine centre; Lees fastened on the ball, beat the opposing backs:** and ,easily bested Wignall, scoring the first goal 'after 25 minutes' play. - Having drawn first blood, the visibors now settled down to their game and took up the attack. Smith, Pember- ton and Makin got plenty to do to clear the on- slaught on their citadel, but the visitors were not to be kept out. Smith, of Latchford, beat Ogden, raced down the right, and from near the corner-flag, made a capital centre, which completely beat Wignall. He thus scored the visitors' second goal. From the centre kick there was a short spell of midfield play, and the visitors got into the home quarters. Lees again scored. At half-time the visitors were leading by three goals to nil.

On resu-ming the second portion, the visitors were the first to attack, but did not give Wig- nail niuch trouble. Then the home team were beginning to show signs of distress. They were not able to keep up the pace they started with; and the visitors, having fairly got the measure of their opponents, were chiefly attacking the home goal. The local players made occasional raids on the visitors' quarters, only to be driiven back by Stubbs and Bardsley. After 20 minttee nlay, Lees made a splendid individual attemnt. Receiving•the ball in his own half of the field, he dribbled down, and beat the opposing backs. Wignall left his charge to meet him, and Lees had no difficulty in placing the ball into the empty goal, thus performing the "hat trick." The same player scored again before the finish. The final whistle left Latchford winners by five goals to none.

Pemberton, Makin. Parkinson and Robinson played well for the 'home team, and Bardsley, Downs, Webb, Smith and Lees were the pick of the visitors. Lees scored four goals out of the five gained by his side.
WARRINGtON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. Weaver Refining Co. v. Weston.

This match was played at Acton Bridge, on the ground of the former club, before a good crowd of spectators. The home team winning the toss, Hulse set the balL rolling for the visi- tors, and the home half-backs gaining* posses- sion served their 'forwards_well. The visitors' defence was soon in difficulties, and underwent a prolonged and severe attack, when Barnes deliberately handled' in the dreaded area. Aspey gave Nancollis no chance with the re- sulting kick. From the centre kick the play was very fast and exciting, the ball travelling from end to end. Brooks, racing away on the right, made a fine centre, and Leicester received the ball and beat Nancollis a second time. The visitors were not allowed to settle down to their usual style of play, and were mainly on the defence. From a brief raid on the right by Conway, Johnson cleared with a huge - kick. Evans obtained the ball and made a judicious pass to Aspey, who scored the third goal. The visitors now made an attempt on the home de- fence, but they could not break through, John- sen and Woodward being equal* to all emer- gencies. Evans, the home centre, made a fine' individual effort, and, after beating several opponents, he finished up with a low drive, which Nancollis had no chance to save. Half- time arrived with the home team leading by four goals to none. On resuming, the play was not of the same stapdaal as in the first half. The visitors ap- peared to be disheartened with the score piled up against them, and wild kicking and poor shooting when within range of goal were their weak points. Johnson, the left back of the home team, had the misfortune to 'displace his kneecap early in this half, .and had to retire Talbot played a splendid game for the visitors at centre-half. Leicester and Aspey added goals for the Refiners, and they ran' out winners by six goals to none. Weaver Refining Co.—Mills; D. Woodward and Johnson; H. Newton, Wilkinson and W. New- ton; Brooks, A. Johnson, Evans, Aspey and , Leicester.
Weston—Nancollis ; Barnes and Woods; Hope, Talbot and L. Aspey ; J. Smith, Leach, Hulse, Kirkham and Conway.
Daresbury v. Great Sankey.

Played at Moore, on the ground of the former club. The home team was only weakly repre- sented, five of the regular members failing to turn up, while the Sankey Club had a good side out. Davenport made his first appearance in goal, to the exclusion af Colquhoon, and Kelly was unable to play. The following were the players : Daresbury—Plumpton; De Prez and J. Hough, ton; Foster, Ball and Ryder; Fleet, A. Rough- ton, Adams, H. Foster and A. Ryder. ' Great Sankey—Davenport; Glover and Ste- , phens; Payne, Gardiner and Houghton; Dar- lington, H. Ditchfield, J. Ditchfield, Houghton and Poulter. The. homesters won the toss and J. Ditchfield set the ball rolling. The superiority of the visitors was soon in evidence, and from a grand centre by Houghton, Darlington scored the first goal after five minutes', play. From the eantre kick some fine combination by the visi- tors was seen, the home team being completely outplayed. Plumpton, in the home goal, did some splendid work. On one "occasion he made three or four successive saves in fine style. For a time infringement of the offside rule by the visitors caused the game to be a bit slack. J. Ditchfield, by an individual run, scored the seconT goal, and Poulter quickly added a third from short range. From a free-kick for a foul charge, Glover scored the finest goal of the 'match from 30 yards' range, the ball just enter- ing at the far corner of the. net under the bar, with the goalkeeper completely beaten all the way: Darlington, Poulter and. J. Ditchfield added other goals before half-time, when the score was seven goals to none, in favour of the visitors.

On resuming, the home team made several attempts to beat the visitcr§' defence, but Glover and Stephens were equal to the work which,came their way. Play for a time was a little quiet. Poulter, however, livened Up, beat the defence, and again baffled ,Plumpton. Shortly after De Prez had to concAle a corner, which was well placed by Houghton, and .Gar- diner headed a fine number nine goal. J. Ditch- field scored a tenth, and as Houghton was going through he was fouled in the penalty area, and he scored from the free-kick. Occasional breakaways by. the home forwards was cheered by their supporters. and the only time Davenport was called upon to handle the ball, he infringed one of the laws of the game by carrying the ball, but no score took place, and Poulter scored goal 140. 12 for the visitors. From now up to the finish play was very tame, the visitors being afraid of registering another goal, as they con- sidered it would be unlucky, and the game ended in their favour by twelve goals to none. Plimpton, De Prez and J. Houghton were the best players for the home team.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE
N CT ES.

The Daresbury Club opened their League fix- tures when they received a visit from the Great Sankey Club. The home club were unfortunate in not being able to turn out their best eleven, having to play four reserves. The visitors were nearly at full strength, Kelly being the only absentee. The result of the match went very much in favour of the visitors, who never allowed the home players much scope. Their longer experience of the game was of great advantage to them, and they piled up seven goals in the first half., and added five others in the Second portion, winning the match by twelve goals to nil. For the home club Plumpton kept a remarkable goal, despite the number of shots that went past him. For the visitors, the goals were scored by Poulter (4), J. Ditohfield (3), Darlington (2), Houghton, Gardiner and Glover (one each).

div.head: One-sided Game.
div.p: A One-sided Game.

At Acton Bridge, the Weaver Refining Com- pany and the Weston Clubs were engaged in League strife for the first time, and a one-sided game was witnessed. During the match it was unfortunate -that an accident should have hap- pened to Johnson, one of the home defenders. He had his kneecap displaced, and this will keep him out of the team for a few weeks. In the first portion the Weaver lads scored four goals,, and during the second half they scored two more and were winners by six goals to nil.

div.head: Adult School's Fine Win.
div.p: Adult School's Fine Win.

At Folly-lane the Adult School team were entertained by the reserves of Crosfield's Recs., and a--very good game ensued. Good play was shown by both teams. The honours in the first half went .to the home team, with one goal to nil in their favour. During the second portion the Adult School boys reversed matters and eventually won by three goals to one. The result was a very satisfactoi7 conclusion to the visitors, as in the two previous matches they had played drawn games, with the Weaver Refining Company, and the Great Sankey teams. Thus they have new managed to place a win to their credit.
The Soldiers Are Defeated.

The Orford Barracks team and Stockton Heath met on the Barracks Ground, and after the display of the " Heathens " the Previous week the Soldiers made a very good show against their opponents, doing the most pressing. during the first half, and were leading at half- time. During the second half the " Heathens " showed to better advantage and, were able to pull the game round in their favour, and won the match by five goals to two goals for the Soldiers.

Shuttleworth's Four Goals. Fairfield and St. Barnabas' were opposed to each other at Orford-road. The, visitors were superior to their opponents and were leading at half-time by three goals to none. The home players performed much better in the second half and goals Were scored- by Broadhurst and Hughes, while Shuttleworth scored four goals and Bevan two for the visitors, who won by six goals against two.

div.head: St. John's Still Unbeaten.
div.p: St. John's Still Unbeaten.

•.• • • • Bank Quay Recs. and Orford St. John's met at Lovely-lane, and a keen match was played. The Recs. made determined efforts to be the first team to lower the visitors' colours, but they failed in their attempt. The St. John's .played a sound game in defence, and they improved their position on the League chart by register- ing another win. Rankinson scored in the first half, and Tickle did the same in the second, and the St. John's won the match by two goals against none.

To-day's Match Items. To-day the Stockton Heath Club have to re- play the drawn cup-tie with the Lymm Ama- teurs, at Lymm. The Latchford Club will have Lostock Gralam as visitors to Thelwall-lane, in a Cheshire League fixture. As the visitors are a very strong team, great,interest is being taken in the match. Neither side have yet lost a match this season, and therefore a fine game should ,be witnessed. The visitors are always great favourites when visiting the town, as their reputation is well known. It only needs a• fine day and there will be a good crowd to witness the game. The following players will represent the home club: Robinson and J. C. Bardsley; Downs, Webb and Carter; Smith, Haspell, Lees. Fogg and , Taylor. Reserves, H. Stubbs and Siddall.
FIXTURES FOR TO-DAY. North Cheshire League. Latchford v. Lostock Gralam—J. Smallwood. Crosfield's Recs. v. Altrineham Lads—S. Breese
Warrington and District League. Weston v. Daresbury—R. Gough. Fairfield v. Emmanuel—J. Sherlock. Excelsior v. Orford St. John's—T. Pittam.
Cheshire Amateur Cup-tie Replay. Lymm Amateurs v. Stockton Heath—W Barnett.
• CHESHIRE AMATEUR SENIOR CUP.
Brooklands v. Latchford.

The match between the above clubs, in the first round of the Cheshire Amateur Senior Cup, took place on the 'Atkinson-road Ground, Sale. The home team was at full Strength. while the visitors were minus two of their selected players in Robinson and Haspell, their places being taken by Stubbs and Siddall, of the ,reserves. who played with credit to themselves 4 and the club. The following players faced each other, under the supervision of Referee B. Phillips;— Brookla.nds—Wignall; Smith and Pemberton; Levy, Makin and Ogden; Greenhalgh, Taylor, Edwards, Robinson and Parkinson. Latchford—Kite; J. C. Bardsley and H. Stubbs; Downs, Webb and Carter; Smith, Sid- dall, Lees, Fogg and Taylor. There was only a moderate attendance of spectators when Lees set the ball rolling. Straightaway the home half-backs put their forwards in possession, and during the first 15 minutes the visitors were hard pressed. Bardsley played a very effective game at back. Kite had no very difficult shots to contend with: The visitors' half-back line now began to be

div.head: Orford Barracks v. Stockton Heath.
div.p: Orford Barracks v. Stockton Heath.
A rearranged fixture was brought forward, and this was the first meeting of these two clubs. It toolc•place on the Soldiers' grouNd at Orford. The following players lined out under Referee Kite:
Orford Barracks--Moodie; Busby and Stevens;

Anslow, Staples and Pressland ; Campbell, Bir- kinhead, Forshaw, Trafford and Sansby. Stockton Heath—Simcock ; Gosling and Mor- timer; Gifford, Denny and Magill; Antrobus, Lockhart, Jones, Smith and Parr. The Heathens were successful in naming the coin, and Forshaw started for the home team. The opening exchanges were in favour of the Soldiers. Forshaw, leading an attack on the visitors' goal, only missed the mark by inches in the first few minutes. From the goal kick, a good combined run on behalf of the visitors by Jones, Smith and Parr, ended in the latter run- ning the ball over the goal line. For a few min- utes play was evenly contested, and the home forwards gradually worked the ball down the field, being ably led by Trafford, the latter neatly passing out to Forshaw, and he defeated the Heathens' goalkeeper with an easy shot. This reverse roused the visitors, and they made a determined attack on the home goal, through some good passing movements by. Antrobus and Lockhart. The latter sent in a difficult. shot, which Moodie saved very cleverly. A corner fell to the visitors, which was finely placed„and ended in a melee in front of goal. The ball came out to Gosling, and he returned a low ground shot, thus equalising. Both teams now played very hard to obtain the lead, Campbell, Birkinhead and Forshaw ,making a bold effort to break through,' but were driven back by Denny and Gosling in turn. A fine effort on the home right was nipped in the bud by Magill, and a foul against Trafford gave relief to the visitors' defence for a short period, as the Sol- diers were just now showing the better form. A. swinging pass by Campbell was taken up by Sansby, who passed on to Trafford, when well placed, and he beat Simcock. The home team thus took the lead, and half-time arrived: Bar- racks, two Foals ;_ Heathens, one goal. .

On resuniing the visitors made a great im- ,provement on their display of the. first portion of the game. They set up an irresistible attack on the home goal. T. Smith hit the cross-bar with a rattling shot, took a first time kick at the rebound. and placed his side on level terms. Jones spoiled a good opening by getting into an off-side position. The home team, led by For- shaw, made an attempt to break through, but Denny and Gosling soon placed them on the de- fensive. The next move was by the visitors, and Jones placed the Heathens, in front with a well-judged shot. From now the home team played a beaten game, and the Heathens made a continuous abtack on their goal. The score was further augmented by Smith and Lockhart, and the visitors ran out easy winners by five goals to two goals.

div.head: Crosfield's v. Adult School.
div.p: Crosfield's v. Adult School.

This match took place at Folly-lane. The home team won the toss. Dykes kicked off, and tracks were at once made for the home citadel, but met with a stout defence, which eventually led to a corner to the School lads. This was well cleared by Chesters, and' Munn carried the play into the visitors' half. After some even exchanges in midfield, the home team scored the first goal.by Munn, after 20 minutes' play. From the centre kick the visitors played a hard game, but failed to get on equal terms. At half-time Crosfield's were leading by one goal to none. The School lads, at the restart, made a strong attack on the home goal, and Jones was very busy dealing with all kinds of shots. Hunter was now playing a fine game for the visitors, sending in some good shots. Webb put through for the School and equalised the score. Play now ruled hard and fast on both sides, each striving hard for the lead. Banner was suc- cessful in placing his side in front with a good shot. Shortly after Webb put the result beyond doubt by scoring a third goal. At the final whistle the Adult School were declared winners by three goals to Crosfield's one. The home. team were best served by Jones, Chesters, Scott and Munn, and for the Adult School, Welsby, Garnett, Hunter, Lee, Banner and Webb were most prominent.

div.head: Bank Quay Recs. v. Orford St. John's.
div.p: Bank Quay Recs. v. Orford St. John's.

Played, at Lovely-lane ground, and a keen struggle was witnessed by a fair crowd of spec- tators. The John's captain was successful in , tbe -choice of goals. The Recs. kicked off, and at once made an attack, and, but for a timely clearance by W. Smith, the John's citadel would have fallen. End-to-end play followed, the de- fence on both sides prevailing, and neither goal:- keeper Were called upon. Welsby on one occa- sion sent in a rasping shot, which grazed the 'visitors' cross-bar. A few inches lower, and it would have been a certain score. As the game proceeded it became of a bustling nature, the referee having to administer several cautions. Half-time arrived without any legitimate score having been made. On resuming the game was fast and exciting, both sets of players going into it ding-dong. The Recs.' defenders conceded a corner, which was very well placed by J. Smith, and Hankin- son drew, first blood for the visitors. From the centre kick the Recs. carried the play into the visitors' quarters, but failed to beat the :visit- ors' defence. Millward and W. Smith kicked aid tackled in fine style. The ,outside right of the Recs. now played a fine game, and 'raced away down the wing, and centring from near the corner flag, the ball hit the far upright and travelled back across the goalmoutly into play again. Then Millward cleared the danger with a good lune up the field. The John's now had a turn at the opposite end, and the home defence held out for a while, until Tickle, in a favour- able position, scored a second goal for the visit- ors. A few minutes before time play became rough, and the referee had to give several free kicks and speak to the players on both sides. Time was called with Orford St. John's winners by two goals to hone.' A. Booth, A. WelSby and the outside right were the most prominent for the Recs., and W. Smith, T. tickle, and Han- kinson played a good game for Orford St. John's.
FRIENDLY FIXTURES.
Padgate United v. Higher Walton.

Padgate United were at home to Higher Wal- ton, and succeeded in recording •their first vic- tory. They made the game secure in the first half by scoring three goals, and thus led at half- time by 3-0. The visitors held their own in the second half, each team scoring twice. The game ended in favour of Padgate by 5-2.

Although beaten, Higher Waltob played well *and kept the ball on the move, but were well held by the Padgate defence. Padgate gave a trial to two new players in R. Norke (goal) and J. Holcroft (left back), who both gave satisfac- tion. The goals for Padgate were scored by T. Williams (2), John Houghton (2), and S. Hard- man.

The whole team played well and have been selected en bloc for this afternoon's game at Padgate, when a stiff proposition is encountered in the visit of the Warrington Adult School, who are doing so well in the local League.
Orford Athletic v. Fairfield United.
The Fairfield -United Club, having no League fixture to fulfil, splayed a friendly match with the 011ord Athletic Club at Orford ground. The teams were as follow :

Orford Athletic—Holden; Slater and Trantor; Rigby, Devine and Oxley; Wilkinson, Newton, Woodhouse, Platt and Wills. Fairfield United--G leave ; Rowlands and Woodhouse; Banner, Hamblett and Dooley; Simcoek-, Collins, Challinor, Appleton and Sim. kin. . . Referee, S. C. Essenhigh.

The home captain won the toss and \decided to play with the sun at their backs. Challinor set the ball rolling. The visitors were the first to become- aggressive. The home backs relieved and an attempt was made to lower the visitors' goal, when Hamblett cleared the danger with a. long shot, which Holden saved. Simcock re- ceived the ball on the right, and passed inside to Collins, who quickly snapped up the chance offered and scored for the Fairfield lads. A few even exchanges now took place, and both sets of forwards spoilt chances by getting into off- side positions. Platt received from Oxley and put the home team on equal terms. Half-time was called with the score one goal each. After the restart, it was soon evident th.t keen rivalry existed between both sets of players, and play was very fast. The Fairfield boys missed chances of adding to their score by selfish play, which kept their right wing prac- tically idle. Owing to their eagerness the players were continually in an off-side position, and good play Was thrown away. A corner to the visitors was nicely placed by Simcock, and several players missed an easy chance of'adding to the score. The remainder of the game was evenly distributed, and the match ended in a draw of one goal each. The goalkeepers on both sides did very well, as also did Woodhouse, Collins, Banner and Dooley for the Fairfield team. Slater, Trantor, Rigby and Oxley were the pick of the home team.

Grappenhall St. Wilfred's v. Widnes S. Marie's. Grappenhall St. Wilfred's entertained Wid- nes St. Marie's on Saturday, and were defeated by two goals to nil, after a strenuous and fast game. Widnes pressed, only to be repulsed by Evans and Massey. Richards got going for the .home team, the ball just going outside the post. Prior to the interval, however, Widnes showed improved form, and after a neat forward move- ment scored with a fine dropping shot. Imme- diately afterwards Widnes were awarded a penalty, but Shakeshaft saved in grand style, the interval arriving with the visitors leading by one goal to nil.

In the second half Grappenhall improved, and frequently raided the Widnes end, but could not equalise. In the closing stages Win- nes attacked, and again scored. The Grappen- hall forwards made strenuous efforts to reduce the lead, but the Widnes defence held out.

ST. HELENS AND DISTRICT THURSDAY LEAGUE. St. Helens Co-op. v. Warrington Co-op. Played at St. Helens on Thursday. The home team won the toss and played down the slope. Before the game had been in progress ten minutes- St. Helens took the lead. This reverse put new life into the visitors, and after some. clever work Thornton equalised With a beauti- ful shot. Even play was the order for sometime, and then Savage put on goal number two for the Warrington "Co-opers," after some capital work. St. Helens equalised, and the first halg ended: St. Helens,, two goals; Warrington two. In the second half some good combination was seen, and at times play became very excit- ing. Both defences, however, .held out until about ten minutes from time, when Rutter scored for Warrington, who eventually ran out winner S by three goals to two. Latchford 8.8. v. Grappenhall S.S.

Grappenhall won their maic)-1 with Latchford, at Latchford. C. Clayton was the first to score, but Walton soon equalised. Half-time arrived with the score 3-1 in favour of Latchford. Resuming, the home team pressed. for some time and, Wilkinson scored. FOden soon after- wards got possession and scored the second goal for Grappenholl. The visitors were by far hay- - ing the best of the game, and Sh4eshaft scored . three goals in a very short time, and in the last few minutes Barton- scored Grappenhall's sixth goal. Result: Grappcnhall, six; Latch- -- ford, four.

div.head: Fairfield v. St. Barnabas'.
div.p: Fairfield v. St. Barnabas'.

This match was played at Orford-road. The visitors won the toss and Hughes set the ball rolling. Play was at *nice carried into the home territory, when Shuttleworth caused a sensa- tional opening by scoring in the first minute. From the kick the home players did not seem able to Make much headway against the visit- ors' half-backs, and were driven back on ,their own goal. Shuttleworth worked himself a good position and scored a second goal. The visit- ors continued to hold the upper hand, and did not allow the home players much latitude. Near the interval Bevan registered a third point. At half-time the visitors were leading by three goals to none.

‘ln the second portion t e Fairfield lads had More of the game and sox good efforts were made by their players and met with success. Broadhurst and Hughes scored goals, and Shut- tleworth and Bevan added further goals for the visitors. The game ended: St. Barnabas', six goals; Fairfield, two goals.

div.head: TEAMS FOR TO-DAY.
div.p: TEAMS FOR TO-DAY.

Grappenhall St. Wilfred's play WidneF Juniors at Widnes, and will be represented by: R. Shakeshaft; W. Masse Y and J. Peters; A. E. Evans, T. Woodward and F. Booth; J. Thomvs, F. Woodcock, J. Richards, H. Parr and W. Cameron. Reserves: F. Parr, T. Fairhurst and R. B. Howells.

Padgate 'United meet Warrington Adult School at Padgate. The Padgate team will be: R. Norke ; J. Warburton and J. Holcroft; R. Hankinson, W. Wadsworth (capt.), and T. Wil-. hams; tames Houghton, A. Derbyshire, John Houghton, J. Rigby and S. Hardman. Adult School team: Welsby ; Garnett and Spencer; J. Leigh, W. Hunter and Clarke; Rhodes, Dyke-s, Gregson, Webb .and Banner. Reserves: Rowe and Jackson.

SHOTS AT THE GOAL. Lees scored four goals again last•week. Smith, the Latchford right winger, can make grand centres. Smith's goal was a.beauty, wasn't it? Lees has scored ten goals in three matches for Latchford.
Bardsley played a great game in his first match. Poulter scored four times against Daresbury. J. Ditchfield also got two good goals.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 11, 1913.
E.I.JC/OLIS
St. James', Latchford.

A prettily decorated church and large con- gregations were features at the harvest festiN at at St. James', Latchford, on Sunday. The choir sang splendidly Barnby's anthem, "Ye shall go out with joy," the solo .being taken by Master John Grant. Mr. E. Davies played the accompaniments. The preachers were, the Rev. J. H. Garnett, St. Peter's, Warrington, in the morning,. and the Rev. P. A. Screeton, St. Paul's, Seacombe, and formerly vicar of the church, in the evening.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Guild.
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Guild.

The above society opened the winter session on Monday evening, when the Rev.. W. Reid gave a lecture on "St. Aldan, Apostle to North- umbria." In a clear and interesting manner the lecturer sketched out the early efforts made to Christianise England by the various Roman and Celtic monks. Special attention was drawn to the work of St. Aidan, the Celtic monk, who made his way from lona to Lindis- farne (Holy Island), and, working from thence, (lid so much to establish Christianity through- out Northumbria. The lives and conditions of the people, their manners, and customs were all touched upon and emphasised, also the great missionary work undertaken and accomplished by St. ,Aidan. Mr. Lewsey presided over a good gathering.

div.head: Cairo Street Chapel.
div.p: Cairo Street Chapel.

The safe in-gathering of the harvest was joy- fully and thankfully celebrated at the Ca!ro- street Chapel on Sunday. The Rev. Dr. Me' tor preached, and his sermon in the evening vas a most striking one. An account of it will found under another heading in this column. There were crowded congregations, and the scheme of decoration was modest, though ex- tremely pretty. The talented choir dispensed special music and with splendid taste and expression they rendered, in the morning, the anthem "0 lovely " peace" (Handel), and in the evening Look on the fields" (Charles Macpherson). Mr. James Muir proved a most capable accompanist and his work at the organ materially assisted the choir. The offertories went to the organ reno- vation fund.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Festival.
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Festival.

-- Large congregations attended St. John's Pres- byterian Church on Sunday in connection with the harvest festival. The edifice was daintily decorated by the ladies of the congregation. The choir most ably rendered special music, including the anthem "Praise His Holy Name" (Simper). A quartet, "Blessed is that happy land" (Nichol), was rendered by the Misses Dewar and Snailham, and Messrs. Aitken and Gillespie. Mr. Aitken gave the solo, "The Lord is my Shepherd," and Mr. Gillespie ren- dered "Radiant morn." Mr. A. G. Lewsey ' made an admirable conductor and organist. The Rev. W. Reid preached in the evening from the parable of the tares. The object of that parable, he said, was a warning against expectation of finding an altogether unmixed in the world, or in the Church. good society Revivals, and even martyrdoms, did not escape the feature of failure, and man's remedy was always a drastic one, he being ever ready -to root out heretics. Christ's policy of com- mand to His servants was to allow the mixed crop to grow until the harvest. Upon closer scrutiny this was seen 'to be imperative, because of the close resemblance between wheat and tare.

It was unfortunate the word "tare" had been introduced, as the "retch" was dissimilar to wheat and not unwholesome, whereas the "darnel," whilst to some extent poisonous, closely resembled the good grain at one point of its life's history. The preacher showed how, while so diverse in nature, the roots of both were closely intertwined, and how impossible it was to uproot or even disturb the one apart from the other. Christ had reserved to Himself the office and functions of judge, and to judge each other was outside the province and com- petence of man. The bar of God's justice lay across the life of each individual.

div.head: "Michaelmas Religion."
div.p: "Michaelmas Religion."

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell, writing of Michael- mas and harvest festivals in his magazine for the Burtonwood parish, says "Of late years Michaelmas has developed a religion all its own—the religion of the material. "The beautiful festival of St. Michael and All Angels has been displaced by the vulgar show of St. Georgius, the husbandman. The end of September is given up to coarsely and over-decorated churches and the demoralising religious dissipation of 'harvest festivalling.' ‘,.Let us go and see the decorations at St. Sepulchre's and hear Mr. Chadband preach.' Such is the speech of those who systematically ignore public worship and their, duty towards God's Church throughout the year, but who be- come suddenly- enthused about Michaelmas and full of religious unction, of a kind, when the churches reek of the smell of apples, and the atmosphere is foetid with the heavy odour of giant vegetables. The churches are full, of course; the plates (or bags) are full too—of copper—` Alexander,. the coppersmith, did me much evil. This Michaelmas religion is both dangerous and insufferable. Surely the Church should know better than to cater for it, and its vulgarisms, mainly with a view to swollen offer- ' tories, which deservedly fall so far short? The argument that it is well to get people to invade the churches under any conditions, if not pre- text, is altogether at fault.. "There is a religion which does no good, a churchgoing which does harm—a statement pre- eminently true of harvest •festival Church hunt- ing. Truth to tell, we think the popularity of the harvest .service is on the wane. With the departure, the earlier the better, of Michaelmas religion, as it now it:3, St. Michael and All Angels will have the opportunity of once more entering into their own.

div.head: "Present Day Ellorality."
div.p: "Present Day Ellorality."

Lecturing at Cairo-street Chapel on Sunday evening on "Present-day Morality," Dr. Mellor asked what did that consist of and upon what did it depend? It depended on custom and con- vention, On public opinion and on the standards accepted, without question, from the social class to which we belonged. Very seldom did our so-called moral life rise above these levels, and that remained true even when, we had made allowance in full for all the sincere efforts after genuine -personal goodness, which, in face 'of tremendous difficulties, were undoubtedly made in the world. Thousiands of people in society to-day could not afford to be good, even as good as they would like, to be. To live out the beSt• morality that, was in them would not pay; it would be to court poverty, and to-day poverty was the Unforgiveable sin. How could a. man be unreservedly generous, sympathetic and kindly :when he had the in- terests of business to consider first of all, and when the more he had achieved of material goods the more was his mind haunted by the fear of ending his days in the workhouse? There was not much chance for genuine moral- ity until we had a society in which any man who so wished could choose poverty as his ideal. If a man to-day desired to emulate St. Francis of Assisi lie would indubitably be sent to gaol for being "without visible, means of subsist- ence," and if a man tried to live his life in strict accordance with the precepts of the Christian gospel he would probably be com- mitted to an asylum. In our municipal and civic life this same eon- ventional morality led us every day not only to do actually things that were bad—for ex- ample, men seeking the confidence of their fellows, made promises which they knew they could not fulfil—but also blind us perpetually to the true proportion of needs and events, so that it was actually possible for men to talk of borrowing money to build a new Town Hall, whilst all the time the town they lived in was in dire need of new and decent sanitary arrange- ments. Men could talk of beautifying the place by a new building, whilst it was actually on record that the death-rate amongst infants was higher than it ought to be because the sanitary arrangements were so bad, and there, was no money to construct a new sewer. Thai

div.head: Brick Street Mission.
div.p: Brick Street Mission.

The above mission held their annual harvest festival on Sunday, Mr. W. Mort, of Lymm, being the preacher, morning and evening, and at both services Mr. Mort was greatly appreci- ated. In the afternoon the school was thrown open for the scholars, and a very pleasing address was given b'Y Councillor James Shaw (superintendent). Mr. George Gough gave a bass solo in fine style, and his effort was much appreciated, as also was Miss J. Riley's solo, "A little talk with Jesus." In the evening the misgion was well filled. The Mission choir ren- dered two special anthems in excellent style. On the following Monday evening a fruit banquet and Concert was held, when the follow- ing took part in the evening's programme: Misses. E. Lightfoot, E. Shaw, Messrs. W. Bar- ton, jun., S. Gallop, H. Santley. and J. H. Bibby. Mr. W. Wright, sen., presided, and addressed the gathering.

div.head: Golborne Street B3ptist Church
div.p: Golborne Street B3ptist Church

Harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sunday at the Golborne-street Baptist Church. The edifice had been beautifully ,decorated by the ladies, under the superintendence of Mrs. H. Buckby. The gifts of fruit and flowers were in excess of last year, and the abundance, in addition to the charming setting, lent a pictur- esque appearance to the church. The preacher for the day was the Pastor, tie Rev. H. Ogden. In the morning Mr. Ogden took his subject from Genesis i. 12, "And the earth brought forth grass and herb yielding seed after his kind." The preacher declared that men considered every factor in the harvest but God. On Mon- day, if the theme was allowed to rest on the lord's Day, Lancashire would discuss cotton. Every factor counted in cotton except God. The church in the evening was full, when Mr. Ogden again preached. On Monday night a suc- cessful sale of fruit and vegetables took place. The flowers and some fruit were sent to the , Infirmary, the Workhouse and the Fever Hos- pital.

div.head: Harvest Festival at Parish Church.
div.p: Harvest Festival at Parish Church.

The harvest thanksgiving services at the Parish Church, Warrington, were concluded on Sunday, when a marked feature was the excel- lent attendances at each of the services. Holy Communion was celebrated, and at the morn- ing service the Vicar of Banks, Southport, the Rev. Herman F. S. Collier, preached. The Rector, during the afternoon, addressee the scholars from Church-street and Fairfield Sunday Schools at a special service for the young, and at the evening service the Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson, Principal of the Training College, interested the congregation with a forceful discourse based upon the text: " Man shall not live by bread alone." Temptation, he said, was the lot of most people. If you will only do this, you will he better. It is not quite straight, honest, or honourable, but it will give you so much more than you have got at the present moment. Temptation came, with all its terrible force, and we have two things set against each other— bread and the Word of God. We must always remember that, when faced with a similar temptation in His humanity, Christ conquered. While we offered thanksgiving for temponil blessings, we should not forget that these do hot represent the whole of life. Man needs something for the higher part of his nature, 8 well as for the lower, food for the soul as well as for the body. This festival should inspire us with the thought that there is a greater pur- pose than merely working for the things of this world. The choir rendered some very fine and appro- priate music, their work being one of • the features of the festival. "I am the bread of life," to Eyre's setting in "E" flat, was most tastefully rendered at the morning service. Spohr's masterpiece, "Great and, wonderful are all Thy works," was the feature of the evening, and it was sung with the proper taste and expression. Mr. F. M. Darby accomplished excellent work on the organ. The church had been eaortif ally decorated with Nature's embellishments by members nf the congregation. It was announced that .t5O was required for the Assistant Clergy Fund, on behalf of which was the collection, and this Was raised by the aid of generous donations. The collections on Thursday totalled £5 6s. 81. and on Sunday £24 7s.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
Warrington Workingmen's Association. N.A. CENTRE. A POOR WEEK-END.

Last week-end was spoiled by the weather. Sunday morning, when the downpour was heaviest, kept members from venturing out. However, itwas *hat was wanted, fgr the fish in the canals were entirely out of condition, and even if .it is late in the season for the fish-to come on, ,it is far better for anglers to take a few that are right than to take quantities that are not 4t. Strange to say, the roach and perch in the Still water at Long Barn are in better condition than any we have handled' lately. Why not members who reside this way give this water a trial, instead. of going 'farther afield? We know fair roach, perch and chub ar6 to be taken here with very little trouble. A couple of members tried that water last week and their baits were maggots that had been left over from the Previous week and a piece of bread, and they returned with a dozen fair roach and perch, ,which had given fair sport, because as we mention, they were in first-rate condition.

div.head: CHESTER.
div.p: CHESTER.

Both the canal and river were off here; sport was at its worst. Several members who. fished the Dee returned ,without a scale. There is no doubt the rain will do some good. We know of one member at least who has visited the Dee on ten different occasions and has not yet placed anything on the set board. One or two mem- bers who have tried the canal report that sport is 'very flat, as a gudgeon, one dace and two roach for two days' fishing are not worth the journey. We have better results nearer home.

div.head: GOWY.
div.p: THE GOWY.

Members who journey to the Gowy had a poor week-end; the best we have heard of were three roach, 140 z., 11oz. 6dr. and 10oz. 7dr., respectively. Here again the fresh should do anglers a good turn, and if we have no more rain until week-end members should catch the stream " fining " down, and results should im- prove, as tradition says October is about the best maggot month in the year for this stream.

div.head: NORTON.
div.p: NORTON.

Although fish have not been taken in quan- tities here, we are glad to report they are im- proving in .weight. Mr. J. Green has now weighed one in that places him first on the list, Mr. T. Dixon coming second. Mr, H. Moore had .a fair catch last week-end; taking about a dozen nice sizeable fish, while Mr. J. Myers was responsible for an eel 10oz. 7dr. Of course, this does not come on the board, as Mr. C. Morton has already one in of llb. 7oz. Several members have had nice fish during the week, but not in any quantity, and nothing to upset those already weighed in.

div.head: GAS METER RENTS.
div.p: GAS METER RENTS.
Council Approve of Schome to
Abolish these Rates.
MORE GAS FOR SLOT USERS.

Gas profits, as allocated to the relief of the rates, were again discussed at Warrington Town Council on Tuesday. The discussion arose on the recommendation of the Gas Com- mittee, "that an additional 5 feet of gas per penny be allowed to consumers in the borough supplied by means of prepayment meters; that all meter rents be abolished as and from the 31st day of October next."

Councillor GOUGH intimated that he was now willing to withdraw the motion about the matter standing in his name, as the committee had realised the gross' injustice that had been done to slot meter users. .

Alderman JOHN EVAN $: I do not think there has been injustice. Councillor GOUGH: Your resolution to give five feet more proves it. (Hear, hear.) Alderman JOHN EVANS : The committee pro- posed a I,eduction in the price of gas that was rejected by the Council, and the committee now bring forward this proposition. You are re- minded that we are abolishing meter rents. Councillor DICKENSON : What will be the posi- tion of ratepayers who own their own meters. Alderman TINNION : The meters will,be bought from _them at a fair allowance.

div.head: COULD REDUCE THE PRICE.
div.p: COULD REDUCE THE PRICE.

Councillor OSBORNE was pleased the Gas Com- mittee had adopted the suggestion to abolish the meter rents.. He was still of the opinion that the Gas Committee could well afford to reduce the price of gas, and he could not see why they should not follow out the strong wish expressed at the last Council meeting. When the 'resolution was referred back, it was understood the committee would reconsider the matter, and he was led to believe a reduction would be made in the price of gas. Independ- ent of abolishing the meter rents, the public had not got a penny concession. , Alderman TINNION : Of course they have. Councillor OSBORNE : Considering the amount of profit made, I had hoped a reductiqn would have been -made in the price, and seeing • that we are likely to make a considerable profit in the future, something shOuld be done. (Hear, hear.) •

div.head: REDUCED BY £5,000.
div.p: REDUCED BY £5,000.

Councillor ROBERTS said the proposed conces- sions would reduce the profits of the Gas Com- mittee by £5,000, or equal to a sd. rate. If the Council at the same time insisted on reducing the price, the Council must take the responsi- bility. If they had a reduction they would con- sequently have an increase in the rates in similar proportion.

I contend, he added, that the ratepayer, apart from the gas consumer, is entitled to considera- tion in regard to the distribution of the gas Profits. His credit is at stake, and it would be him who would be called upon to contribute if there was a deficiency. Councillor OSBORNE : Does it actually cost £5,000?

Councillor ROBERTS I may be a little out. Councillor OSBORNE : I think you are a con- siderable amount out. Councillor ROBERTS added that it would cost several thousands, and he thought they were entitled to ask for another yeat to see how the concessions worked.

div.head: ENORMOUS PROFITS.
div.p: ENORMOUS PROFITS.

Councillor PEMBERTON said it was a matter how far' they could charge the gas consumer to provide enormous profits to relieve the rates. These did not let them see the true state of the rates. He understood the rates actually came to 10s. 6d. in the but because they got the profits from the trading under- takings, the rates were only Bs. The MAYOR thought they should be very cautious in what they were doing. Councillor HAWTHORN said people who did not use ,gas got benefit from the profits that Went to relieve the rates. They were making big pro- fits and paying income tax 'upon it, whereas that could be. avoided by reducing the- profits and giving more concessions to the gas con- sumers.

div.head: RENTS GOING UP.
div.p: RENTS GOING UP.

Councillor LINDLEY said by reducing the price of-gas they would give the best possible, handle to the property owners to put up the rents. Was it wise to charge the working man Id. per week less for gas, and allow the property owners to put up rents 3d. per week?. Alderman TINNION said the committee wanted to put all consumers on an equitable basis. The cost of removing the meter rents would be £1,258, and to reduce the gas Id. would cost £1,296, so thdre was little difference between the two schemes. They also proposed to give a sum equal to £2,263 to the slot meter users. Thus the total amount the committee were to give was £3,589. They thought that a 'suffi- ciently large sum, considering the unsatisfac.: tory position of the residual and fuel marEefs. The resolution was adopted.
